The thoracic cage is rigid with well-developed accessory muscles
The ribs are more horizontal and breathing depends mainly on the diaphragm
The tongue and occiput are relatively larger
originalOptions: The airway is narrowest at the subglottic/cricoid area
The cervical spine is relatively straight
The thoracic cage is rigid with well-developed accessory muscles
The ribs are more horizontal and breathing depends mainly on the diaphragm
The tongue and occiput are relatively larger
questions.correctAnswer: C) The thoracic cage is rigid with well-developed accessory muscles
questions.correctAnswerText: The thoracic cage is rigid with well-developed accessory muscles
questions.explanation: The paediatric chest wall is compliant, with horizontal ribs and poorly developed accessory muscles, so children rely on the diaphragm. This is why retractions appear early in respiratory distress.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a standard intraosseous (IO) access site?
questions.explanation: Standard IO sites are the proximal tibia (most common first choice), distal tibia, proximal humerus, and the distal femur (paediatric only). The femoral neck is not an IO insertion site.

questions.text: You are alone with a patient in suspected cardiac or respiratory arrest. After checking for danger and before sending for help, what is the next step?
questions.explanation: After scene safety, responsiveness is assessed. The rescuer then shouts for help or activates the emergency response and checks breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds.

questions.text: All of the following are true regarding confirmation of endotracheal tube (ETT) position EXCEPT:
options: Visualizing the tube passing through the oesophagus
Direct visualization of the tube passing through the vocal cords
originalOptions: Visualizing the tube passing through the oesophagus
Direct visualization of the tube passing through the vocal cords
questions.correctAnswer: B) Visualizing the tube passing through the oesophagus
questions.correctAnswerText: Visualizing the tube passing through the oesophagus
questions.explanation: A tube passing into the oesophagus is a misplacement, not a confirmation. Correct placement is confirmed by passage through the vocal cords and, most reliably, by continuous waveform capnography together with clinical checks.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to intraosseous line insertion?
options: Previous IO attempt in the same bone
Infection (osteomyelitis or cellulitis) over the insertion site
originalOptions: Previous IO attempt in the same bone
Infection (osteomyelitis or cellulitis) over the insertion site
questions.correctAnswer: E) Fluid leakage from the line
questions.explanation: Leakage is a post-insertion complication (extravasation or malposition), not a pre-insertion contraindication, and the line should be stopped and another site chosen. The other options are contraindications to placement.

questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to IV thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke?
options: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
Seizure at onset with residual post-ictal deficits
originalOptions: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
Seizure at onset with residual post-ictal deficits
questions.correctAnswer: C) Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
questions.correctAnswerText: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
questions.explanation: Ischaemic stroke or serious head trauma within the previous 3 months is an absolute exclusion. Recent major surgery, pregnancy, minor or rapidly improving symptoms, and seizure at onset with residual deficits are relative cautions.

questions.text: A crushed trauma patient is hypotensive and tachycardic with no external bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: Rapid infusion of 2 L warmed crystalloid followed by CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Complete history and secondary survey before any intervention
xABCDE with cervical-spine protection, presumed hemorrhagic shock, large-bore IV/IO access, activation of a massive transfusion protocol, eFAST, and portable chest and pelvic radiographs
Immediate transfer to radiology for contrast CT before resuscitation
Vasopressor infusion to restore blood pressure
originalOptions: Rapid infusion of 2 L warmed crystalloid followed by CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Complete history and secondary survey before any intervention
xABCDE with cervical-spine protection, presumed hemorrhagic shock, large-bore IV/IO access, activation of a massive transfusion protocol, eFAST, and portable chest and pelvic radiographs
Immediate transfer to radiology for contrast CT before resuscitation
Vasopressor infusion to restore blood pressure
questions.correctAnswer: C) xABCDE with cervical-spine protection, presumed hemorrhagic shock, large-bore IV/IO access, activation of a massive transfusion protocol, eFAST, and portable chest and pelvic radiographs
questions.correctAnswerText: xABCDE with cervical-spine protection, presumed hemorrhagic shock, large-bore IV/IO access, activation of a massive transfusion protocol, eFAST, and portable chest and pelvic radiographs
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic hypotension is hemorrhagic until proven otherwise, and the occult sources are the chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, and long bones. Treatment is blood products and bleeding control, not repeated crystalloid loading or CT.

questions.text: A 17-year-old is found unconscious in a swimming pool. He is unresponsive with abdominal breathing at 16/min, BP 80/50 mmHg, and HR 49/min. In addition to hypoxemia, which condition must be considered earliest?
questions.explanation: Cervical spine injury must be assumed in any unconscious patient after a diving or fall mechanism until it is excluded. Hypotension with bradycardia and diaphragmatic breathing suggests a cervical cord lesion with neurogenic shock.

questions.text: A 26-year-old seat-belted driver has mild abdominal tenderness, hypoactive bowel sounds, and questionable liver dullness. The abdominal X-ray shows free air. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Careful observation for further evidence of intra-abdominal injury
Suspected ruptured diaphragm with pneumothorax; chest tube insertion
Contrast study of the gastrointestinal tract
originalOptions: Careful observation for further evidence of intra-abdominal injury
Suspected ruptured diaphragm with pneumothorax; chest tube insertion
Contrast study of the gastrointestinal tract
questions.explanation: Free intraperitoneal air indicates hollow-viscus perforation, which is a surgical emergency regardless of how stable the patient appears. Observation or further diagnostic studies only delay definitive treatment.

questions.text: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks of gestation is involved in a car accident. BP is 120/70 mmHg, HR is 107/min, and the FAST examination is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate cesarean section in the operating room
Monitor the mother and fetus for a minimum of 4 hours
Immediate cesarean section in the emergency department
Discharge if laboratory tests are normal
CT of the abdomen and pelvis
originalOptions: Immediate cesarean section in the operating room
Monitor the mother and fetus for a minimum of 4 hours
Immediate cesarean section in the emergency department
Discharge if laboratory tests are normal
CT of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.correctAnswer: B) Monitor the mother and fetus for a minimum of 4 hours
questions.correctAnswerText: Monitor the mother and fetus for a minimum of 4 hours
questions.explanation: A stable pregnant trauma patient with a negative FAST requires at least 4 hours of maternal and fetal monitoring because placental abruption may present late. Kleihauer-Betke testing is added if the mother is Rh-negative.

questions.text: After high-speed blunt trauma, a patient remains hypotensive and tachycardic despite initial crystalloid. FAST shows free fluid in Morison's pouch. What is the most appropriate management?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
Activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to emergency laparotomy
originalOptions: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
Activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to emergency laparotomy
questions.correctAnswer: E) Activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to emergency laparotomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to emergency laparotomy
questions.explanation: Persistent hypotension with a positive FAST indicates intraperitoneal hemorrhage, which requires urgent operative control. CT is reserved for hemodynamically stable patients, and DPL is rarely needed when FAST is available.

questions.text: A patient has a gunshot wound to the center of the abdomen. Which organ is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The small bowel occupies the largest volume of the central abdomen and is the organ most commonly injured in penetrating gunshot wounds. The actual injury still depends on the entry site and trajectory.

questions.text: A patient with a stab wound to the lower chest is hypotensive with muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and jugular venous distension constitute Beck's triad of tamponade. In tension pneumothorax, breath sounds are unilaterally absent, while in massive hemothorax the neck veins are flat.

questions.text: In a patient with suspected traumatic cardiac tamponade, which bedside investigation is the best rapid diagnostic adjunct?
options: CT of the chest with contrast
eFAST with a focused pericardial view
originalOptions: CT of the chest with contrast
eFAST with a focused pericardial view
questions.correctAnswer: D) eFAST with a focused pericardial view
questions.correctAnswerText: eFAST with a focused pericardial view
questions.explanation: eFAST rapidly detects pericardial fluid at the bedside. In an unstable penetrating-trauma patient it must not delay surgical decompression.

questions.text: A patient with a penetrating chest wound and confirmed cardiac tamponade is hemodynamically unstable. What is the definitive management?
options: Emergency thoracotomy or operative pericardial decompression
originalOptions: Emergency thoracotomy or operative pericardial decompression
questions.correctAnswer: B) Emergency thoracotomy or operative pericardial decompression
questions.correctAnswerText: Emergency thoracotomy or operative pericardial decompression
questions.explanation: Traumatic tamponade requires surgical decompression and repair of the cardiac injury. Pericardiocentesis is only a temporizing bridge when surgical care is not immediately available.

questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to performing a CT scan in a trauma patient?
options: Positive FAST in a stable patient
Pelvic fracture in a stable patient
originalOptions: Positive FAST in a stable patient
Pelvic fracture in a stable patient
questions.explanation: CT requires transport and time, so it is reserved for hemodynamically stable patients. An unstable patient needs resuscitation and hemorrhage control, not "scan and plan".

questions.text: A chest radiograph of a trauma patient is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: ERATLSdiaphragmaticrupture.png ]
questions.explanation: A large gastric air-fluid level projects in the lower half of the left hemithorax, mildly displacing the heart to the right. There is also left lower zone atelectasis and a basal pleural effusion.

questions.text: All of the following belong to the secondary survey EXCEPT:
options: Selective CT imaging in a stable patient
originalOptions: Selective CT imaging in a stable patient
questions.explanation: FAST is an adjunct to the primary survey used to detect hemorrhage during resuscitation. History, complete examination, and selective CT belong to the secondary survey, which follows stabilization.

questions.text: An 8-year-old child has a penetrating knife wound to the abdomen and a positive FAST scan. What is the next step?
options: Transfer to the operating room immediately
originalOptions: Transfer to the operating room immediately
questions.correctAnswer: D) Transfer to the operating room immediately
questions.correctAnswerText: Transfer to the operating room immediately
questions.explanation: A penetrating abdominal wound with a positive FAST indicates hemoperitoneum and a significant intra-abdominal injury. Operative exploration is required rather than imaging or observation.

questions.text: What does the acronym FAST represent in trauma assessment?
options: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
originalOptions: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
questions.correctAnswer: B) Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
questions.correctAnswerText: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
questions.explanation: In trauma, FAST is a bedside ultrasound examination of the pericardial, hepatorenal, splenorenal, and pelvic views to detect free fluid. "Face, Arm, Speech, Time" is the stroke mnemonic.

questions.text: What does the acronym FAST represent in stroke assessment?
options: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services
originalOptions: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma
Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services
questions.correctAnswer: E) Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services
questions.correctAnswerText: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services
questions.explanation: FAST is a rapid recognition tool for stroke, and the "T" reminds the rescuer to call emergency services and note the last-known-well time. It is not a complete neurological examination.

questions.text: A hemodynamically stable patient has a penetrating wound just left of the sternum at the fifth intercostal space. Which rapid bedside study should be performed during the trauma assessment?
questions.correctAnswer: C) eFAST including a pericardial view
questions.explanation: A parasternal wound in the cardiac box requires exclusion of pericardial fluid, which eFAST provides rapidly while serial examination continues. Formal echocardiography or operative evaluation follows if suspicion persists.

questions.text: What is the initial imaging modality of choice in an unstable trauma patient with suspected hemoperitoneum?
options: CT of the abdomen with contrast
originalOptions: CT of the abdomen with contrast
questions.explanation: FAST is performed at the bedside without leaving the resuscitation area. Contrast CT is the definitive study for stable patients, and a negative FAST does not exclude intra-abdominal injury.

questions.text: A 22-year-old man with a gunshot wound to the left chest has BP 80/40 mmHg, which improves to 122/84 mmHg after 2 L of Ringer's lactate. HR is now 100/min and RR is 28/min. A closed tube thoracostomy drains a small amount of blood with no air leak. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: The patient responded to resuscitation and the tube drained little blood, so the next step is reassessment. Deterioration or ongoing bleeding would prompt urgent operative management.

questions.text: A mechanically ventilated trauma patient suddenly develops hypotension, high airway pressures, and absent breath sounds on one side, consistent with tension pneumothorax. What is the immediate management?
options: Chest radiograph followed by tube thoracostomy
Immediate needle or finger decompression followed by tube thoracostomy
originalOptions: Chest radiograph followed by tube thoracostomy
Immediate needle or finger decompression followed by tube thoracostomy
questions.correctAnswer: B) Immediate needle or finger decompression followed by tube thoracostomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate needle or finger decompression followed by tube thoracostomy
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and decompression must not wait for imaging. Positive-pressure ventilation accelerates the tension, so increasing PEEP would worsen it.

questions.text: According to current ATLS guidance, where should needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax be performed?
questions.correctAnswer: E) 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
questions.explanation: The 4th–5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line fails less often because the chest wall is thinner there. The 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line is the older, traditional site.

questions.text: Which of the following defines massive hemothorax?
options: More than 1000 mL of blood on initial drainage or more than 100 mL/hour
More than 1000 mL of blood on initial drainage or more than 200 mL/hour
More than 1500 mL of blood on initial drainage or ongoing loss of about 200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours
More than 500 mL of blood on initial drainage or more than 200 mL/hour
More than 2000 mL of blood on initial drainage only
originalOptions: More than 1000 mL of blood on initial drainage or more than 100 mL/hour
More than 1000 mL of blood on initial drainage or more than 200 mL/hour
More than 1500 mL of blood on initial drainage or ongoing loss of about 200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours
More than 500 mL of blood on initial drainage or more than 200 mL/hour
More than 2000 mL of blood on initial drainage only
questions.correctAnswer: C) More than 1500 mL of blood on initial drainage or ongoing loss of about 200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours
questions.correctAnswerText: More than 1500 mL of blood on initial drainage or ongoing loss of about 200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours
questions.explanation: These are the classic thresholds that prompt urgent operative consultation for thoracotomy. The decision also rests on physiology and transfusion requirements, not on volume alone.

questions.text: After a trauma, a chest tube immediately drains 1700 mL of blood. What definitive management should be considered?
options: Insertion of a second chest tube and observation
CT of the chest before any intervention
Observation with a repeat chest radiograph
originalOptions: Insertion of a second chest tube and observation
CT of the chest before any intervention
Observation with a repeat chest radiograph
questions.explanation: Immediate drainage above 1500 mL meets the classic threshold for operative control of ongoing intrathoracic hemorrhage. Resuscitation continues alongside surgical preparation.

questions.text: An elderly man has 4 stab wounds above the nipple line. He is intubated, a chest tube drains 700 mL of blood, and 2 L of normal saline is given. BP is now 60/0 mmHg and HR is 160/min. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Persistent shock despite a chest tube and fluid resuscitation indicates ongoing intrathoracic hemorrhage that needs operative control. Imaging or transfer would delay hemorrhage control in a patient who is peri-arrest.

questions.text: After chest trauma, subcutaneous emphysema extends to the neck and the patient does not improve after chest-tube insertion. Which injury should be suspected?
questions.explanation: A persistent large air leak or failure of lung re-expansion despite a functioning chest tube suggests a major tracheobronchial disruption. It is confirmed by bronchoscopy and usually needs operative repair.

questions.text: What is the initial management of a suspected massive traumatic hemothorax?
options: Immediate thoracotomy without a chest tube
Large-bore chest tube with blood-product resuscitation and urgent surgical consultation
originalOptions: Immediate thoracotomy without a chest tube
Large-bore chest tube with blood-product resuscitation and urgent surgical consultation
questions.correctAnswer: E) Large-bore chest tube with blood-product resuscitation and urgent surgical consultation
questions.correctAnswerText: Large-bore chest tube with blood-product resuscitation and urgent surgical consultation
questions.explanation: A large-bore tube drains the blood and quantifies ongoing loss, and it should not be delayed for imaging. Warmed blood products and early thoracic surgical involvement accompany it.

questions.text: Where is a chest tube inserted for traumatic hemothorax?
options: Within the safe triangle, at the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
originalOptions: Within the safe triangle, at the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
questions.correctAnswer: C) Within the safe triangle, at the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
questions.correctAnswerText: Within the safe triangle, at the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
questions.explanation: The safe triangle is bounded by the lateral edge of pectoralis major, the lateral edge of latissimus dorsi, and the 5th intercostal space. Insertion here avoids vital structures.

questions.text: Which of the following is appropriate in the management of flail chest?
options: Analgesia, judicious fluid therapy, and ventilatory support when needed
Placement of a sandbag over the flail segment
Immediate surgical fixation of all fractured ribs
originalOptions: Analgesia, judicious fluid therapy, and ventilatory support when needed
Placement of a sandbag over the flail segment
Immediate surgical fixation of all fractured ribs
questions.correctAnswer: A) Analgesia, judicious fluid therapy, and ventilatory support when needed
questions.correctAnswerText: Analgesia, judicious fluid therapy, and ventilatory support when needed
questions.explanation: The main problem is pain, impaired ventilation, and underlying pulmonary contusion. Excessive fluid worsens contusion, and weights or strapping further restrict ventilation.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes a flail chest?
options: One rib fractured at three sites
One fractured rib on the right and one on the left
Three consecutive ribs, each fractured at two or more sites, producing a paradoxically moving segment
Fractures of ribs 10–12 with liver injury
originalOptions: One rib fractured at three sites
One fractured rib on the right and one on the left
Three consecutive ribs, each fractured at two or more sites, producing a paradoxically moving segment
Fractures of ribs 10–12 with liver injury
questions.correctAnswer: D) Three consecutive ribs, each fractured at two or more sites, producing a paradoxically moving segment
questions.correctAnswerText: Three consecutive ribs, each fractured at two or more sites, producing a paradoxically moving segment
questions.explanation: A free-floating chest-wall segment moves paradoxically, inward on inspiration. The clinical problem is pain, impaired ventilation, and underlying pulmonary contusion.

questions.text: Which finding is characteristic of massive hemothorax?
options: Hyperresonance to percussion with absent breath sounds
Dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, and hypotension with flat neck veins
Tracheal deviation toward the affected side with hyperresonance
Muffled heart sounds with clear lungs
originalOptions: Hyperresonance to percussion with absent breath sounds
Dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, and hypotension with flat neck veins
Tracheal deviation toward the affected side with hyperresonance
Muffled heart sounds with clear lungs
questions.correctAnswer: B) Dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, and hypotension with flat neck veins
questions.correctAnswerText: Dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, and hypotension with flat neck veins
questions.explanation: Massive hemothorax produces hemorrhagic shock, so the neck veins are flat from hypovolemia and percussion is dull. Hyperresonance with distended neck veins indicates tension pneumothorax.

questions.text: Why can a normal initial chest radiograph in a child not exclude significant thoracic injury?
options: Pulmonary contusion is never visible on radiographs
Rib fractures are always visible on the first film
The mediastinum in children is fixed
The compliant chest wall transmits force to the lungs, causing contusion or rib/cartilage injury without a visible fracture
originalOptions: Pulmonary contusion is never visible on radiographs
Rib fractures are always visible on the first film
The mediastinum in children is fixed
The compliant chest wall transmits force to the lungs, causing contusion or rib/cartilage injury without a visible fracture
questions.correctAnswer: E) The compliant chest wall transmits force to the lungs, causing contusion or rib/cartilage injury without a visible fracture
questions.correctAnswerText: The compliant chest wall transmits force to the lungs, causing contusion or rib/cartilage injury without a visible fracture
questions.explanation: Pediatric chest-wall compliance allows major intrathoracic injury with few external or radiographic signs. A normal film therefore does not exclude significant injury.

questions.text: In open pneumothorax, air preferentially enters the pleural space through the chest wall defect when its diameter is at least what proportion of the tracheal diameter?
options: Half of the tracheal diameter, regardless of tissue resistance
originalOptions: Half of the tracheal diameter, regardless of tissue resistance
questions.explanation: When the defect reaches about two-thirds of the tracheal diameter or more, air follows the path of least resistance through the wound rather than through the trachea. This impairs ventilation.

questions.text: What is the initial management of an open pneumothorax?
options: A three-sided (vented) occlusive dressing followed by a chest tube at a separate site
A fully sealed four-sided occlusive dressing
Primary closure of the wound in the emergency department
originalOptions: A three-sided (vented) occlusive dressing followed by a chest tube at a separate site
A fully sealed four-sided occlusive dressing
Primary closure of the wound in the emergency department
questions.correctAnswer: A) A three-sided (vented) occlusive dressing followed by a chest tube at a separate site
questions.correctAnswerText: A three-sided (vented) occlusive dressing followed by a chest tube at a separate site
questions.explanation: The vented dressing acts as a one-way flutter valve and prevents conversion to tension pneumothorax. A fully sealed dressing traps air and may cause tension.

questions.text: Which rib fractures generally require the greatest force and signal a high risk of associated injuries?
questions.explanation: Ribs 1–3 are protected by the shoulder girdle, so their fracture implies a high-energy mechanism. It raises suspicion for great-vessel, brachial plexus, and intrathoracic injury.

questions.text: Which finding best differentiates cardiac tamponade from tension pneumothorax as the cause of hypotension?
questions.explanation: Breath sounds are unilaterally absent in tension pneumothorax and generally present and equal in tamponade. Jugular venous distension, tachycardia, and a narrow pulse pressure may occur in both.

questions.text: A trauma patient has both a suspected tension pneumothorax and a head injury. What takes priority?
options: Complete neurological assessment with GCS first
Immediate decompression of the tension pneumothorax during the Breathing step, before neurological assessment
originalOptions: Complete neurological assessment with GCS first
Immediate decompression of the tension pneumothorax during the Breathing step, before neurological assessment
questions.correctAnswer: E) Immediate decompression of the tension pneumothorax during the Breathing step, before neurological assessment
questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate decompression of the tension pneumothorax during the Breathing step, before neurological assessment
questions.explanation: Life threats are treated in ABCDE order, and hypoxia worsens secondary brain injury. The head injury is then managed while avoiding hypoxia and hypotension.

questions.text: A penetrating lower-chest injury causes unilateral reduced chest movement and decreased breath sounds without tension physiology. What is the initial definitive pleural treatment?
questions.explanation: Traumatic hemothorax or pneumothorax is treated definitively with a chest tube. Diaphragmatic and thoracoabdominal injury should also be considered with a lower-chest wound.

questions.text: A 32-year-old man was trapped under a car for 2 hours. He has cool, mottled, insensate extremities, firm hard muscles, and absent pulses below the femoral level. Which intervention is most likely to improve limb salvage?
options: Immediate transfer to a trauma center
originalOptions: Immediate transfer to a trauma center
questions.explanation: Prolonged crush produces compartment syndrome, with tense muscles, neurological deficit, and absent pulses. Emergency fasciotomy is time-critical for limb salvage.

questions.text: An 18-year-old struck on the back of the leg by a car can walk and has minimal swelling, normal pulses, normal motor examination, and no fracture on X-ray, but he reports persistent pain. Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion to the injury is the earliest and most reliable feature, and a normal distal pulse does not exclude it. The patient should not be discharged, and fasciotomy is definitive treatment.

questions.text: A construction worker falls 9 meters. HR is 124/min, BP 80/40 mmHg, and SpO₂ 89%. He has an occipital skull fracture, gurgling breathing, diminished breath sounds on the right, no jugular venous distension, a deformed knee, and an arm fracture. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Endotracheal intubation with inline cervical spine stabilization
Reduction and splinting of the extremity injuries
Insertion of a 32F chest tube on the right
originalOptions: Endotracheal intubation with inline cervical spine stabilization
Reduction and splinting of the extremity injuries
Insertion of a 32F chest tube on the right
questions.correctAnswer: B) Endotracheal intubation with inline cervical spine stabilization
questions.correctAnswerText: Endotracheal intubation with inline cervical spine stabilization
questions.explanation: Gurgling respiration indicates an unprotected airway, and airway control takes priority with cervical protection. Decreased breath sounds are addressed in the Breathing step that follows.

questions.text: A trauma patient with spinal cord injury has flaccid lower extremities, no rectal tone, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Which feature is expected in spinal shock, as distinct from neurogenic shock?
options: Flaccid paralysis with loss of deep tendon reflexes
originalOptions: Flaccid paralysis with loss of deep tendon reflexes
questions.correctAnswer: E) Flaccid paralysis with loss of deep tendon reflexes
questions.correctAnswerText: Flaccid paralysis with loss of deep tendon reflexes
questions.explanation: Spinal shock is a temporary loss of all cord function below the lesion. Neurogenic shock is the hemodynamic state of hypotension and bradycardia from loss of sympathetic tone.

questions.text: A patient with spinal cord injury has warm skin, HR 70/min, and BP 60/40 mmHg, and hemorrhage has been excluded. Which statement about management is correct?
options: Large-volume crystalloid alone is the treatment of choice
Vasopressors such as norepinephrine are indicated with judicious fluid administration
originalOptions: Large-volume crystalloid alone is the treatment of choice
Vasopressors such as norepinephrine are indicated with judicious fluid administration
questions.correctAnswer: C) Vasopressors such as norepinephrine are indicated with judicious fluid administration
questions.correctAnswerText: Vasopressors such as norepinephrine are indicated with judicious fluid administration
questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock results from loss of vascular tone, so volume alone is usually insufficient and may cause pulmonary edema. Bleeding must be excluded first because it is far more common in trauma.

questions.text: A young construction worker falls from a height of two stories and sustains bilateral calcaneal fractures. Which diagnostic study is the next step?
questions.explanation: Bilateral calcaneal fractures result from axial loading and are associated with thoracolumbar spine compression fractures. The spine must therefore be evaluated.

questions.text: A 25-year-old man opens his eyes to pain, moans periodically, and has the left arm reach toward the painful stimulus. The right arm does not respond and the legs are stiffly extended. What is the GCS?
questions.explanation: Eye opening to pain scores 2 and moaning (incomprehensible sounds) scores 2. The best motor response is localization, which scores 5, giving 2 + 2 + 5 = 9.

questions.text: A patient opens his eyes to command, moves his arms and legs on command, and is disoriented in conversation. What is the GCS?
questions.explanation: Eye opening to command scores 3, obeying commands scores 6, and confused conversation scores 4, giving 3 + 6 + 4 = 13.

questions.text: A patient's eyes open to voice, speech consists of inappropriate words, and he localizes pain. What is the GCS?
questions.explanation: Eye opening to voice is 3, inappropriate words is 3, and localizing pain is 5, giving a total GCS of 11. Withdrawal rather than localization would score M4 and give 10.

questions.text: A 40-year-old motorcyclist with isolated head injury has unequal dilated pupils, eye opening to pain, incomprehensible sounds, and abnormal flexion. BP is 130/80 mmHg with noisy breathing. What are the GCS and the immediate management?
options: GCS 9; observe and repeat the examination
GCS 7; mannitol and CT before addressing the airway
GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
GCS 5; burr-hole decompression in the emergency department
originalOptions: GCS 9; observe and repeat the examination
GCS 7; mannitol and CT before addressing the airway
GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
GCS 5; burr-hole decompression in the emergency department
questions.correctAnswer: C) GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
questions.correctAnswerText: GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
questions.explanation: E2 + V2 + M3 = 7, and unequal dilated pupils with falling consciousness indicate impending herniation. Airway control comes first, and hyperventilation is only a brief rescue measure.

questions.text: A 21-year-old man thrown from a horse has a facial injury and a GCS of 9. Despite suction and an oropharyngeal airway, he continues to snore. What is the next step?
options: CT of the head before airway intervention
originalOptions: CT of the head before airway intervention
questions.explanation: Persistent obstruction despite basic maneuvers shows the airway cannot be maintained, so a definitive airway is required. Pre-intubation GCS components are documented, and CT follows once the patient is stable.

questions.text: Which statement about moderate brain injury is correct?
options: CT is indicated only if a neurological deficit is present
If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
Discharge depends on clinical examination alone
originalOptions: CT is indicated only if a neurological deficit is present
If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
Discharge depends on clinical examination alone
questions.correctAnswer: D) If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
questions.correctAnswerText: If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
questions.explanation: Moderate injury is GCS 9–13, all patients need CT, and serial neurological examination is mandatory. Deterioration prompts the severe-injury pathway of airway control, ICP management, and neurosurgical consultation.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an indication for CT of the brain after minor head injury?
options: Two or more episodes of vomiting
GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
originalOptions: Two or more episodes of vomiting
GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
questions.correctAnswer: B) A single episode of vomiting
questions.explanation: By the Canadian CT Head Rule, vomiting becomes an indication only with two or more episodes. A single episode is not sufficient on its own.

questions.text: All of the following statements about subdural hematoma are correct EXCEPT:
options: It worsens if the patient is taking anticoagulants
It carries high morbidity and mortality because of the underlying brain injury
It needs rapid evacuation if CT shows a midline shift of more than 5 mm
It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
originalOptions: It worsens if the patient is taking anticoagulants
It carries high morbidity and mortality because of the underlying brain injury
It needs rapid evacuation if CT shows a midline shift of more than 5 mm
It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
questions.correctAnswer: E) It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
questions.correctAnswerText: It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
questions.explanation: Subdural hematoma results from torn bridging veins. Middle meningeal artery injury, usually after temporal bone fracture, causes epidural hematoma.

questions.text: All of the following statements about epidural hematoma are correct EXCEPT:
options: It is associated with skull fracture
It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
It has a lenticular (biconvex) shape on CT
It is associated with a lucid interval
originalOptions: It is associated with skull fracture
It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
It has a lenticular (biconvex) shape on CT
It is associated with a lucid interval
questions.correctAnswer: C) It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
questions.correctAnswerText: It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
questions.explanation: Epidural hematoma arises from the middle meningeal artery and is lens-shaped on CT. Bridging-vein tears cause subdural hematoma, which is crescent-shaped.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a definitive airway?
questions.explanation: A definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea that protects against aspiration. A laryngeal mask is a supraglottic device and does not fully protect the airway.

questions.text: A patient with head trauma, a depressed skull fracture, gurgling respirations, and vomitus on the face has a low GCS. After supplemental oxygen and jaw elevation, what is the next step?
options: Obtain a lateral cervical spine X-ray
originalOptions: Obtain a lateral cervical spine X-ray
questions.explanation: Gurgling indicates fluid in the airway, and it must be cleared before ventilation can be effective. Failure to suction prevents airway management and risks aspiration.

questions.text: A 17-year-old helmeted motorcyclist has GCS 7, BP 140/92 mmHg, HR 88/min, and RR 18/min. Appropriate immobilization should include a semirigid cervical collar and:
options: Soft collar in place of the rigid collar
originalOptions: Soft collar in place of the rigid collar
questions.explanation: A rigid collar with a long board and head blocks is standard for transport of a patient with possible spinal injury. The patient should be removed from the board as soon as practical to limit pressure and respiratory complications.

questions.text: Cervical spine injury should be assumed in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Isolated chest pain is not a criterion for presuming cervical injury. Multisystem trauma, altered consciousness, neurological deficit, and significant blunt injury above the clavicles are.

questions.text: Which finding precludes clinical clearance of the cervical spine without imaging?
options: Absence of a painful distracting injury
originalOptions: Absence of a painful distracting injury
questions.explanation: NEXUS and Canadian C-spine criteria require a normal level of alertness for clinical clearance. An obtunded patient cannot be cleared clinically and requires imaging.

questions.text: Which of the following alone is NOT sufficient to clear the cervical spine and remove the collar?
options: Absence of pain with voluntary movement
originalOptions: Absence of pain with voluntary movement
questions.correctAnswer: A) A negative cervical spine X-ray
questions.explanation: Plain films miss a substantial proportion of cervical injuries. Clearance requires clinical criteria, with CT or MRI when indicated.

questions.text: Which statement is correct regarding rigid cervical collars in isolated penetrating neck trauma?
options: They are mandatory in all cases
They must be applied before airway assessment
They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
They are indicated only when an anterior neck hematoma is present
originalOptions: They are mandatory in all cases
They must be applied before airway assessment
They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
They are indicated only when an anterior neck hematoma is present
questions.correctAnswer: D) They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
questions.correctAnswerText: They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
questions.explanation: Isolated penetrating neck trauma rarely causes unstable spinal injury. A collar can hide expanding hematoma and hinder airway management.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT generally used in acute traumatic brain-injury care?
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation worsens intracranial hemorrhage and requires reversal in head injury. Hyperosmolar agents, anticonvulsants, sedation, and isotonic fluids are part of acute management.

questions.text: In a trauma patient with cerebral edema, why should hypercarbia be avoided?
options: It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
originalOptions: It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.correctAnswer: E) It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.correctAnswerText: It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.explanation: CO₂ is a potent cerebral vasodilator, so hypercarbia raises intracranial pressure. The target PaCO₂ is 35–40 mmHg, with brief hyperventilation reserved for herniation.

questions.text: In managing a head-injured patient, what is the most important initial step?
questions.explanation: Airway comes first in the ABCDE sequence. Hypoxia and hypotension are the most damaging secondary insults to an injured brain.

questions.text: A 73-year-old man falls down stairs. He is hypotensive and tachycardic, opens his eyes to voice, is confused, and has clear fluid dripping from the ear with mastoid ecchymosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Otorrhea of cerebrospinal fluid with mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign) is the classic sign of basilar skull fracture. Hypotension, however, should still prompt a search for hemorrhage elsewhere.

questions.text: A motorcyclist with severe facial fractures and GCS 6 arrives in the emergency department. What is the immediate management?
options: CT of the head and face before airway management
Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
Maxillofacial reduction before any airway intervention
originalOptions: CT of the head and face before airway management
Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
Maxillofacial reduction before any airway intervention
questions.correctAnswer: D) Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
questions.correctAnswerText: Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
questions.explanation: Facial fractures with GCS 6 imply a difficult airway and an unprotected airway. Traumatic brain injury and cervical spine injury must be presumed.

questions.text: A facial-trauma patient with initial hypoxemia and GCS 10 is intubated with cervical-spine protection and becomes physiologically stable. What should be done next?
options: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
originalOptions: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
questions.correctAnswer: B) Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
questions.explanation: Once the patient is stabilized, CT is the investigation of choice for acute intracranial and cervical injury. Neurosurgical and maxillofacial teams are involved early.

questions.text: A trauma patient has BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 125/min, SpO₂ 89%, and is unresponsive to voice. A foot is deformed and the opposite arm has a large laceration. What is the best next step?
options: Apply a tourniquet to the deformed foot
Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
originalOptions: Apply a tourniquet to the deformed foot
Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
questions.correctAnswer: E) Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
questions.correctAnswerText: Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
questions.explanation: The unresponsive, hypoxic patient needs airway control, while the bleeding arm laceration needs direct control simultaneously. The deformed foot is a closed injury and does not require a tourniquet.

questions.text: A hemodynamically unstable patient has a narrow-complex tachycardia of 180/min. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Instability from a tachyarrhythmia mandates immediate synchronized cardioversion. Adenosine and vagal maneuvers are reserved for stable patients.

questions.text: All of the following are adjuncts to the primary survey of a trauma patient EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CT requires transport and a relatively stable patient, so it belongs to the secondary survey. ECG, ABG, FAST, and portable radiographs are primary-survey adjuncts.

questions.text: As the first doctor receiving a trauma patient in the emergency room, what is the most important task?
options: Write the specific details of the injury
Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
originalOptions: Write the specific details of the injury
Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
questions.correctAnswer: D) Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
questions.correctAnswerText: Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
questions.explanation: The first clinical priority is identification and treatment of immediate life threats. History and documentation follow stabilization.

questions.text: What is the appropriate initial volume of crystalloid for a pediatric trauma patient in shock?
questions.explanation: The traditional initial pediatric bolus is 20 mL/kg of warmed isotonic crystalloid, followed by reassessment. In hemorrhagic shock, blood products are started early rather than repeating large crystalloid volumes.

questions.text: Which screening radiographs are traditionally obtained in the initial assessment of a multiply injured patient?
questions.explanation: The classic trauma series comprises a lateral cervical spine, an AP chest, and an AP pelvis. Current practice is selective and relies on CT according to stability and local protocol.

questions.text: In the initial assessment of trauma patients, which of the following does NOT affect circulation?
options: Second-degree burn of 20% body surface area
originalOptions: Second-degree burn of 20% body surface area
questions.explanation: Isolated brain injury does not cause hypotension, so shock should prompt a search for hemorrhage or another cause. Spinal cord injury causes neurogenic shock, and the other options reduce effective circulating volume or cardiac output.

questions.text: In the initial assessment of trauma patients, which of the following does NOT affect ventilation?
questions.explanation: Tamponade impairs circulation by restricting cardiac filling, not ventilation. The other options directly impair air entry or lung expansion.

questions.text: Maintaining a target systolic blood pressure of 80–90 mmHg in active hemorrhage without traumatic brain injury, until surgical hemostasis is achieved, is known as:
questions.explanation: Permissive hypotension is a component of damage-control resuscitation. It avoids disrupting early clot, and it is not used in traumatic brain injury, where cerebral perfusion pressure must be maintained.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an immediately life-threatening thoracic injury identified and treated during the primary survey?
questions.explanation: Esophageal rupture is serious but is usually identified in the secondary survey. Airway obstruction, tension and open pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, and tamponade are the immediate threats.

questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes a mass-casualty incident from a multiple-casualty incident?
options: A multiple-casualty incident exceeds the facility's resources
A mass-casualty incident can be handled with the usual resources
In a mass-casualty incident, only the most severely injured are treated, regardless of survivability
A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
originalOptions: A multiple-casualty incident exceeds the facility's resources
A mass-casualty incident can be handled with the usual resources
In a mass-casualty incident, only the most severely injured are treated, regardless of survivability
A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
questions.correctAnswer: E) A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
questions.correctAnswerText: A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
questions.explanation: In a multiple-casualty incident, resources are adequate and the most seriously injured are treated first. A mass-casualty incident overwhelms capacity.

questions.text: Which principle applies to triage in a mass-casualty incident?
options: Allocate the most time and equipment to the most severely injured, including those with unsurvivable injuries
Treat patients in order of arrival
Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
Treat children before all other patients
originalOptions: Allocate the most time and equipment to the most severely injured, including those with unsurvivable injuries
Treat patients in order of arrival
Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
Treat children before all other patients
questions.correctAnswer: C) Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
questions.correctAnswerText: Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
questions.explanation: The goal shifts from the best outcome for one patient to the best outcome for the greatest number. Committing disproportionate resources to one patient reduces total lives saved.

questions.text: A patient with multiple stab wounds has BP 89/40 mmHg and is irritable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypotension with altered behavior after multiple stab wounds indicates major blood loss. Tamponade and tension pneumothorax must still be actively excluded during the Breathing and Circulation steps.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT included in the primary survey?
questions.explanation: The primary survey is limited to identifying and treating immediate life threats. A detailed history (AMPLE) belongs to the secondary survey.

questions.text: A patient with diabetes and hypertension has fever, hypotension, and turbid urine draining from a Foley catheter. Which shock state is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fever and hypotension with a urinary catheter and turbid urine point to a urinary source of sepsis. Treatment is cultures, early antimicrobials, resuscitation, and source control.

questions.text: A patient has dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hemoptysis, and pulmonary embolism is strongly suspected. What is the imaging study of choice?
questions.explanation: CTPA is the first-line confirmatory test in a stable patient with a high pre-test probability. V/Q scanning is preferred in pregnancy, renal impairment, or contrast allergy.

questions.text: Which of the following is essential before passing a urinary catheter in a male trauma patient?
options: Perform a retrograde urethrogram in every patient
originalOptions: Perform a retrograde urethrogram in every patient
questions.correctAnswer: C) Examine the rectum and perineum
questions.explanation: Rectal and perineal examination excludes signs of urethral injury, namely a high-riding prostate, perineal bruising, and a scrotal hematoma. Blood at the meatus likewise warrants a retrograde urethrogram before catheterization.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to Foley catheter insertion in a trauma patient?
questions.explanation: Urinary retention is an indication for catheterization. The other findings suggest urethral disruption and require a urethrogram first.

questions.text: What does the AMPLE history mnemonic stand for in the trauma secondary survey?
options: Airway, Medications, Pain, Last meal, Events
Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
Age, Medications, Previous surgery, Labs, Environment
originalOptions: Airway, Medications, Pain, Last meal, Events
Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
Age, Medications, Previous surgery, Labs, Environment
questions.correctAnswer: D) Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
questions.correctAnswerText: Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
questions.explanation: AMPLE is the focused history obtained in the secondary survey. Pregnancy is included under past medical history, and the event history covers the environment and mechanism.

questions.text: What is the most common type of shock in trauma patients?
questions.explanation: Hypotension after trauma is hemorrhagic until proven otherwise. Tension pneumothorax and tamponade must still be excluded during the primary survey.

questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolytic therapy?
options: Ischemic stroke more than 3 months earlier
originalOptions: Ischemic stroke more than 3 months earlier
questions.explanation: Any prior intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication because of the risk of recurrent intracranial bleeding. The other options are relative contraindications or are not contraindications.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an indication for intubation?
options: GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
Severe maxillofacial injury with impending airway obstruction
originalOptions: GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
Severe maxillofacial injury with impending airway obstruction
questions.correctAnswer: C) GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
questions.correctAnswerText: GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
questions.explanation: A GCS of 8 or less is the threshold for intubation. A patient with a higher GCS needs intubation only if the airway is unprotected or deterioration is anticipated.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an objective sign of airway obstruction?
options: Use of accessory muscles of respiration
originalOptions: Use of accessory muscles of respiration
questions.explanation: Neck vein distention reflects a circulatory problem such as tamponade or tension pneumothorax. Stridor, accessory-muscle use, paradoxical movement, and cyanosis are objective signs of airway obstruction.

questions.text: Which statement about trauma patients with comorbidities is false?
options: In elderly patients, normal vital signs may mask significant shock
They warrant a lower threshold for imaging and admission
They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
originalOptions: In elderly patients, normal vital signs may mask significant shock
They warrant a lower threshold for imaging and admission
They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
questions.correctAnswer: D) They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
questions.correctAnswerText: They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
questions.explanation: Patients with comorbidities have poor reserve and benefit from care at a higher-level trauma center. Transfer is appropriate when their needs exceed local capability.

questions.text: Which statement about the emergency management of trauma patients is correct?
options: The specific injury must be identified before management begins
The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
A detailed history must precede resuscitation
Diagnosis must be established before treatment
Unstable patients should undergo CT first
originalOptions: The specific injury must be identified before management begins
The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
A detailed history must precede resuscitation
Diagnosis must be established before treatment
Unstable patients should undergo CT first
questions.correctAnswer: B) The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
questions.correctAnswerText: The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
questions.explanation: Management follows the same ABCDE sequence of treating the greatest threat to life first. It does not depend on knowing the specific injury.

questions.text: Which statement about the classes of hemorrhagic shock is false?
options: Class IV: more than 40% blood loss
Class I: normal heart rate and blood pressure
Class I: less than 5% blood loss
originalOptions: Class IV: more than 40% blood loss
Class I: normal heart rate and blood pressure
Class I: less than 5% blood loss
questions.correctAnswer: E) Class I: less than 5% blood loss
questions.correctAnswerText: Class I: less than 5% blood loss
questions.explanation: Class I corresponds to a loss of less than 15% of blood volume, which the body absorbs with little physiological change.

questions.text: Which statement about airway management in trauma is false?
options: Endotracheal intubation helps protect the airway
Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
Endotracheal intubation allows control of ventilation
originalOptions: Endotracheal intubation helps protect the airway
Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
Endotracheal intubation allows control of ventilation
questions.correctAnswer: C) Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
questions.correctAnswerText: Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
questions.explanation: Intubation is indicated when airway protection, oxygenation, ventilation, or severe neurological compromise requires it, not simply because trauma occurred.

questions.text: How should the airway be opened in a trauma patient with possible cervical spine injury?
options: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway in every patient
Flexing the neck over a pillow
originalOptions: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway in every patient
Flexing the neck over a pillow
questions.correctAnswer: A) Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
questions.correctAnswerText: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
questions.explanation: Jaw thrust opens the airway without extending the neck. Head-tilt/chin-lift is avoided when cervical injury is suspected.

questions.text: Which rapid adjuncts help identify occult hemorrhage in an unstable trauma patient?

eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
originalOptions: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
questions.correctAnswer: D) eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
questions.correctAnswerText: eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
questions.explanation: These bedside studies identify the main hidden sources of bleeding without leaving the resuscitation area. A baseline hemoglobin cannot exclude acute hemorrhage, and unstable patients should not go to CT.

questions.text: How is hemorrhage from an unstable pelvic fracture managed?
options: Repeated rocking of the pelvis to assess stability
Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
Urinary catheter insertion in all patients
originalOptions: Repeated rocking of the pelvis to assess stability
Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
Urinary catheter insertion in all patients
questions.correctAnswer: B) Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
questions.correctAnswerText: Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
questions.explanation: Circumferential compression reduces pelvic volume and tamponades venous and bony bleeding. Definitive control is by pelvic packing, angioembolization, or surgery according to physiology and resources.

questions.text: Which statement about traumatic diaphragmatic injury is FALSE?
options: Blunt trauma can produce a large diaphragmatic tear
It may be misinterpreted as hemothorax on chest radiograph
Even small tears require surgical repair
A nasogastric tube coiled in the chest is a diagnostic clue
The right diaphragm is injured more often than the left

questions.correctAnswer: E) The right diaphragm is injured more often than the left

questions.explanation: Left-sided injury is more common because the liver protects the right hemidiaphragm. The injury can be missed initially and later present as herniation of bowel or stomach into the thorax.

questions.text: An unresponsive patient regains a pulse after defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation, and the post-shock ECG shows third-degree AV block with a slow ventricular rate. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation: With a pulse present, symptomatic complete heart block is treated with transcutaneous pacing (± dopamine/epinephrine infusion) rather than defibrillation or chest compressions, which are reserved for pulseless rhythms.
questions.note: Without a pulse, this is PEA: resume CPR and give epinephrine; routine pacing during established arrest is not recommended.

questions.text: The recovered ECG shows P waves marching out independently from QRS complexes at a faster rate than the ventricular rate, with no fixed relationship between P and QRS. What is the diagnosis? [img: ERArrhythmia1.png ]
options: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
originalOptions: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
questions.explanation: Complete AV dissociation — P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular escape rate — defines third-degree AV block, unlike Mobitz I/II where some P waves still conduct.

questions.text: Which statement correctly differentiates Mobitz type I from Mobitz type II second-degree AV block?
options: Mobitz I has a constant PR interval with sudden dropped beats; Mobitz II shows progressive PR prolongation
Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
originalOptions: Mobitz I has a constant PR interval with sudden dropped beats; Mobitz II shows progressive PR prolongation
Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

questions.correctAnswer: D) Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
questions.correctAnswerText: Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
questions.explanation: Mobitz I reflects reversible AV-nodal delay with progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat; Mobitz II is an infranodal block with fixed PR intervals and a higher risk of progressing to complete heart block.

questions.text: A 12-lead ECG shows a constant PR interval of 240 ms with every P wave followed by a QRS complex. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A fixed PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction (no dropped beats) defines first-degree AV block, a partial delay rather than an interruption of conduction.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia2.png ] The ECG shows constant PR intervals with intermittent nonconducted P waves in a patient with an acute anterior wall MI. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
originalOptions: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
questions.correctAnswer: E) Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
questions.correctAnswerText: Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
questions.explanation: Mobitz II or high-grade AV block complicating anterior MI reflects extensive infranodal conduction system damage and can progress abruptly to complete block/asystole, so urgent pacing readiness and cardiology evaluation are required rather than observation or AV-nodal blocking drugs.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia3.png ] An asymptomatic 29-year-old has first-degree AV block on this ECG with no other conduction disease. What is the best next step?
options: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
originalOptions: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
questions.correctAnswer: C) No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
questions.correctAnswerText: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
questions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic first-degree AV block requires no acute intervention beyond identifying reversible causes (e.g., AV-nodal blocking drugs); cardioversion and defibrillation are irrelevant since this is not a tachyarrhythma

questions.text: What are the defining ECG features of complete (third-degree) AV block?
options: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
originalOptions: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
questions.correctAnswer: B) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
questions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
questions.explanation: In third-degree block, P waves and QRS complexes occur completely independently (AV dissociation), with the atrial rate faster than the escape ventricular rate; the escape QRS is narrow if junctional, wide if ventricular/infranodal.

questions.text: What ECG finding is diagnostic of complete (third-degree) heart block?
options: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
originalOptions: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.correctAnswer: E) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.explanation: The hallmark of complete heart block is total dissociation of atrial and ventricular activity — P waves and QRS complexes occur independently at their own rates.

questions.text: A patient develops Mobitz II AV block complicating an acute anterior wall MI. When is a permanent pacemaker indicated?
options: Only if the patient develops asystole
Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves
If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
originalOptions: Only if the patient develops asystole
Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves
If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
questions.correctAnswer: C) If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
questions.correctAnswerText: If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
questions.explanation: Anterior MI causing Mobitz II/high-grade block indicates extensive septal/infranodal damage with a high risk of sudden complete block or asystole; if it persists after reversible causes are addressed, permanent pacing is indicated.

questions.text: A patient has atrial fibrillation of unknown duration and is hemodynamically stable. What anticoagulation strategy should precede elective cardioversion?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
No anticoagulation needed if cardioversion restores sinus rhythm
Anticoagulation is only needed after cardioversion, not before
originalOptions: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
No anticoagulation needed if cardioversion restores sinus rhythm
Anticoagulation is only needed after cardioversion, not before
questions.correctAnswer: A) Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
questions.correctAnswerText: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
questions.explanation: For AF ≥48 hours or of unknown duration, guidelines require ≥3 weeks anticoagulation before and ≥4 weeks after elective cardioversion (or TEE exclusion of thrombus with periprocedural anticoagulation), because stroke risk depends on atrial stasis duration, not on restoration of sinus rhythm.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia4.png] A hemodynamically stable patient has atrial flutter with a ventricular rate around 130/min and no heart-failure symptoms. What is the best initial treatment?
options: A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control
originalOptions: A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control
questions.correctAnswer: D) A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control
questions.correctAnswerText: A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control
questions.explanation: In stable atrial flutter, rate control with a beta-blocker (or diltiazem/verapamil if LVEF is preserved) is first-line; cardioversion is reserved for instability, and adenosine only transiently unmasks flutter waves without terminating the rhythm.

questions.text: Which arrhythmia is most commonly associated with thyrotoxicosis?
questions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis sensitizes atrial myocardium and is a classic reversible cause of atrial fibrillation; thyroid function should be checked in all new-onset AF.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] A patient has had palpitations for 1 week due to atrial fibrillation, with no syncope, heart failure, or chest pain. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: In stable AF with preserved LVEF, IV diltiazem provides acute ventricular rate control; cardioversion is not first-line without addressing anticoagulation given the AF duration is ≥48 hours, and defibrillation is inappropriate for a non-shockable rhythm with a pulse.

questions.text: Which finding alone is NOT considered an ACLS sign of hemodynamic instability in a patient with atrial flutter?
questions.correctAnswer: C) A high ventricular rate alone
questions.explanation: ACLS instability criteria require hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure attributable to the arrhythmia; a fast rate by itself, without these findings, does not define instability.

questions.text: In a patient with atrial fibrillation, which factor determines whether rate control or rhythm control is prioritized, and how should ventricular rate be managed if AF is hemodynamically stable?
options: If AF causes instability, perform immediate synchronized cardioversion; if stable, choose rate or rhythm control based on symptoms/comorbidities, using a beta-blocker as an acute rate-control option (diltiazem/verapamil reserved for LVEF >40%)
All stable AF patients require immediate cardioversion regardless of duration
Diltiazem is preferred over beta-blockers regardless of ejection fraction
Digoxin is always first-line for rate control
originalOptions: If AF causes instability, perform immediate synchronized cardioversion; if stable, choose rate or rhythm control based on symptoms/comorbidities, using a beta-blocker as an acute rate-control option (diltiazem/verapamil reserved for LVEF >40%)

questions.explanation: Unstable AF mandates immediate cardioversion; in stable AF, management is individualized, and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are restricted to patients with LVEF above 40% to avoid worsening heart failure.

questions.text: A hemodynamically stable patient with atrial fibrillation has an LVEF of 30%. Which agent should be avoided for ventricular rate control?
questions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers have negative inotropic effects and should be avoided when LVEF is below 40%; beta-blockers (if compensated), digoxin, or amiodarone in decompensated states are preferred alternatives.

questions.text: A patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Which class of drugs must be avoided?
options: Class Ia antiarrhythmics such as procainamide
Isolated AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
Class III antiarrhythmics such as ibutilide

Isolated AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
Class III antiarrhythmics such as ibutilide
questions.correctAnswer: B) Isolated AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
questions.correctAnswerText: Isolated AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
questions.explanation: AV-nodal blocking agents can preferentially slow AV-node conduction while leaving the accessory pathway unopposed, accelerating ventricular conduction and precipitating ventricular fibrillation; procainamide or cardioversion are used instead.

questions.text: What is the primary indication for emergency electrical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation?
options: AF diagnosed incidentally on a routine ECG
AF lasting less than 12 hours regardless of symptoms
Recurrent paroxysmal AF with prior successful rate control
AF causing hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, or ongoing ischemia)
