questions.correctAnswerText: AF causing hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, or ongoing ischemia)
questions.explanation: Emergency synchronized cardioversion is reserved for AF causing hemodynamic compromise; stable AF is managed with rate/rhythm-control strategies and appropriately timed anticoagulation.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] What rhythm is shown on this 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: The tracing shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm without discrete P waves, replaced by fine fibrillatory baseline oscillations — diagnostic of atrial fibrillation.

questions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a heart rate of 32/min and a palpable pulse. Which of the following are acceptable therapeutic options if the initial drug is ineffective?
options: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Immediate chest compressions regardless of pulse
Observation only, since bradycardia is never treated pharmacologically
originalOptions: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Immediate chest compressions regardless of pulse
Observation only, since bradycardia is never treated pharmacologically
questions.correctAnswer: A) Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
questions.correctAnswerText: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
questions.explanation: Atropine is first-line for symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse; if ineffective, transcutaneous pacing and/or a chronotropic infusion are next-line options per the adult bradycardia algorithm.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] An adult patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse and poor perfusion. What is the correct approach to management?
options: Chest compressions, invasive airway, transcutaneous pacing

questions.correctAnswerText: Support ABCs and give atropine; if ineffective, use transcutaneous pacing and/or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion
questions.explanation: Since the patient has a pulse, chest compressions and defibrillation are not indicated; the adult bradycardia algorithm proceeds from atropine to pacing/chronotropic infusion if there is inadequate response.

questions.text: What defines sinus arrest, and how does its ECG pause differ from a sinoatrial exit block?

Sinus arrest requires a pause exceeding 10 seconds to be diagnosed

questions.text: What is the first-line medication to treat symptomatic bradycardia?
questions.explanation: Atropine is the first drug given in the adult symptomatic bradycardia algorithm because it reverses excessive vagal tone at the SA/AV node; beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers would worsen bradycardia.

questions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise. What is the correct atropine dosing and next step if ineffective?
options: Atropine 5 mg IV bolus, single dose
Atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg

questions.explanation: Current ACLS bradycardia dosing is atropine 1 mg IV push every 3-5 minutes (max 3 mg); persistent symptomatic bradycardia despite atropine warrants pacing or a chronotropic infusion while reversible causes are treated.

questions.text: Which of the following is an EXTRINSIC (reversible) cause of bradycardia rather than intrinsic SA-node disease?
options: Increased vagal tone or drug effect
originalOptions: Increased vagal tone or drug effect
questions.correctAnswer: A) Increased vagal tone or drug effect
questions.correctAnswerText: Increased vagal tone or drug effect
questions.explanation: Extrinsic bradycardia results from reversible factors like vagal stimulation, drugs, hypothyroidism, or raised ICP, distinguishing it from intrinsic structural SA-node disease such as sick sinus syndrome or fibrosis.

questions.text: Which of the following is a pathological, intrinsic cause of bradycardia rather than a normal physiological variant?
options: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
originalOptions: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
questions.explanation: Sick sinus syndrome reflects intrinsic structural SA-node disease (typically idiopathic fibrosis), unlike athletic bradycardia, sleep-related bradycardia, or respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which are normal physiological findings.

questions.text: How is sinus arrhythmia defined, and what does a non-phasic pattern suggest in the context of sick sinus syndrome?
options: It is a fixed P-P interval with no respiratory variation; non-phasic forms are always benign

It is SA-node rhythm with P-P interval variation exceeding 120 ms; the classic phasic (respiratory) form is benign, but a non-phasic form in SSS suggests intrinsic SA-node dysfunction, often with sinus pauses or tachy-brady syndrome
It requires a pause exceeding 3 seconds to diagnose
It is defined only by heart rates below 40 bpm

questions.text: What is the first clinical issue assessed in the bradycardia algorithm?

Whether the bradycardia is causing cardiopulmonary compromise/poor perfusion

questions.explanation: The bradycardia algorithm begins by determining whether the slow rate is causing symptomatic hypoperfusion, since this determines whether pharmacologic/electrical treatment is needed or the patient can be observed.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia6.png] A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presents with palpitations. and she is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step for management?
questions.explanation: In stable AF, rate control is first-line; diltiazem is preferred over a beta-blocker in this asthmatic patient to avoid bronchospasm, while adenosine and atropine have no role in AF.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia19.png] A 73-year-old ICU patient becomes unresponsive with a tachyarrhythmia on ECG and a blood pressure of 70/40. What is the best next step for management?
questions.explanation: A tachyarrhythmia causing severe hypotension and unresponsiveness is unstable; immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated rather than pharmacologic rate/rhythm control

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia7.png] A patient becomes unresponsive and the ECG shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate next step?
options: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR
originalOptions: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR
questions.correctAnswer: E) Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR

questions.explanation: Pulseless VF is a shockable rhythm requiring immediate unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR; synchronized cardioversion applies only to tachyarrhythmias with a pulse.

questions.text: How is adult asystolic cardiac arrest managed?
options: Confirm true asystole in at least two leads, begin/continue high-quality CPR, give epinephrine as soon as possible and every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes
Transcutaneous pacing as the first intervention

questions.explanation: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm; management relies on high-quality CPR and epinephrine, with a search for reversible causes (Hs and Ts), rather than defibrillation or routine pacing.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] A young athlete collapses and the his ECG. What is the rhythm?
questions.explanation: The twisting QRS axis around the isoelectric baseline is characteristic of torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT associated with QT prolongation (e.g., congenital long-QT syndrome in a young patient).

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia9.png] An 85-year-old previously healthy woman presents with recurrent syncope, the last episode an hour ago. Her ECG shows a fixed PR interval with intermittently nonconducted P waves. What type of block does she have?
questions.explanation: A constant PR interval with sudden, unpredicted dropped QRS complexes (no progressive lengthening) defines Mobitz type II, an infranodal block with a high risk of progression to complete heart block — consistent with her syncope.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] An ICU patient becomes unresponsive with no pulse and is not breathing. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: Pulseless polymorphic VT (torsades) is treated as a shockable rhythm; immediate defibrillation takes priority over airway management or drug administration.

questions.text: Which intervention provides the greatest immediate survival benefit in ventricular fibrillation?
options: Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
originalOptions: Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
questions.correctAnswer: E) Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
questions.correctAnswerText: Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
questions.explanation: Time to defibrillation is the strongest predictor of survival in VF; CPR maintains perfusion until a shock can be delivered, while drugs and airway management are adjunctive.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] A patient with a family history of sudden cardiac death has this ECG rhythm. What is the rhythm, and what should be evaluated?

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia10.png] What two abnormalities are shown on this ECG?

questions.text: What is the most important immediate precursor/risk factor for pulmonary embolism?
options: Deep-vein thrombosis, usually from the proximal lower-extremity or pelvic veins

questions.correctAnswerText: Deep-vein thrombosis, usually from the proximal lower-extremity or pelvic veins
questions.explanation: Most pulmonary emboli originate from DVT in the proximal leg or pelvic veins embolizing to the right heart and pulmonary circulation, distinct from left atrial thrombus (which embolizes systemically, e.g., in AF).

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia11.png] An athletic patient presents with a racing heart sensation and stable vitals. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. What do you give?
questions.explanation: For a stable, regular narrow-complex (likely SVT) tachycardia, vagal maneuvers followed by IV adenosine is first-line; diltiazem/verapamil are second-line alternatives, and atropine/amiodarone have no role here.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia12.png] A patient has normal vital signs with a heart rate of 170/min. The ECG shows a regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia. What do you give?
questions.explanation: In stable, regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia (presumed VT with a pulse), an antiarrhythmic infusion such as amiodarone is appropriate with expert consultation; diltiazem/verapamil should be avoided in wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia13.png] Progressive PR-interval prolongation followed by a dropped QRS complex identifies which rhythm?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
questions.explanation: Progressive PR lengthening culminating in a nonconducted P wave, with the cycle then repeating, is the defining feature of Mobitz I (Wenckebach) block.

questions.text: What are the symptoms/signs of tachycardia (HR >150 bpm) that indicate urgent treatment?
options: A heart rate consistently above 150 bpm on its own
Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure attributable to the tachyarrhythmia
originalOptions: A heart rate consistently above 150 bpm on its own
Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure attributable to the tachyarrhythmia
questions.correctAnswer: B) Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure attributable to the tachyarrhythmia
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure attributable to the tachyarrhythmia
questions.explanation: Urgent treatment (synchronized cardioversion) is guided by signs of hemodynamic compromise caused by the tachyarrhythmia, not by rate alone.

questions.text: A patient has a tachyarrhythmia with a rate above 150 bpm but is asymptomatic with normal blood pressure and mentation. How should this be classified?
options: Stable, since rate alone does not meet ACLS instability criteria
originalOptions: Stable, since rate alone does not meet ACLS instability criteria
questions.correctAnswer: C) Stable, since rate alone does not meet ACLS instability criteria
questions.correctAnswerText: Stable, since rate alone does not meet ACLS instability criteria
questions.explanation: Since instability requires hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischemic pain, or heart failure attributable to the arrhythmia, an asymptomatic patient with normal perfusion despite a fast rate is managed as stable.

questions.text: A patient is found pulseless with an organized rhythm on the monitor. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate high-quality CPR, epinephrine as soon as possible and every 3-5 minutes, and treatment of reversible Hs and Ts (no defibrillation)
originalOptions: Immediate high-quality CPR, epinephrine as soon as possible and every 3-5 minutes, and treatment of reversible Hs and Ts (no defibrillation)

questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate high-quality CPR, epinephrine as soon as possible and every 3-5 minutes, and treatment of reversible Hs and Ts (no defibrillation)
questions.explanation: An organized rhythm without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity (PEA), which is not shockable; management centers on high-quality CPR, epinephrine, and correcting reversible causes.

questions.text: In the treatment algorithm for tachyarrhythmia with a pulse, how should a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia be approached versus an unstable tachyarrhythmia?

Stable narrow-complex tachycardia requires immediate cardioversion regardless of vagal maneuvers

questions.explanation: The presence of instability dictates immediate cardioversion; in stable patients, vagal maneuvers and adenosine are first-line for regular narrow-complex tachycardia before considering rate-control drugs.

questions.text: An unresponsive, pulseless patient develops a shockable rhythm on the monitor. What is the immediate treatment?
options: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation with prompt resumption of high-quality CPR

questions.explanation: A pulseless shockable rhythm (VF/pulseless VT) requires immediate unsynchronized defibrillation, with CPR resumed promptly afterward without pausing to reassess rhythm/pulse first.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia14.png] What rhythm is shown on this recovered ECG?
questions.explanation: The irregularly irregular rhythm without discernible discrete P waves is characteristic of atrial fibrillation.

questions.text: How is a hemodynamically stable, regular narrow-complex tachycardia managed?
options: Begin with vagal maneuvers, then give adenosine if the rhythm remains regular; use synchronized cardioversion if the patient becomes unstable
Diltiazem as first-line before any other measure

questions.correctAnswerText: Begin with vagal maneuvers, then give adenosine if the rhythm remains regular; use synchronized cardioversion if the patient becomes unstable
questions.explanation: Vagal maneuvers can terminate reentrant SVT non-invasively; adenosine is used if vagal maneuvers fail, reserving cardioversion for instability.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia15.png ] What is the diagnosis based on this ECG strip?
questions.explanation: A regular rhythm with a normal P wave preceding every QRS complex, a normal PR interval, and no dropped beats represents a normal sinus rhythm.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia16.png ] The ECG shows an anterior/anteroseptal infarction pattern. Which coronary artery is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Anterior/anteroseptal ST-elevation MI reflects occlusion of the left anterior descending artery, which supplies the anterior wall and interventricular septum.

questions.text: What are the ECG characteristics of multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
options: A regular rhythm with a single P-wave morphology
An irregular rhythm with atrial rate >100/min, at least 3 distinct P-wave morphologies, variable P-P/R-R/PR intervals, and an isoelectric baseline between P waves
Absent P waves with fine fibrillatory baseline

questions.explanation: MAT is defined by ≥3 morphologically distinct P waves with an irregular rate >100/min, most commonly due to underlying pulmonary disease or electrolyte disturbance; the underlying cause should be treated.

questions.text: How can supraventricular tachycardia present atypically compared to classic palpitations?
options: With a widened QRS complex in all cases
originalOptions: With a widened QRS complex in all cases
questions.explanation: Prominent neck pulsations and polyuria. Atrial stretch can increase natriuretic-peptide release and urine output during sustained tachycardia.

questions.text: Which unusual neck and urinary symptoms may occur during supraventricular tachycardia?
options: Jugular venous distension with peripheral edema
Oliguria due to reduced renal perfusion
Prominent neck pulsations ("frog sign") and polyuria from atrial stretch-related natriuretic peptide release

Prominent neck pulsations ("frog sign") and polyuria from atrial stretch-related natriuretic peptide release

questions.correctAnswerText: Prominent neck pulsations ("frog sign") and polyuria from atrial stretch-related natriuretic peptide release
questions.explanation: Simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction against a closed AV valve during SVT produces visible neck pulsations, while atrial stretch increases ANP/BNP release, causing polyuria.

questions.text: How is an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse treated?
options: Immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying the shock
originalOptions: Immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying the shock

questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying the shock
questions.explanation: An unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse (hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischemic pain, or heart failure) requires immediate synchronized cardioversion rather than vagal maneuvers or drug therapy, which are for stable patients.

questions.text: A patient treated for SVT develops transient flushing, chest pressure, and dyspnea immediately after a rapid IV drug push. Which drug most likely caused these effects?
questions.explanation: Adenosine causes brief, self-limited flushing, chest pressure, and dyspnea due to its very short half-life and transient AV-nodal/vasodilatory effects, which resolve within seconds.

questions.text: A conscious, hemodynamically stable patient has regular monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. What is the next treatment?
options: Obtain expert consultation and give an antiarrhythmic infusion (e.g., procainamide, amiodarone, or sotalol); cardiovert if instability develops
originalOptions: Obtain expert consultation and give an antiarrhythmic infusion (e.g., procainamide, amiodarone, or sotalol); cardiovert if instability develops

questions.correctAnswerText: Obtain expert consultation and give an antiarrhythmic infusion (e.g., procainamide, amiodarone, or sotalol); cardiovert if instability develops
questions.explanation: Stable monomorphic VT with a pulse is managed with antiarrhythmic drug therapy under expert guidance; cardioversion is reserved for instability, and defibrillation is inappropriate since the patient has a pulse.

questions.text: A person with alcohol use disorder collapses and is found to be in torsades de pointes. What intervention is most likely to correct the underlying problem?
options: Rewarm the individual to correct hypothermia
Administer naloxone to correct narcotic overdose
originalOptions: Rewarm the individual to correct hypothermia
Administer naloxone to correct narcotic overdose
questions.explanation: Torsades de pointes, especially in a patient with alcohol use (predisposing to hypomagnesemia/hypokalemia), is treated with IV magnesium sulfate even if the measured level is normal; defibrillation is needed if the patient becomes pulseless or unstable.

questions.text: What is ventricular bigeminy?
options: A single isolated PVC occurring randomly
A repeating 1:1 pattern in which each normal conducted beat is followed by a PVC (normal beat-PVC-normal beat-PVC)
Two consecutive PVCs followed by a compensatory pause
originalOptions: A single isolated PVC occurring randomly
A repeating 1:1 pattern in which each normal conducted beat is followed by a PVC (normal beat-PVC-normal beat-PVC)
Two consecutive PVCs followed by a compensatory pause
questions.correctAnswer: C) A repeating 1:1 pattern in which each normal conducted beat is followed by a PVC (normal beat-PVC-normal beat-PVC)
questions.correctAnswerText: A repeating 1:1 pattern in which each normal conducted beat is followed by a PVC (normal beat-PVC-normal beat-PVC)
questions.explanation: Bigeminy describes the fixed alternating pattern of one sinus beat followed by one PVC, repeating throughout the rhythm strip.

questions.text: What is the underlying etiology of torsades de pointes?
options: Prolonged QT interval, congenital or acquired (e.g., QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, marked bradycardia)
Shortened PR interval with an accessory pathway
A macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid isthmus

A macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid isthmus
questions.correctAnswer: A) Prolonged QT interval, congenital or acquired (e.g., QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, marked bradycardia)
questions.correctAnswerText: Prolonged QT interval, congenital or acquired (e.g., QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, marked bradycardia)
questions.explanation: Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic VT that occurs in the setting of QT prolongation, commonly precipitated by electrolyte disturbances, certain drugs, or congenital long-QT syndromes.

questions.text: What is the first-line treatment for a drug-resistant, stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse that persists despite antiarrhythmic therapy?
options: Repeat the same antiarrhythmic at a higher dose indefinitely
originalOptions: Repeat the same antiarrhythmic at a higher dose indefinitely
questions.correctAnswer: D) Synchronized cardioversion with expert support
questions.explanation: Stable monomorphic VT that persists despite (or cannot receive) antiarrhythmic therapy should be electrically cardioverted (synchronized, since a pulse is present); unsynchronized shocks are reserved for pulseless or polymorphic VT.

questions.text: How many consecutive premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are required to define ventricular tachycardia?
options: A single PVC repeated every other beat
originalOptions: A single PVC repeated every other beat
questions.explanation: Three or more consecutive PVCs at a rate typically 140-240 bpm defines (non-sustained, if <30 seconds) ventricular tachycardia.

questions.explanation: Stable monomorphic VT with a pulse is initially managed with an antiarrhythmic infusion under expert guidance; synchronized cardioversion is reserved for if instability develops.

questions.text: Which of the following are recognized morphology-based classifications of ventricular tachycardia?
questions.explanation: VT is classified by QRS morphology into monomorphic (uniform beat-to-beat morphology), polymorphic (varying morphology, including torsades with QT prolongation),

questions.text: A patient has ventricular tachycardia with a heart rate of 300/min, blood pressure 94/78, and no chest pain. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassess perfusion carefully; if instability (e.g., a narrow pulse pressure suggesting poor perfusion) is present despite the absence of chest pain, perform synchronized cardioversion rather than relying on drug therapy
Lidocaine as sole therapy regardless of hemodynamic status

questions.explanation: A rate of 300/min with a narrow pulse pressure raises concern for inadequate perfusion despite the absence of chest pain; stability must be judged by the full clinical picture, not a single reassuring symptom.

questions.text: Which drugs must be avoided in a patient with WPW syndrome who develops atrial fibrillation?
options: Class III antiarrhythmics such as ibutilide
AV-nodal blocking agents (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
originalOptions: Class III antiarrhythmics such as ibutilide
AV-nodal blocking agents (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)

questions.correctAnswerText: AV-nodal blocking agents (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
questions.explanation: In pre-excited AF, AV-nodal blockers can preferentially block the AV node while accelerating conduction down the accessory pathway, risking degeneration into ventricular fibrillation; procainamide or cardioversion is used instead.

questions.text: What is a delta wave on ECG?
options: A notched, tall R wave in the inferior leads
A slurred initial upstroke of the QRS complex from early ventricular activation through an accessory pathway
A widened, deep S wave in the lateral leads
A biphasic P wave in lead V1

questions.correctAnswerText: A slurred initial upstroke of the QRS complex from early ventricular activation through an accessory pathway
questions.explanation: The delta wave reflects pre-excitation — early ventricular depolarization via an accessory pathway bypassing the AV node's normal conduction delay — and, with a short PR interval, is diagnostic of WPW.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia18.png ] What is the diagnostic ECG triad of Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation?
options: Prolonged PR interval, narrow QRS, and absent P waves
Sawtooth flutter waves with a fixed AV conduction ratio
Irregularly irregular rhythm with fibrillatory waves

questions.correctAnswerText: Short PR interval, a delta wave (slurred initial QRS upstroke), and a widened QRS complex
questions.explanation: The accessory pathway bypasses the AV node's conduction delay (short PR) and causes early, slurred ventricular depolarization (delta wave), widening the QRS complex.

questions.text: What is the primary risk associated with WPW syndrome?
options: Rapid antegrade accessory-pathway conduction during atrial fibrillation degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death
originalOptions: Rapid antegrade accessory-pathway conduction during atrial fibrillation degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death
questions.correctAnswer: C) Rapid antegrade accessory-pathway conduction during atrial fibrillation degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death
questions.correctAnswerText: Rapid antegrade accessory-pathway conduction during atrial fibrillation degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death
questions.explanation: In pre-excited AF, the accessory pathway can conduct extremely rapidly to the ventricles (unimpeded by AV-nodal delay), risking degeneration into VF — this is why AV-nodal blocking drugs are dangerous in this setting.

questions.text: How is a hemodynamically stable case of atrial fibrillation initially managed?
options: Assess duration, stroke risk, heart failure/LVEF, blood pressure, and pre-excitation; use appropriate ventricular rate control and an anticoagulation/rhythm strategy as indicated
Give amiodarone as a universal first-line agent regardless of other factors
Perform immediate cardioversion regardless of duration
Withhold all treatment until symptoms worsen

questions.correctAnswerText: Assess duration, stroke risk, heart failure/LVEF, blood pressure, and pre-excitation; use appropriate ventricular rate control and an anticoagulation/rhythm strategy as indicated
questions.explanation: Stable AF management is individualized based on AF duration, LVEF, stroke risk, and pre-excitation status; amiodarone is not a universal first-line choice.

questions.text: What are the ECG characteristics of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
options: A regular, uniform QRS morphology throughout
A rapid wide-complex tachycardia with continuously changing QRS morphology and axis, with torsades de pointes being the form associated with a prolonged QT
A narrow-complex tachycardia with absent P waves

A rapid wide-complex tachycardia with continuously changing QRS morphology and axis, with torsades de pointes being the form associated with a prolonged QT

questions.correctAnswer: B) A rapid wide-complex tachycardia with continuously changing QRS morphology and axis, with torsades de pointes being the form associated with a prolonged QT
questions.correctAnswerText: A rapid wide-complex tachycardia with continuously changing QRS morphology and axis, with torsades de pointes being the form associated with a prolonged QT
questions.explanation: Polymorphic VT shows beat-to-beat variation in QRS morphology/axis; when this occurs with QT prolongation, it is specifically termed torsades de pointes.

questions.text: What are the ECG characteristics of a premature ventricular complex (PVC)?
options: A narrow QRS preceded by an early, abnormal P wave
A regular rhythm with progressive PR prolongation

Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm

questions.explanation: PVCs arise from ventricular ectopic foci, producing an early, wide, bizarre QRS without a preceding P wave, and the post-ectopic pause creates the "skipped beat" sensation patients report.

questions.text: A 55-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolaemia, and known stable angina, presents with chest pain radiating to both arms. What ECG finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Stable angina is demand ischaemia on a fixed plaque without myocardial infarction, so the ECG and troponin are typically normal. Persistent ST depression suggests NSTE-ACS, ST elevation suggests STEMI or vasospasm, and Q waves indicate an old infarct.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognised life-threatening complication of acute coronary syndrome?
options: Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VF or pulseless VT)
Papillary-muscle rupture with acute severe mitral regurgitation
Ventricular free-wall rupture with cardiac tamponade
originalOptions: Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VF or pulseless VT)
Papillary-muscle rupture with acute severe mitral regurgitation
Ventricular free-wall rupture with cardiac tamponade
questions.explanation: ACS complications are electrical (VF, pulseless VT, high-grade AV block), pump failure (acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock), and mechanical (papillary-muscle rupture, septal rupture, free-wall rupture). Tension pneumothorax is not a complication of MI.

questions.text: What is the most clinically important adverse effect of nitroglycerin?
questions.explanation: Dose-related vasodilation causes hypotension, which is the most clinically important effect and can lead to syncope. Headache is very common but not dangerous, and reflex tachycardia is a secondary response.

questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with chest pain. She has a history of previous deep vein thrombosis and is not pregnant. Pulmonary embolism is suspected. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation: CTPA is the first-line confirmatory test for suspected PE in a non-pregnant patient with no contrast contraindication. V/Q scanning is preferred only in pregnancy, significant renal impairment, or contrast allergy, and CXR, ECG, and echocardiography cannot confirm PE.

questions.text: A patient presents with tearing chest pain and a difference in blood pressure between the two arms. What is the best initial medication?
questions.explanation: Tearing chest pain with an inter-arm BP difference indicates aortic dissection, which requires IV beta-blockade first (target heart rate 60–70 bpm, systolic BP 100–120 mmHg) to reduce aortic shear stress. Antiplatelets, anticoagulants, and thrombolytics are contraindicated, and a vasodilator is added only after heart-rate control.

questions.text: A diabetic patient presents with dyspnoea but no chest pain. Which diagnosis must NOT be missed?
questions.explanation: Diabetic patients, especially those with autonomic neuropathy, often present with silent or atypical ACS in which dyspnoea is the anginal equivalent. The other options are pain-predominant conditions and are not the critical diagnosis to exclude.

questions.text: An older farmer develops central chest pain while working. The pain subsides after a 10-minute rest and returns when he resumes work. His ECG and troponin are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Predictable exertional pain that is relieved by rest, with normal ECG and troponin, indicates stable angina (demand ischaemia on a fixed plaque with no infarction). Unstable angina presents with new, crescendo, or rest pain, and NSTEMI requires a troponin rise.

questions.text: A patient with confirmed STEMI is in an ambulance. A non-PCI hospital and a PCI-capable hospital are each about 15 minutes away. What is the best management?
options: Take him to the non-PCI hospital for fibrinolysis
Take him to the nearest hospital with CABG capacity
Take him to the nearest emergency department and wait for serial troponins
Transfer him directly to the PCI-capable hospital for primary PCI
Give fibrinolytics in the ambulance, then take him to the non-PCI hospital
originalOptions: Take him to the non-PCI hospital for fibrinolysis
Take him to the nearest hospital with CABG capacity
Take him to the nearest emergency department and wait for serial troponins
Transfer him directly to the PCI-capable hospital for primary PCI
Give fibrinolytics in the ambulance, then take him to the non-PCI hospital
questions.correctAnswer: D) Transfer him directly to the PCI-capable hospital for primary PCI
questions.correctAnswerText: Transfer him directly to the PCI-capable hospital for primary PCI
questions.explanation: Primary PCI is preferred when the anticipated first-medical-contact-to-device delay is 120 minutes or less, and the patient should not be detoured to a non-PCI hospital. Fibrinolysis is reserved for when the delay to PCI exceeds 120 minutes.

questions.text: What is the definitive reperfusion treatment for an eligible STEMI patient at a PCI-capable centre?
questions.explanation: In STEMI the goal is reperfusion, and primary PCI within 90 minutes of arrival is the preferred strategy at a PCI-capable centre. Fibrinolysis is used only when timely PCI is not available.

questions.text: An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. The most likely location of the myocardial infarction is: [img: ERChestInferiorMI.jpg ]
questions.explanation: ST elevation in II, III and aVF localises the infarct to the inferior wall (usually RCA), with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. Lateral infarcts involve I, aVL, V5–V6, anterior or septal infarcts involve V1–V4, and posterior MI shows reciprocal ST depression in V1–V2.

questions.text: Which of the following medications used in coronary artery disease relieves symptoms but has no proven effect on mortality or morbidity?
questions.explanation: Nitrates relieve angina through vasodilation but have not been shown to improve survival. Aspirin and statins reduce cardiovascular events in established CAD, and beta-blockers improve prognosis after MI.

questions.text: A patient has ischaemic chest pain. The ECG shows no ST-segment elevation (normal, ST depression, or T-wave inversion) and the troponin level is elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: NSTEMI is myocardial injury with a troponin rise without ST elevation. Unstable angina has a normal troponin, and STEMI requires ST elevation or hyperacute T waves.

questions.text: Chest pain radiating to the jaw and relieved by sitting forward is most likely due to:
questions.explanation: Pericarditis pain is classically worse when lying supine and relieved by sitting forward, and may radiate to the neck, back, or jaw. Stable angina is exertional and relieved by rest or GTN, not by posture.

questions.text: Chest pain that is reproducible on palpation of the chest wall most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Pain reproduced by chest-wall palpation points to a musculoskeletal cause and lowers the probability of ACS (LR ≈ 0.3). It does not exclude ACS on its own, since about 15% of ACS patients also have chest-wall tenderness.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the three types of angina?
options: All three types have a raised troponin from myocardial necrosis and differ only in the duration of pain
Stable angina: rest pain with transient ST elevation; unstable angina: predictable exertional pain; vasospastic angina: pain with a troponin rise
Stable angina: rest pain from plaque rupture; unstable angina: exertional pain relieved by rest; vasospastic angina: exertional pain treated first-line with beta-blockers
Unstable angina differs from stable angina by a raised troponin, and vasospastic angina is treated first-line with beta-blockers

Stable angina: predictable exertional pain relieved by rest or GTN; unstable angina: new, crescendo, or rest pain without troponin rise; vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina: episodic rest pain from coronary spasm with transient ST elevation

Stable angina: rest pain from plaque rupture; unstable angina: exertional pain relieved by rest; vasospastic angina: exertional pain treated first-line with beta-blockers

questions.correctAnswerText: Stable angina: predictable exertional pain relieved by rest or GTN; unstable angina: new, crescendo, or rest pain without troponin rise; vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina: episodic rest pain from coronary spasm with transient ST elevation
questions.explanation: Stable angina is demand ischaemia on a fixed plaque, and unstable angina is plaque rupture with partial thrombosis but a normal troponin; a troponin rise defines NSTEMI. Vasospastic angina is treated with calcium channel blockers or nitrates, and beta-blockers are generally avoided.

questions.text: All of the following are life-threatening causes of chest pain EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Costochondritis is a benign musculoskeletal cause of chest pain. Aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, PE, and oesophageal rupture are all immediately life-threatening.

questions.text: In a patient with suspected acute myocardial infarction, which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: Treatment should be delayed until cardiac biomarker results are available
An ECG should be performed immediately (within 10 minutes of arrival)
Aspirin should be given as soon as MI is suspected
Serial ECGs should be compared rather than relying on a single tracing
originalOptions: Treatment should be delayed until cardiac biomarker results are available
An ECG should be performed immediately (within 10 minutes of arrival)
Aspirin should be given as soon as MI is suspected
Serial ECGs should be compared rather than relying on a single tracing
questions.correctAnswer: A) Treatment should be delayed until cardiac biomarker results are available
questions.correctAnswerText: Treatment should be delayed until cardiac biomarker results are available
questions.explanation: STEMI is diagnosed from the ECG, and reperfusion must not wait for troponin or other enzyme results, because time is muscle. Biomarkers are sent in parallel with treatment, not before it.

questions.text: A patient with a previous history of myocardial infarction attends the cardiology clinic for a routine check-up. He is asymptomatic, and his ECG is shown. What is the most appropriate management? [img: ERChestnoacutetherapy.png ]
questions.explanation: A fixed PR interval above 200 ms with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV block, which is benign and needs no treatment when asymptomatic. Pacing is reserved for symptomatic bradycardia, asymptomatic Mobitz II, or complete heart block.

questions.text: What is abdominal angina, and what is its classic presentation?
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia with sudden severe pain out of proportion to the examination
Chronic mesenteric ischaemia with postprandial pain, food fear (sitophobia), and weight loss
Mesenteric venous thrombosis in hypercoagulable states
originalOptions: Acute mesenteric ischaemia with sudden severe pain out of proportion to the examination
Chronic mesenteric ischaemia with postprandial pain, food fear (sitophobia), and weight loss
Mesenteric venous thrombosis in hypercoagulable states
questions.correctAnswer: B) Chronic mesenteric ischaemia with postprandial pain, food fear (sitophobia), and weight loss
questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia with postprandial pain, food fear (sitophobia), and weight loss
questions.explanation: Abdominal angina is the gut equivalent of cardiac angina: atherosclerotic mesenteric stenosis cannot meet the increased demand after a meal. Acute mesenteric ischaemia instead presents with sudden, severe pain out of proportion to the examination.

questions.text: A patient presents with sudden-onset tearing chest pain radiating to the back. This is classically associated with:
questions.explanation: Aortic dissection typically causes abrupt, severe tearing pain that is maximal at onset and radiates to the back. Myocardial infarction causes pressure-like pain that builds more gradually, and pericarditis pain is positional.

questions.text: What is the most common initiating event of acute coronary syndrome?
options: Fixed atherosclerotic stenosis with demand ischaemia
Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with superimposed thrombosis
Aortic dissection extending into the coronary ostium
originalOptions: Fixed atherosclerotic stenosis with demand ischaemia
Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with superimposed thrombosis
Aortic dissection extending into the coronary ostium
questions.correctAnswer: C) Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with superimposed thrombosis
questions.correctAnswerText: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with superimposed thrombosis
questions.explanation: ACS results from plaque rupture (less commonly erosion) followed by platelet activation and thrombus formation, causing partial or complete vessel occlusion. Fixed-plaque demand ischaemia causes stable angina, and spasm causes Prinzmetal angina.

questions.text: A patient with a tachyarrhythmia (ECG shown) has hypotension and ischaemic chest discomfort. What is the immediate treatment? [img: ERChestisc.png ]
options: Immediate synchronised cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying treatment
originalOptions: Immediate synchronised cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying treatment
questions.correctAnswer: A) Immediate synchronised cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying treatment
questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate synchronised cardioversion, with sedation if feasible without delaying treatment
questions.explanation: This is Atrial Fibrillation. Hypotension and ischaemic chest pain are unstable features, so an unstable tachyarrhythmia requires immediate synchronised cardioversion. Drug therapy and vagal manoeuvres are for haemodynamically stable patients.

questions.text: An ECG shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment? [img: ERChestacutepericarditis.png ]
options: An NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) or aspirin, plus colchicine
originalOptions: An NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) or aspirin, plus colchicine
questions.correctAnswer: D) An NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) or aspirin, plus colchicine
questions.correctAnswerText: An NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) or aspirin, plus colchicine
questions.explanation: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression indicates acute pericarditis, treated with an NSAID plus colchicine (aspirin is preferred after MI), which reduces symptom duration and recurrence. Reperfusion is for STEMI with regional convex elevation and reciprocal changes, and corticosteroids are second-line.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional 8 D's of stroke care?
questions.explanation: The 8 D's are Detection, Dispatch, Delivery, Door, Data, Decision, Drug (or device), and Disposition. Defibrillation belongs to cardiac arrest care, not stroke care.

questions.text: Nitroglycerin should be avoided or used with extreme caution in all of the following situations EXCEPT:
options: Tadalafil use within the past 48 hours
Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
originalOptions: Tadalafil use within the past 48 hours
Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
questions.correctAnswer: E) Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
questions.correctAnswerText: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
questions.explanation: Nitrates are indicated for ongoing angina when blood pressure permits. They cause severe hypotension in preload-dependent states (RV infarction, severe aortic stenosis), in baseline hypotension, and after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours).

questions.text: A patient with STEMI has been referred for primary PCI and the catheterisation laboratory is activated. Which medication regimen should be started while preparing for PCI?
options: Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
originalOptions: Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
questions.correctAnswer: C) Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
questions.correctAnswerText: Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
questions.explanation: Aspirin is given immediately, with clopidogrel whenever PCI is planned and initial anticoagulation with heparin or LMWH, along with a high-intensity statin. Warfarin is not an acute anticoagulant in ACS, and nitrates, morphine, and oxygen are given only for specific indications.

questions.text: Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression is seen in:
questions.explanation: Pericarditis causes diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression (and PR elevation in aVR). Tamponade shows low-voltage QRS and electrical alternans, and benign early repolarisation lacks PR depression and is stable on serial ECGs.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most common ECG finding in acute pulmonary embolism?
questions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. S1Q3T3 is classic but rare, and RBBB, right axis deviation, and P pulmonale are less common, non-specific findings.

questions.text: What is the key chest X-ray finding in acute aortic dissection?
options: Visceral pleural line with absent lung markings
originalOptions: Visceral pleural line with absent lung markings
questions.explanation: A widened mediastinum with an abnormal aortic contour is the classic radiographic finding in aortic dissection, although a normal CXR never excludes it and CT aortography is the diagnostic study. A water-bottle silhouette indicates a large pericardial effusion.

questions.text: A patient with diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolaemia presents with ischaemic chest pain, and the ECG shows lateral T-wave inversions. What is the best next step?
options: Discharge with an outpatient stress test
Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
originalOptions: Discharge with an outpatient stress test
Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
questions.correctAnswer: E) Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
questions.correctAnswerText: Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
questions.explanation: T-wave inversion without ST elevation suggests NSTE-ACS, which is managed with monitoring, aspirin, anti-ischaemic therapy, and serial ECG and troponin with risk stratification (e.g. HEART or TIMI score). Fibrinolysis is indicated only for STEMI, and the timing of invasive management depends on risk.

questions.text: Which leads primarily represent the anterior wall of the left ventricle?
questions.explanation: V3–V4 overlie the anterior wall (LAD territory), V1–V2 the septum, and V5–V6 and I/aVL the lateral wall. V1–V4 together are often described as the anteroseptal/anterior territory.

questions.text: Which myocardial territory is involved when ST elevation is seen in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5 and V6)? [img: ERChestlateralwall.png ]
questions.explanation: Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 face the lateral wall (circumflex or diagonal/LAD territory), and extension of the changes through V3–V6 is described as anterolateral. The inferior wall is represented by II, III and aVF, and posterior infarction appears as reciprocal ST depression in V1–V2.

questions.text: Which medication should be avoided in inferior myocardial infarction because of possible right ventricular infarction and preload dependence?
questions.explanation: Nitrates reduce preload, which can cause severe hypotension and even arrest in a preload-dependent RV infarction (confirmed by ST elevation in V4R) and after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use. Aspirin and antiplatelet therapy remain indicated, and oxygen is given only when SpO₂ is below 95%.

questions.text: How is a posterior myocardial infarction recognised on the standard 12-lead ECG, and how is it best confirmed?
options: ST elevation in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
ST elevation in II, III and aVF, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
Pathological Q waves in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V3R–V4R)
ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6, confirmed by posterior leads V7–V9
originalOptions: ST elevation in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
ST elevation in II, III and aVF, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
Pathological Q waves in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V3R–V4R)
ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6, confirmed by posterior leads V7–V9
questions.correctAnswer: B) ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
questions.correctAnswerText: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
questions.explanation: Posterior MI appears on the standard ECG only as reciprocal changes in V1–V3, and ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9 gives direct confirmation. Right-sided leads (V4R) are used to confirm right ventricular infarction.

questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolytic therapy in ACS?
options: Ischaemic stroke more than 3 months ago
originalOptions: Ischaemic stroke more than 3 months ago
questions.explanation: Fibrinolysis can precipitate catastrophic bleeding in suspected aortic dissection, so it is an absolute contraindication. Pregnancy, current anticoagulant use, and an ischaemic stroke more than 3 months ago are relative contraindications.

questions.text: Which of the following patients meets the criteria for fibrinolytic therapy?
options: A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
A patient with STEMI who presents directly to a PCI-capable centre with an expected door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes
originalOptions: A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
A patient with STEMI who presents directly to a PCI-capable centre with an expected door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes
questions.correctAnswer: C) A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
questions.correctAnswerText: A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
questions.explanation: Fibrinolysis is indicated for STEMI (≥1 mm ST elevation in two contiguous leads) within the time window when timely PCI is not available. It is not used for NSTEMI or unstable angina, and primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered promptly.

questions.text: A patient with STEMI arrived at a non-PCI hospital 30 minutes ago. The nearest PCI-capable centre is 45 minutes away, and the decision is made to transfer him for PCI. What is the maximum acceptable time from first medical contact to PCI?
questions.explanation: When the patient presents to a non-PCI hospital, transfer for primary PCI is appropriate if the first-medical-contact-to-device time is 120 minutes or less; beyond that, fibrinolysis should be given. The 90-minute target applies only to direct presentation to a PCI-capable hospital.

questions.text: What is the target door-to-balloon time for a patient presenting directly to a PCI-capable hospital?
questions.explanation: The door-to-balloon target for primary PCI is within 90 minutes of arrival. Thirty minutes is the door-to-needle target for fibrinolysis, and 120 minutes is the first-medical-contact-to-device threshold used in transfer decisions.

questions.text: A haemodynamically stable asthmatic patient has atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response and no heart failure (ECG shown). What is the most appropriate first treatment? [img: ERChestdiltiazem.png ]
questions.explanation: Stable AF is managed with rate control, and a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is preferred in asthma because beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm. Cardioversion is for unstable patients, adenosine is for regular narrow-complex SVT, and amiodarone is reserved for AF with reduced ejection fraction (EF < 40%).

questions.text: Which leads are used for rapid ECG-axis determination?
questions.explanation: Leads I and aVF divide the frontal plane into quadrants (I positive and aVF positive = normal axis; I positive and aVF negative = leftward axis; I negative and aVF positive = right axis). Lead II is used to resolve borderline left axis deviation.

questions.text: How many large squares are there in 1 second of an ECG tracing at the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s?
questions.explanation: One large square equals 0.20 s, so 1 second contains 5 large squares (25 mm). A small square equals 0.04 s.

questions.text: What is the heart rate on the regular ECG strip shown, in which each R–R interval spans two large squares? [img: ERECG150beats.png ]
questions.explanation: Heart rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares between consecutive R waves = 300 ÷ 2 = 150 beats/min.

questions.text: How many large squares are there in 1 minute of ECG tracing?
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, 1 second contains 5 large squares, so 1 minute contains 5 × 60 = 300. This is the basis of the 300 rule for heart rate.

questions.text: How many small squares are there in 1 minute of ECG tracing?
questions.explanation: One small square equals 0.04 s, so 60 ÷ 0.04 = 1500. This is the basis of the 1500 rule for precise rate calculation.

questions.text: How many small squares correspond to 1 mV of amplitude on a standard ECG?
questions.explanation: The standard calibration is 10 mm/mV, and each small square (1 mm) equals 0.1 mV, so 10 small squares equal 1 mV.

questions.text: Which method is used to calculate the heart rate from a regular rhythm on an ECG?
options: 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
1500 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
300 divided by the number of small squares between consecutive R waves
The number of QRS complexes in one large square multiplied by 300
The R–R interval in seconds multiplied by 60
originalOptions: 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
1500 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
300 divided by the number of small squares between consecutive R waves
The number of QRS complexes in one large square multiplied by 300
The R–R interval in seconds multiplied by 60
questions.correctAnswer: A) 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
questions.correctAnswerText: 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
questions.explanation: The 300 rule applies to regular rhythms. The 1500 rule requires small squares (1500 ÷ small squares), and the heart rate is 60 divided by the R–R interval in seconds, not multiplied by it.

questions.text: Calculate the ventricular rate on the regular ECG strip shown. [img: ERECG180beats.png ]
questions.explanation: An R–R interval of about 1.7 large squares gives 300 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 180 beats/min using the 300 rule.

questions.text: What ECG findings define right bundle branch block? [img: ERECGRBBB.png ]
options: QRS ≥120 ms with broad notched R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6 and a deep S wave in V1
QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with an rSR′ pattern in V1 and normal terminal forces
Short PR interval with a delta wave and a widened QRS
Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves
originalOptions: QRS ≥120 ms with broad notched R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6 and a deep S wave in V1
QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with an rSR′ pattern in V1 and normal terminal forces
Short PR interval with a delta wave and a widened QRS
Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves
questions.correctAnswer: B) QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
questions.correctAnswerText: QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
questions.explanation: RBBB requires a QRS ≥120 ms with late right-ventricular forces (rsR′ in V1–V2) and a broad terminal S wave in the left-sided leads. Option C describes incomplete RBBB, and option A describes LBBB.

questions.text: What diagnostic difficulties can arise when a patient has LBBB on the ECG?
options: It abolishes P waves, preventing rhythm interpretation
It shortens the PR interval and mimics pre-excitation
It produces diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, mimicking pericarditis
It produces a dominant R wave in V1, mimicking posterior MI
It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
originalOptions: It abolishes P waves, preventing rhythm interpretation
It shortens the PR interval and mimics pre-excitation
It produces diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, mimicking pericarditis
It produces a dominant R wave in V1, mimicking posterior MI
It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
questions.correctAnswer: E) It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
questions.correctAnswerText: It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
questions.explanation: LBBB alters ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation, so ischaemic ST changes are hard to interpret. Clinical context, serial biomarkers, and validated criteria such as modified Sgarbossa are used, and a new LBBB with chest pain is managed as a STEMI equivalent.

questions.text: Which set of ECG findings supports the diagnosis of right ventricular hypertrophy?
options: Sokolow-Lyon voltage ≥35 mm with left axis deviation and lateral strain pattern
Left axis deviation with deep S waves in V1 and tall R waves in V5–V6
Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
Tall R wave in aVL with ST depression and T-wave inversion in I and aVL
Pathological Q waves in V1–V4 with ST elevation
originalOptions: Sokolow-Lyon voltage ≥35 mm with left axis deviation and lateral strain pattern
Left axis deviation with deep S waves in V1 and tall R waves in V5–V6
Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
Tall R wave in aVL with ST depression and T-wave inversion in I and aVL
Pathological Q waves in V1–V4 with ST elevation
questions.correctAnswer: C) Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
questions.correctAnswerText: Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
questions.explanation: RVH is recognised by right axis deviation and a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S >1), often with a right ventricular strain pattern. Option A describes LVH.

questions.text: What are the ECG characteristics of left bundle branch block?
options: QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
QRS ≥120 ms; rSR′ pattern in V1; broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with a delta wave and short PR interval
QRS ≥120 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm
Narrow QRS with a tall R wave in V1 and ST depression in V1–V3
originalOptions: QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
QRS ≥120 ms; rSR′ pattern in V1; broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with a delta wave and short PR interval
QRS ≥120 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm
Narrow QRS with a tall R wave in V1 and ST depression in V1–V3
questions.correctAnswer: A) QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
questions.correctAnswerText: QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
questions.explanation: LBBB shows a broad monophasic or notched R wave in the lateral leads and a deep QS or rS in V1–V3, with ST–T changes opposite to the QRS direction. Option B describes RBBB, and option D describes TCA toxicity.

questions.text: A patient with chest pain has a normal ECG and elevated cardiac troponin. This most likely suggests:
questions.explanation: NSTEMI is myocardial infarction with a raised troponin and no ST elevation (the ECG may be normal, or show T inversion or ST depression). Unstable angina is the closest alternative, but its troponin is normal.

questions.text: A patient with suspected inferior MI has ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF and in lead V4R. Which drug is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: ST elevation in V4R indicates right ventricular infarction, which is preload-dependent, so nitrates can cause profound hypotension. Nitrates are also contraindicated after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.

questions.text: A patient has an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: An unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse requires immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if feasible. Adenosine is for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, and unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless VT or VF.

questions.text: What rhythm is shown on the ECG strip? [img: ERECGMAT.png ]
questions.explanation: MAT is an irregular tachycardia with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and variable PR intervals. Atrial fibrillation is the closest alternative, but it has no discernible P waves.

questions.text: The ECG shows constant PR intervals with intermittent non-conducted P waves and dropped QRS complexes. What is the diagnosis? [img: ERECGsecAVblockM2.png ]
options: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
originalOptions: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
questions.correctAnswer: A) Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
questions.correctAnswerText: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
questions.explanation: A constant PR interval before a suddenly dropped QRS defines Mobitz II. Mobitz I shows progressive PR lengthening before the dropped beat.

questions.text: An ECG shows diffuse concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation in all leads. What is the diagnosis and treatment? [img: ERECGpericarditis.png ]
questions.explanation: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression that does not follow a coronary territory indicates pericarditis, treated with an NSAID plus colchicine. STEMI shows convex elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal depression.

questions.text: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF indicates infarction of which wall?
questions.explanation: Leads II, III, and aVF face the inferior wall of the left ventricle, typically supplied by the right coronary artery.

questions.text: A haemodynamically stable patient has a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia (ventricular tachycardia). Which treatment is most appropriate? [img: ERECGamiodarone.png ]
questions.explanation: Stable monomorphic VT is treated with IV antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, procainamide, lidocaine, or sotalol). Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for unstable VT, and defibrillation for pulseless VT.

questions.text: Which of the following describes the ECG characteristics of sinus arrhythmia?
options: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves
Inverted P waves before every QRS with a shortened PR interval
Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
Progressive PR lengthening with intermittently dropped QRS complexes
Regular P–P intervals with variable QRS morphology
originalOptions: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves
Inverted P waves before every QRS with a shortened PR interval
Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
Progressive PR lengthening with intermittently dropped QRS complexes
Regular P–P intervals with variable QRS morphology
questions.correctAnswer: C) Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
questions.correctAnswerText: Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
questions.explanation: In sinus arrhythmia the P, QRS, and T morphology is normal and only the R–R timing varies, rising with inspiration and falling with expiration. Non-respiratory variation suggests pathology.

questions.text: Which characteristic ST-segment morphology is seen with digoxin effect?
options: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Osborn waves at the J point
Peaked T waves with a widened QRS
originalOptions: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Osborn waves at the J point
Peaked T waves with a widened QRS
questions.explanation: Digoxin effect produces a scooped ST depression ("reverse tick") with a shortened QT, and is a benign finding at therapeutic levels. Digoxin toxicity instead causes arrhythmias.

questions.text: A report states "possible left axis deviation" (lead I positive, aVF negative). Which finding confirms true left axis deviation?
questions.explanation: When lead I is positive and aVF is negative, a negative lead II confirms true left axis deviation (about −30° to −90°). A positive lead II means the axis is borderline and may still be normal.

questions.text: Which ECG findings suggest an early repolarization pattern?
options: Convex ST elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression and evolving Q waves
J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a pseudo-RBBB pattern
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Scooped ST depression with a shortened QT interval
originalOptions: Convex ST elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression and evolving Q waves
J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a pseudo-RBBB pattern
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Scooped ST depression with a shortened QT interval
questions.correctAnswer: B) J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
questions.correctAnswerText: J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
questions.explanation: Early repolarization is a benign pattern, most common in young males and athletes, that is stable on serial ECGs. Pericarditis is the closest alternative, but it shows PR depression and diffuse changes.

questions.text: A patient has first-degree heart block on ECG (PR >200 ms, all P waves conducted). What is the immediate management?
questions.explanation: First-degree AV block is a benign finding in which every impulse is conducted, so no treatment is needed unless it is symptomatic or drug-induced.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a pathological Q wave?
options: Depth >25% of the following R-wave amplitude
originalOptions: Depth >25% of the following R-wave amplitude
questions.explanation: A pathological Q wave is ≥40 ms wide and deeper than 25% of the R wave. A Q wave narrower than 40 ms is physiological, and any Q wave in V1–V4 is considered pathological.

questions.text: All of the following shorten the QT interval EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism prolongs the QT interval (via bradycardia). Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, and increased sympathetic tone (fever, hyperthyroidism) shorten it.

questions.text: An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AF shows chaotic atrial activity with no P waves, a fibrillatory baseline, and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. MAT is also irregular, but it has at least three distinct P-wave morphologies.

questions.text: Which option correctly defines a pathological Q wave and lists conditions that can produce pseudoinfarction Q waves?
options: Width <40 ms and depth <25% of the R wave; causes: MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms only; causes: hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, digoxin effect, cardiac tamponade
Depth ≥2 mm in leads III and aVR only; causes: PE, pericarditis, early repolarization, Brugada syndrome
Width <40 ms and depth >50% of the R wave; causes: hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, TCA toxicity
originalOptions: Width <40 ms and depth <25% of the R wave; causes: MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms only; causes: hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, digoxin effect, cardiac tamponade
Depth ≥2 mm in leads III and aVR only; causes: PE, pericarditis, early repolarization, Brugada syndrome
Width <40 ms and depth >50% of the R wave; causes: hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, TCA toxicity
questions.correctAnswer: B) Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
questions.correctAnswerText: Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
questions.explanation: Pathological Q waves represent myocardial scar. Pseudoinfarction Q waves occur in WPW (negative delta wave), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB, severe LVH, and acute myocarditis.

questions.text: Which group of conditions causes shortening of the QT interval?
options: Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics, ondansetron
Hypothyroidism, bradycardia, raised ICP, myocardial ischaemia
Congenital long QT syndrome, hypomagnesaemia, tricyclic antidepressants
Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
originalOptions: Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics, ondansetron
Hypothyroidism, bradycardia, raised ICP, myocardial ischaemia
Congenital long QT syndrome, hypomagnesaemia, tricyclic antidepressants
Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
questions.correctAnswer: E) Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
questions.explanation: These conditions shorten repolarisation. The other options list classic causes of QT prolongation (electrolyte depletion, drugs, and bradycardic states).

questions.text: P mitrale (a broad, notched P wave >0.12 s in lead II) is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: P mitrale reflects left atrial enlargement, as in mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, or left heart failure. COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension cause the tall peaked P pulmonale instead.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognised cause of poor R-wave progression across the precordial leads?
questions.explanation: Loss of anterior forces from anteroseptal infarction (also LVH, LBBB, COPD, and lead misplacement) impairs R-wave progression. Posterior MI, left-sided WPW, RBBB, and the paediatric variant produce tall R waves in V1.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognised cause of a tall R wave in V1?
questions.explanation: Posterior infarction produces a tall R wave in V1–V2 as the mirror image of posterior Q waves. Other causes are RVH, RBBB, left-sided WPW, and dextrocardia. The other options cause poor R-wave progression or deep S waves in V1.

questions.text: An ECG shows both a tall peaked P wave and a broad notched P wave. Which chamber-enlargement pattern does this suggest?
questions.explanation: The tall peaked component reflects right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale) and the broad notched component reflects left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), so both atria are enlarged.

questions.text: What are the normal duration and amplitude of the P wave on ECG?
options: <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
originalOptions: <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
questions.correctAnswer: E) <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
questions.correctAnswerText: <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
questions.explanation: A normal P wave is shorter than 120 ms and lower than 2.5 mm in the limb leads. A longer P wave suggests left atrial enlargement, and a taller one suggests right atrial enlargement.

questions.text: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, what defines a narrow and a wide QRS complex?
options: Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
originalOptions: Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
questions.correctAnswer: C) Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
questions.correctAnswerText: Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
questions.explanation: A QRS of 120 ms or more is wide, suggesting a ventricular origin, bundle branch block, or pre-excitation.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of QT prolongation?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT interval. Hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and hypothermia prolong it, as do many drugs.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognised cause of left axis deviation?
questions.explanation: Left axis deviation (lead I positive, aVF negative) occurs with left anterior fascicular block, LVH, inferior MI, and ventricular pacing. The other options cause right axis deviation.

questions.text: In which limb lead are the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave normally predominantly negative?
questions.explanation: Lead aVR looks at the heart from the right shoulder, opposite to the normal direction of depolarisation, so all its waves are normally negative.

questions.text: When can the normally negative complexes in lead aVR become predominantly positive?
questions.correctAnswer: E) Dextrocardia or right-arm/left-arm limb-lead reversal
questions.explanation: Both conditions invert the normal limb-lead vectors. They are distinguished by precordial R-wave progression, which is lost in dextrocardia and normal in limb-lead reversal.

questions.text: Which is NOT a component of the FAST stroke recognition tool?
questions.explanation: FAST consists of Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call emergency services. Seizures can accompany stroke but are not a recognition sign in this tool.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute dysarthria suggestive of stroke, with no available medical history. Which immediate bedside test must not be missed?
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia can mimic acute stroke and is rapidly correctable, so glucose is checked first. The stroke pathway (last-known-well time, urgent brain imaging) proceeds in parallel.

questions.text: A stroke patient presents with intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus, ataxia, and a contralateral motor deficit. Which arterial territory is affected?
questions.explanation: Cerebellar and brainstem signs (intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus, ataxia) with a contralateral motor deficit localise to the posterior circulation. MCA strokes produce contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia or neglect, not cerebellar signs.

questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to IV thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke?
options: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
originalOptions: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
questions.correctAnswer: B) Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
questions.correctAnswerText: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
questions.explanation: Ischaemic stroke or serious head trauma within the last 3 months is an absolute exclusion. Recent major surgery, pregnancy, seizure at onset, and minor or rapidly improving symptoms are relative considerations.

questions.text: Which standardized tool is used for the clinical neurological assessment of stroke severity in the Emergency Department?
questions.explanation: The NIHSS quantifies stroke deficits and is the standard severity assessment in the stroke team pathway. The Cincinnati scale is a prehospital recognition tool (face, arm, speech), and the GCS and AVPU assess conscious level only.

questions.text: All of the following are relative exclusion criteria for IV thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke EXCEPT:
