options: Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
originalOptions: Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
questions.explanation: Platelets < 100,000/µL (like INR > 1.7 and therapeutic anticoagulation) is an absolute exclusion. The other options are relative exclusions.

questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) therapy in acute ischaemic stroke?
questions.explanation: Severe uncontrolled hypertension (classically ≥ 185/110 mmHg despite treatment) is an exclusion. The other options are within the treatment window or are normal findings.

questions.text: All of the following are contraindications to thrombolysis in acute stroke EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The platelet exclusion threshold is < 100,000/µL, so a count between 100,000 and 150,000 is not a contraindication. Onset 5 hours ago is outside the standard window, INR > 1.7 and active bleeding are exclusions, and a stroke within 3 months is an absolute exclusion.

questions.text: A patient with acute stroke has a large established multilobar infarct on brain imaging. How does this finding affect eligibility for IV thrombolysis?
options: It is an absolute contraindication in all cases
It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
It is an indication to give a double dose of the thrombolytic
It has no effect on thrombolysis decisions
It mandates repeat CT at 24 hours before any treatment
originalOptions: It is an absolute contraindication in all cases
It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
It is an indication to give a double dose of the thrombolytic
It has no effect on thrombolysis decisions
It mandates repeat CT at 24 hours before any treatment
questions.correctAnswer: B) It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
questions.correctAnswerText: It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
questions.explanation: A large established infarct increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation. In current practice it is treated as a relative caution rather than a fixed stand-alone exclusion.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the "D"s of stroke care?
questions.explanation: The 8 D's are Detection, Dispatch, Delivery, Door, Data, Decision, Drug (or device), and Disposition. Defibrillation belongs to arrest management, not the stroke chain.

questions.text: A patient has isolated left-hand weakness with pronator drift and no sensory loss. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Isolated contralateral weakness with pronator drift and intact sensation indicates a lesion of the motor cortex or corticospinal pathway, here on the right. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia and incoordination rather than weakness, and parietal lesions cause sensory deficits.

questions.text: Which of the following arteries is NOT part of the circle of Willis?
questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries unite to form the basilar artery and supply the circle only indirectly, so they are feeding vessels rather than components of the ring. The ring is formed by the internal carotid, anterior and posterior cerebral, and the anterior and posterior communicating arteries.

questions.text: A patient with diabetes and hypertension presents with vertigo, double vision, and difficulty speaking. The symptoms resolve within 1–2 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis and affected vessel?
questions.explanation: Vertigo, diplopia, and dysarthria point to posterior-circulation ischaemia, and complete resolution within a short window defines a TIA. MCA events cause contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia, or neglect.

questions.text: A patient presents with thunderclap headache, photophobia, vomiting, neck stiffness, and blood pressure 190/110 mmHg. Subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected and urgent non-contrast CT head is arranged. Which listed IV agent is appropriate if controlled blood-pressure reduction is required?
questions.explanation: Nicardipine is the preferred titratable IV antihypertensive in SAH, allowing controlled reduction while avoiding hypotension. Ceftriaxone treats meningitis, and ketorolac, platelets, and vitamin K have no role in blood-pressure control.

questions.text: A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presents with sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and nausea. What is the most important immediate step in the Emergency Department?
questions.explanation: Connective tissue disease raises the risk of aneurysmal rupture and arterial dissection, so sudden severe headache is treated as SAH until proven otherwise. After ABC stabilisation, urgent non-contrast CT is highly sensitive in the first 6 hours, and LP is reserved for a negative CT with persistent suspicion.

questions.text: A woman presents with headache. Which of the following is the correct match?
options: Unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation – Tension-type headache
originalOptions: Unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation – Tension-type headache
questions.explanation: Meningism from blood irritating the meninges accompanies SAH, usually with thunderclap onset. Band-like pain is tension-type, periorbital pain with lacrimation is cluster, and early-morning headache suggests raised intracranial pressure.

questions.text: Can severe hyperglycaemia (above 300 mg/dL) cause a decreased level of consciousness?
options: Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
No, only hypoglycaemia lowers the level of consciousness
No, it affects consciousness only in non-diabetic patients
Yes, but only through direct neuronal toxicity of glucose
No, unless the glucose exceeds 1,000 mg/dL
originalOptions: Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
No, only hypoglycaemia lowers the level of consciousness
No, it affects consciousness only in non-diabetic patients
Yes, but only through direct neuronal toxicity of glucose
No, unless the glucose exceeds 1,000 mg/dL
questions.correctAnswer: A) Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
questions.correctAnswerText: Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
questions.explanation: Severe hyperglycaemia impairs consciousness through hyperosmolar dehydration or DKA, where acidosis disrupts neuronal metabolism. Hyperglycaemia is therefore a recognised cause of altered mental status.

questions.text: Which of the following diseases is NOT among those that must be reported immediately to health authorities?
questions.explanation: Cholera, plague, poliomyelitis, and yellow fever are the classic immediately reportable diseases. Meningitis is not part of this group (national notification lists may vary).

questions.text: A patient has a brief, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by complete spontaneous recovery without a persistent neurological deficit. What is this event called?
questions.explanation: TLOC is a spontaneous, self-limited loss of awareness and postural tone with prompt, complete recovery. It is termed syncope when caused by transient global cerebral hypoperfusion. Coma is prolonged unarousable unresponsiveness, typically more than 1 hour.

questions.text: A person collapses after prolonged standing in a hot, crowded environment. What is the likely diagnosis and initial management?
options: Drug-induced orthostatic hypotension – IV vasopressor infusion
Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
originalOptions: Drug-induced orthostatic hypotension – IV vasopressor infusion
Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
questions.correctAnswer: E) Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
questions.correctAnswerText: Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
questions.explanation: Prolonged standing and a hot, crowded setting are typical orthostatic triggers of reflex (vasovagal) syncope. Management is supportive: lay the patient supine, elevate the legs, assess ABCs and glucose, and exclude dangerous causes.

questions.text: Which of the following best defines a Stokes-Adams attack?
options: A gradual faint after prolonged standing, preceded by pallor and nausea
Exertional syncope from fixed outflow obstruction in severe aortic stenosis
Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
Loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic movements and prolonged post-ictal confusion
Fainting during or immediately after micturition
originalOptions: A gradual faint after prolonged standing, preceded by pallor and nausea
Exertional syncope from fixed outflow obstruction in severe aortic stenosis
Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
Loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic movements and prolonged post-ictal confusion
Fainting during or immediately after micturition
questions.correctAnswer: C) Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
questions.correctAnswerText: Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
questions.explanation: A transient, severe bradyarrhythmia causes abrupt cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid recovery, and the lack of a prodrome distinguishes it from vasovagal syncope. A gradual faint with pallor and nausea is vasovagal, and prolonged post-ictal confusion indicates seizure.

questions.text: A patient faints during or immediately after urination. What is the likely diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
Orthostatic hypotension – inadequate preload from volume depletion
originalOptions: Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
Orthostatic hypotension – inadequate preload from volume depletion
questions.correctAnswer: A) Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
questions.correctAnswerText: Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
questions.explanation: Fainting that is temporally linked to voiding is a situational reflex syncope. Vagal activation lowers vascular resistance and venous return, producing cerebral hypoperfusion.

questions.text: What is reflex (neurally mediated) syncope, and what are its main subtypes?
options: Syncope from an arrhythmia; subtypes are bradyarrhythmic and tachyarrhythmic
Syncope from volume depletion, drugs, or autonomic failure on standing
Syncope from brainstem ischaemia; subtypes are vertebral and basilar
Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
Syncope from mechanical obstruction such as massive PE or aortic dissection
originalOptions: Syncope from an arrhythmia; subtypes are bradyarrhythmic and tachyarrhythmic
Syncope from volume depletion, drugs, or autonomic failure on standing
Syncope from brainstem ischaemia; subtypes are vertebral and basilar
Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
Syncope from mechanical obstruction such as massive PE or aortic dissection
questions.correctAnswer: D) Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
questions.correctAnswerText: Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
questions.explanation: Reflex syncope results from a sudden rise in parasympathetic tone and sympathetic withdrawal, causing bradycardia and/or hypotension. The other options describe cardiac, orthostatic, neurological, and obstructive causes.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of appendicitis?
questions.explanation: Grey Turner sign is flank discolouration from retroperitoneal/pancreatic haemorrhage. Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs are the appendicitis signs.

questions.text: Which sign is elicited by passive extension of the right hip while the patient lies on his left side, and suggests a retrocecal appendix?
questions.explanation: A retrocecal appendix irritates the psoas muscle, so hip extension causes RLQ pain. The obturator sign is pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip. Rovsing sign is RLQ pain on palpation of the LLQ.

questions.text: What proportion of patients with appendicitis present with the full classic picture of fever, nausea/vomiting, RLQ pain, and leukocytosis?
questions.explanation: Only about 20% have the full classic combination. Atypical or muted presentations are common, especially in the elderly.

questions.text: How should a patient with an Alvarado score of 6 be managed?
options: Observation with further imaging and serial examination
originalOptions: Observation with further imaging and serial examination
questions.correctAnswer: B) Observation with further imaging and serial examination
questions.correctAnswerText: Observation with further imaging and serial examination
questions.explanation: A score of 5–6 means possible appendicitis (about 66%), so observe and image. Surgery is reserved for 7–10, and a score of ≤ 4 makes appendicitis unlikely.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute right lower quadrant pain and tenderness at McBurney's point. What is the most likely diagnosis and the appropriate initial management?
options: Acute diverticulitis; oral co-amoxiclav and clear liquids
Renal colic; parenteral NSAIDs and discharge
Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
originalOptions: Acute diverticulitis; oral co-amoxiclav and clear liquids
Renal colic; parenteral NSAIDs and discharge
Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
questions.correctAnswer: E) Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
questions.explanation: McBurney's point tenderness is the classic finding of appendicitis, which needs imaging and early surgical review. Methotrexate would be used only for a stable ectopic pregnancy.

questions.text: Murphy's sign is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Murphy's sign is inspiratory arrest on deep palpation of the RUQ. Appendicitis is assessed with psoas/Rovsing signs instead.

questions.text: A patient presents with afebrile right upper quadrant pain. There is no Murphy sign or jaundice, and ultrasound shows gallstones with acoustic shadowing. The pain has resolved after analgesia and the laboratory results are reassuring. What is the best next step?
options: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent cholecystectomy
originalOptions: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent cholecystectomy
questions.correctAnswer: A) Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.explanation: This is uncomplicated biliary colic. Fever, Murphy sign, jaundice, cholestatic labs, or duct dilation would call for admission and a different pathway.

questions.text: Which statement about biliary colic pain is correct?
options: It is specifically triggered by protein
It always begins exactly 15 minutes after eating
It is typically relieved by food intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
It is typically accompanied by high fever and jaundice
originalOptions: It is specifically triggered by protein
It always begins exactly 15 minutes after eating
It is typically relieved by food intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
It is typically accompanied by high fever and jaundice
questions.correctAnswer: D) It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
questions.correctAnswerText: It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
questions.explanation: Biliary pain is referred to the right infrascapular region. It is commonly precipitated by a fatty meal, but timing and triggers vary. Relief by food suggests peptic ulcer disease, and fever with jaundice suggests cholangitis.

questions.text: Which statement about choledocholithiasis is correct?
options: It is defined by common bile duct dilatation below 5–7 mm
It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
It refers to stones confined to the gallbladder
It is infection of the bile duct diagnosed by Charcot's triad
It is inflammation of the gallbladder wall from cystic duct obstruction
originalOptions: It is defined by common bile duct dilatation below 5–7 mm
It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
It refers to stones confined to the gallbladder
It is infection of the bile duct diagnosed by Charcot's triad
It is inflammation of the gallbladder wall from cystic duct obstruction
questions.correctAnswer: B) It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
questions.correctAnswerText: It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
questions.explanation: Choledocholithiasis is defined by the stone, not by a duct diameter cut-off. Stones in the gallbladder are cholelithiasis, gallbladder inflammation is cholecystitis, and bile-duct infection is cholangitis.

questions.text: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain form the diagnostic triad of which condition?
questions.explanation: This is Charcot's triad of cholangitis, which is infection behind an obstructed bile duct. Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status, and signals suppurative cholangitis needing urgent ERCP decompression. Cholecystitis does not classically cause jaundice.

questions.text: All of the following are true regarding Meckel's diverticulum EXCEPT:
options: It occurs in about 2% of the population
It is located about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve
It is more common in females
It may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue
originalOptions: It occurs in about 2% of the population
It is located about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve
It is more common in females
It may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue
questions.correctAnswer: C) It is more common in females
questions.correctAnswerText: It is more common in females
questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is about twice as common in males, and complications are also more common in males. This is the rule-of-2s trap.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an independent predictor of adverse outcome in upper GI bleeding?
questions.explanation: The adverse threshold is an initial hematocrit < 30%, and even that often underestimates true acute blood loss. A hematocrit < 45% is not a recognised predictor.

questions.text: What does red blood in the nasogastric aspirate of a patient with GI bleeding suggest?
options: A lower GI source such as diverticular bleeding
An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
originalOptions: A lower GI source such as diverticular bleeding
An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
questions.correctAnswer: D) An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
questions.correctAnswerText: An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
questions.explanation: Red blood in NG lavage localises the bleed to the upper GI tract and predicts an adverse outcome. A negative aspirate does not exclude an upper GI bleed.

questions.text: A patient with known cirrhosis presents with haematemesis. Which source must be treated as the cause until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: In cirrhosis, haematemesis is variceal until proven otherwise. It needs a vasoactive drug (octreotide), prophylactic antibiotics, restrictive transfusion, and urgent endoscopy.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes angiodysplasia?
options: Healthy new blood vessels that do not bleed
Mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction after vomiting
Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
originalOptions: Healthy new blood vessels that do not bleed
Mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction after vomiting
Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
questions.correctAnswer: E) Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
questions.correctAnswerText: Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
questions.explanation: Angiodysplasia is a common cause of lower GI bleeding, most often in the right colon of older adults. It is associated with chronic kidney disease and aortic stenosis (Heyde's syndrome).

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of non-specific abdominal pain?
options: It is a diagnosis of exclusion
There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
Symptoms are improving and the patient tolerates oral fluids
originalOptions: It is a diagnosis of exclusion
There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
Symptoms are improving and the patient tolerates oral fluids
questions.correctAnswer: C) There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
questions.correctAnswerText: There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
questions.explanation: Tenderness, if present, is mild and non-localising. Guarding, rigidity, rebound, or a toxic appearance requires a search for a specific serious cause.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of abdominal pain in the emergency department?
questions.explanation: Non-specific abdominal pain accounts for about 34% of ED abdominal pain, followed by appendicitis (28%) and biliary disease (10%).

questions.text: Which is the least typical cause of acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes. Hypertriglyceridaemia and idiopathic disease are established causes. The "I GET SMASHED" mnemonic lists scorpion sting, not snake bite.

questions.text: Stroking the skin of the upper medial thigh in a normal cremasteric reflex causes:
options: Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
Contraction of the scrotal skin only, with no testicular movement
originalOptions: Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
Contraction of the scrotal skin only, with no testicular movement
questions.correctAnswer: B) Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
questions.correctAnswerText: Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
questions.explanation: The reflex is ipsilateral. Its absence supports testicular torsion, although a present reflex does not exclude torsion.

questions.text: Which statement about testicular torsion is FALSE?
options: It presents with a swollen, high-riding testis with a transverse lie
Duplex ultrasound shows absent blood flow
Salvage is 80–100% if detorsion occurs within 6 hours
It is most common at 20–30 years of age
originalOptions: It presents with a swollen, high-riding testis with a transverse lie
Duplex ultrasound shows absent blood flow
Salvage is 80–100% if detorsion occurs within 6 hours
It is most common at 20–30 years of age
questions.correctAnswer: E) It is most common at 20–30 years of age
questions.correctAnswerText: It is most common at 20–30 years of age
questions.explanation: The peak age is 12–16 years, and only about 10% of cases occur after age 20. Salvage falls to about 50% at 12 hours and 0% at 24 hours.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of retroperitoneal haemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Battle sign is mastoid ecchymosis, which indicates a basilar skull fracture. Cullen (periumbilical), Grey Turner (flank), and Fox (inguinal) signs suggest retroperitoneal or pancreatic haemorrhage.

questions.text: Which is NOT a major compartment for occult blood loss causing haemorrhagic shock in an adult?
questions.explanation: The sites of hidden blood loss are "blood on the floor and four more": chest, abdomen/retroperitoneum, pelvis, and long bones. Intracranial bleeding cannot account for profound systemic blood loss in an adult.

questions.text: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
questions.explanation: Smoking is the single strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA, and it also accelerates aneurysm growth. Hypertension and atherosclerosis are contributory only.

questions.text: Which is the most important predictor of abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture?
questions.explanation: Maximum diameter is the strongest predictor, and risk rises sharply above 5.5 cm. Smoking and hypertension raise risk mainly by increasing growth rate.

questions.text: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is typically described by the patient as:
options: Colicky right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder
Burning epigastric pain relieved by food
Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
Postprandial pain with fear of eating
The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
originalOptions: Colicky right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder
Burning epigastric pain relieved by food
Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
Postprandial pain with fear of eating
The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
questions.correctAnswer: E) The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
questions.correctAnswerText: The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
questions.explanation: Rupture classically causes sudden excruciating pain with hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass. The full triad is present in only about half of patients.

questions.text: Which statement about lactate in suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is correct?
options: A normal lactate reliably excludes the diagnosis
Lactate is highly sensitive, so CTA is unnecessary when it is normal
Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
An elevated lactate is required to make the diagnosis
Lactate rises only in chronic mesenteric ischaemia
originalOptions: A normal lactate reliably excludes the diagnosis
Lactate is highly sensitive, so CTA is unnecessary when it is normal
Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
An elevated lactate is required to make the diagnosis
Lactate rises only in chronic mesenteric ischaemia
questions.correctAnswer: C) Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
questions.correctAnswerText: Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
questions.explanation: Lactate can be normal early, before enough bowel is ischaemic to raise it. A high lactate supports severe ischaemia, but a normal value never rules it out.

questions.text: Which best describes the pain of early acute mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
Mild pain with marked rigidity and rebound tenderness
Postprandial pain starting 15–30 minutes after eating and lasting 1–3 hours
Pain relieved promptly by standard analgesia
Localised RLQ pain with periumbilical migration
originalOptions: Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
Mild pain with marked rigidity and rebound tenderness
Postprandial pain starting 15–30 minutes after eating and lasting 1–3 hours
Pain relieved promptly by standard analgesia
Localised RLQ pain with periumbilical migration
questions.correctAnswer: A) Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
questions.correctAnswerText: Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen is the early clue. Rigidity and peritonitis appear late with bowel necrosis, and option C describes chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

questions.text: What is the classic symptom triad of chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
Hypotension, back pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass
Jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension
Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
Pain out of proportion, a soft abdomen, and lactic acidosis
originalOptions: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
Hypotension, back pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass
Jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension
Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
Pain out of proportion, a soft abdomen, and lactic acidosis
questions.correctAnswer: D) Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
questions.correctAnswerText: Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
questions.explanation: This is "abdominal angina", from a fixed mesenteric stenosis that cannot meet post-meal demand. Acute ischaemia instead causes sudden severe constant pain out of proportion to the examination.

questions.text: What is the preferred initial imaging test when acute mesenteric ischaemia is suspected?
questions.explanation: CT angiography is the rapid diagnostic study of choice. It shows vessel occlusion, pneumatosis intestinalis, and absent bowel-wall enhancement.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is WRONG?
options: Bowel strangulation classically causes a lactic metabolic acidosis
Vomiting may independently cause a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
A high lactate supports the diagnosis of mesenteric ischaemia
Pain out of proportion to examination findings is an early feature of acute mesenteric ischaemia
Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
originalOptions: Bowel strangulation classically causes a lactic metabolic acidosis
Vomiting may independently cause a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
A high lactate supports the diagnosis of mesenteric ischaemia
Pain out of proportion to examination findings is an early feature of acute mesenteric ischaemia
Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
questions.correctAnswer: E) Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
questions.correctAnswerText: Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
questions.explanation: Ischaemia produces lactic metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. Any alkalosis in these patients comes from a separate cause, usually vomiting.

questions.text: What is required to establish a diagnosis of shock?
options: Documented hypotension with low cardiac output
Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
originalOptions: Documented hypotension with low cardiac output
Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
questions.correctAnswer: C) Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
questions.correctAnswerText: Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
questions.explanation: Shock is defined by inadequate end-organ perfusion, so no single parameter is required. Hypotension, acidosis and hypoxia may all be absent in compensated shock, and vascular resistance is low in distributive shock.

questions.text: The shock index is calculated as:
questions.correctAnswer: A) Heart rate ÷ systolic blood pressure
questions.explanation: Shock index = HR ÷ SBP (normal 0.5–0.7). A value ≥ 0.9–1.0 suggests occult shock even when the systolic pressure appears normal.

questions.text: A patient who was stabbed multiple times presents with heart rate 130/min, blood pressure 95/70 mmHg and SpO₂ 93%. Which class of haemorrhagic shock does this represent?
questions.explanation: Heart rate > 120 with a falling blood pressure and a narrowed pulse pressure (25 mmHg) indicates Class III (31–40% blood loss), which requires blood transfusion. Class IV shows heart rate > 140 and a markedly low blood pressure.

questions.text: A previously healthy 70-kg man has an estimated acute blood loss of 2 litres. Which statement applies?
options: His urinary output will be at the lower limit of normal
His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
He will have tachycardia with no change in systolic blood pressure
His pulse pressure will be widened
He will have a normal respiratory rate and mental state
originalOptions: His urinary output will be at the lower limit of normal
His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
He will have tachycardia with no change in systolic blood pressure
His pulse pressure will be widened
He will have a normal respiratory rate and mental state
questions.correctAnswer: B) His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
questions.correctAnswerText: His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
questions.explanation: A loss of about 2 L (~30% of blood volume) corresponds to Class III, in which systolic pressure falls and pulse pressure narrows, with tachycardia > 120, tachypnoea, confusion and reduced urine output. Tachycardia with a preserved systolic pressure describes Class II.

questions.text: Which of the following describes Class I haemorrhagic shock?
options: Blood loss of 15–30% with a narrowed pulse pressure
Heart rate > 140/min with negligible urine output
Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
originalOptions: Blood loss of 15–30% with a narrowed pulse pressure
Heart rate > 140/min with negligible urine output
Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
questions.correctAnswer: E) Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
questions.correctAnswerText: Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
questions.explanation: Class I (< 750 mL) is absorbed with essentially normal vital signs. Tachycardia and a narrowed pulse pressure begin in Class II, and hypotension appears in Class III.

questions.text: A trauma patient has Class III haemorrhagic shock. Which of the following findings is NOT expected?
questions.explanation: Urine output is reduced in Class III but becomes negligible only in Class IV (> 40% blood loss). The other findings are all characteristic of Class III.

questions.text: A 34-year-old man pinned by a cement truck has deformities and marked swelling of both thighs. His shock:
options: Cannot be explained without a major arterial injury
Will likely reverse with traction splints
Cannot be explained without a concomitant intra-abdominal injury
Cannot be explained without a concomitant pelvic fracture
Is most likely neurogenic in origin
originalOptions: Cannot be explained without a major arterial injury
Will likely reverse with traction splints
Cannot be explained without a concomitant intra-abdominal injury
Cannot be explained without a concomitant pelvic fracture
Is most likely neurogenic in origin
questions.correctAnswer: B) Will likely reverse with traction splints
questions.correctAnswerText: Will likely reverse with traction splints
questions.explanation: Each femoral fracture can cause 1–2 L of blood loss, so bilateral femoral fractures alone can account for Class III–IV haemorrhage; the long bones are one of the "blood on the floor and four more" sites. Shock of this kind requires blood resuscitation.

questions.text: The "physiologic hypervolaemia" of pregnancy is clinically significant because it:
options: Increases the risk of pulmonary oedema
Reduces the need for blood transfusion
Reduces the crystalloid volume required for resuscitation
Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
Complicates the management of closed head injury
originalOptions: Increases the risk of pulmonary oedema
Reduces the need for blood transfusion
Reduces the crystalloid volume required for resuscitation
Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
Complicates the management of closed head injury
questions.correctAnswer: D) Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
questions.correctAnswerText: Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
questions.explanation: Blood volume expands by about 40–50% in pregnancy, so a pregnant patient can lose considerably more blood before tachycardia or hypotension appear. This masks the severity of haemorrhage while the fetus may already be compromised.

questions.text: Which statement about crystalloid resuscitation in haemorrhagic shock is correct?
options: Large volumes are preferred to restore oxygen delivery
Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
Crystalloid restores oxygen-carrying capacity as effectively as blood
It should be continued until blood pressure is normal, regardless of bleeding control
It is preferred over blood products once haemoglobin falls below 9 g/dL
originalOptions: Large volumes are preferred to restore oxygen delivery
Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
Crystalloid restores oxygen-carrying capacity as effectively as blood
It should be continued until blood pressure is normal, regardless of bleeding control
It is preferred over blood products once haemoglobin falls below 9 g/dL
questions.correctAnswer: B) Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
questions.correctAnswerText: Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
questions.explanation: Crystalloid carries no oxygen and dilutes haemoglobin and clotting factors. In haemorrhagic shock, blood products and definitive haemorrhage control are prioritised, with permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled.

questions.text: Which packed red cells : plasma : platelets ratio is commonly used in massive transfusion for severe haemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Massive transfusion protocols use balanced resuscitation with packed red cells, plasma and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio, which replaces volume and clotting factors together.

questions.text: A patient in shock is not responding to initial fluid resuscitation. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?
options: Repeat crystalloid boluses until the blood pressure normalises
Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
Continue observation, as response is expected to be delayed
Defer resuscitation until CT imaging is completed
originalOptions: Repeat crystalloid boluses until the blood pressure normalises
Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
Continue observation, as response is expected to be delayed
Defer resuscitation until CT imaging is completed
questions.correctAnswer: C) Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
questions.correctAnswerText: Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
questions.explanation: Fluid refractoriness calls for immediate ABCDE reassessment and a search for ongoing haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax or tamponade. Noradrenaline is started for vasodilatory shock, and blood products for haemorrhagic shock.

questions.text: Shortly after urinary catheterisation, a patient develops fever, tachycardia, altered mental status and hypotension. Which type of shock should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Fever with haemodynamic instability in a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter indicates urosepsis. Management is cultures and lactate, antibiotics within the hour, fluids, and noradrenaline to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg if shock persists.

questions.text: A patient with poor oral intake and dehydration is hypotensive, with no fever and no documented source of infection. Which type of shock best fits this presentation?
questions.explanation: Volume depletion from poor intake explains the hypotension, and there is neither fever nor an infective source to suggest sepsis. If fever or an infective source appears, reassess urgently for septic shock.

questions.text: A tachycardic patient with fever remains hypotensive despite initial fluid resuscitation. Which type of shock is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fever with persistent hypoperfusion despite fluids indicates infection-driven vasodilation, which is septic shock. Dehydration alone would be expected to respond to fluid replacement.

questions.text: A child develops a skin reaction, hoarseness and shortness of breath after receiving an antibiotic. After stopping the drug, what is the best next step?
options: IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
originalOptions: IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
questions.correctAnswer: E) IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
questions.correctAnswerText: IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
questions.explanation: This is anaphylaxis with airway involvement, and IM adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving treatment. Corticosteroids, antihistamines and bronchodilators are adjuncts and must not delay it; repeat dosing depends on response and the local protocol.

questions.text: A patient has hypotension, distended neck veins and absent breath sounds on one side. Which type of shock is this?
questions.explanation: Hypotension with raised JVP and unilateral absent breath sounds indicates tension pneumothorax, a mechanical cause of obstructive shock. Cardiogenic shock can also raise the JVP but would not explain the unilateral absent breath sounds.

questions.text: Which of the following constitutes Beck's triad in cardiac tamponade?
options: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
Hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry skin
Hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent unilateral breath sounds
Hypotension, widened pulse pressure and bounding pulse
originalOptions: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
Hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry skin
Hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent unilateral breath sounds
Hypotension, widened pulse pressure and bounding pulse
questions.correctAnswer: A) Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
questions.correctAnswerText: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
questions.explanation: Beck's triad is hypotension, jugular venous distension and muffled heart sounds. The complete triad is often absent, so eFAST should be used to confirm tamponade.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes milrinone?
options: A β-adrenergic agonist producing inotropy with vasoconstriction
An α₁-agonist that raises systemic vascular resistance
A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
A calcium channel blocker with negative inotropic effect
originalOptions: A β-adrenergic agonist producing inotropy with vasoconstriction
An α₁-agonist that raises systemic vascular resistance
A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
A calcium channel blocker with negative inotropic effect
questions.correctAnswer: D) A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
questions.correctAnswerText: A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
questions.explanation: Milrinone raises cAMP independently of β-receptors, so it remains effective in patients taking β-blockers, and it is an "inodilator". Its vasodilation explains the hypotension.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognised complication of central venous catheter insertion?
questions.explanation: Recognised complications include arterial puncture, pneumothorax or haemothorax, malposition with arrhythmia, air embolism, infection and thrombosis. Hypercalcaemia is not related to catheter insertion.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of pulse oximetry?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypertension does not interfere with the optical signal. Inaccuracy arises from poor pulsatile flow (vasoconstriction, shock, hypothermia), dyshemoglobinemias (carboxyhemoglobin reads falsely normal), anemia, and optical interference.

allQuestions.text: All of the following statements regarding pulse oximetry are true, EXCEPT:
options: It provides a continuous noninvasive measurement of pulse rate
It provides a continuous noninvasive measurement of the partial pressure of oxygen
It depends on differential light absorption by oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin
Significant dyshemoglobinemia can affect its accuracy
Excessive ambient light can interfere with its accuracy
originalOptions: It provides a continuous noninvasive measurement of pulse rate
It provides a continuous noninvasive measurement of the partial pressure of oxygen
It depends on differential light absorption by oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin
Significant dyshemoglobinemia can affect its accuracy
Excessive ambient light can interfere with its accuracy
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) It provides a continuous noninvasive measurement of the partial pressure of oxygen
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It provides a continuous noninvasive measurement of the partial pressure of oxygen
allQuestions.explanation: Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin saturation (SpO₂), not PaO₂. The partial pressure of oxygen requires arterial blood gas analysis.

allQuestions.text: You are alone with a patient in suspected cardiac or respiratory arrest. After ensuring scene safety and before sending for help, what is the next step?
allQuestions.explanation: Responsiveness must be established first. Only then is EMS activated, followed by assessment of breathing and pulse.

allQuestions.text: A 21-year-old intoxicated college student turns blue and collapses while eating a hot dog. What is the most likely cause?
allQuestions.explanation: Sudden cyanosis while eating indicates foreign-body airway obstruction, and intoxication increases the risk of aspiration. Cardiac arrest would be a consequence of prolonged obstruction, not the primary cause.

allQuestions.text: A 39-year-old man has a GCS of 6, no facial trauma, a deviated nasal septum, and a full beard. What is the most appropriate airway management?
options: Orotracheal intubation by two operators with in-line cervical spine stabilization
Forced nasotracheal intubation past the deviated septum
Bag-valve-mask ventilation until the beard can be shaved
Bag-valve-mask ventilation until the cervical spine is excluded
originalOptions: Orotracheal intubation by two operators with in-line cervical spine stabilization
Forced nasotracheal intubation past the deviated septum
Bag-valve-mask ventilation until the beard can be shaved
Bag-valve-mask ventilation until the cervical spine is excluded
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Orotracheal intubation by two operators with in-line cervical spine stabilization
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Orotracheal intubation by two operators with in-line cervical spine stabilization
allQuestions.explanation: A GCS of 6 requires a definitive airway, and a deviated septum argues against the nasal route. A beard is not a contraindication to orotracheal intubation, and surgical cricothyrotomy is reserved for failed airway access.

allQuestions.text: A 65-year-old man on a short ladder suddenly collapses and is unresponsive. What is the next step?
options: Call EMS and obtain an AED
Place him in the recovery position
originalOptions: Call EMS and obtain an AED
Place him in the recovery position
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Call EMS and obtain an AED
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Call EMS and obtain an AED
allQuestions.explanation: After unresponsiveness is established, EMS is activated and an AED obtained, then breathing and pulse are assessed. CPR cannot be started before arrest is confirmed.

allQuestions.text: After finding an unresponsive child, shouting for help, and confirming that the child is not breathing but has a pulse, what is the next step?
options: Leave the child to search for an AED
Open the airway by head tilt–chin lift and give rescue breaths
Begin back blows and chest thrusts
originalOptions: Leave the child to search for an AED
Open the airway by head tilt–chin lift and give rescue breaths
Begin back blows and chest thrusts
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Open the airway by head tilt–chin lift and give rescue breaths
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Open the airway by head tilt–chin lift and give rescue breaths
allQuestions.explanation: A palpable pulse with absent breathing is respiratory arrest, which is managed with airway opening and rescue breathing. Compressions are indicated only when the pulse is absent.

allQuestions.text: After finding an unresponsive child with no normal breathing and no definite pulse, and with help already activated, what should the rescuer do next?
options: Leave to search for an AED
Begin back blows and chest thrusts
originalOptions: Leave to search for an AED
Begin back blows and chest thrusts
allQuestions.explanation: The absence of a pulse defines cardiac arrest, so CPR starts immediately. A lone rescuer uses 30:2, and the AED is applied as soon as it is available.

allQuestions.text: After finding someone unresponsive with a pulse but not breathing, you are unable to deliver effective breaths. What is the next step?
options: Repeat head tilt–chin lift and reattempt the breath
Leave the patient to search for an AED
originalOptions: Repeat head tilt–chin lift and reattempt the breath
Leave the patient to search for an AED
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Repeat head tilt–chin lift and reattempt the breath
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Repeat head tilt–chin lift and reattempt the breath
allQuestions.explanation: Ineffective breaths usually result from inadequate airway positioning, so the airway is repositioned first. Compressions are not indicated while a pulse is present.

allQuestions.text: A witnessed adult collapse is followed by loss of consciousness and absent normal breathing. What is the correct resuscitation sequence?
options: Recognize arrest, activate EMS and obtain an AED, begin high-quality CPR (30:2), and defibrillate promptly if the rhythm is shockable
Establish IV access, give epinephrine, begin CPR, then apply the AED
Intubate, begin CPR, call EMS, then apply the AED
Check the pulse for 30 seconds, give rescue breaths first, call EMS, then begin compressions
Perform CPR for 5 minutes, activate EMS, then apply the AED
originalOptions: Recognize arrest, activate EMS and obtain an AED, begin high-quality CPR (30:2), and defibrillate promptly if the rhythm is shockable
Establish IV access, give epinephrine, begin CPR, then apply the AED
Intubate, begin CPR, call EMS, then apply the AED
Check the pulse for 30 seconds, give rescue breaths first, call EMS, then begin compressions
Perform CPR for 5 minutes, activate EMS, then apply the AED
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Recognize arrest, activate EMS and obtain an AED, begin high-quality CPR (30:2), and defibrillate promptly if the rhythm is shockable
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Recognize arrest, activate EMS and obtain an AED, begin high-quality CPR (30:2), and defibrillate promptly if the rhythm is shockable
allQuestions.explanation: Early activation, immediate high-quality CPR, and early defibrillation form the core sequence. Advanced airway or drug therapy must never delay CPR or the first indicated shock.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following findings in a child indicates a currently patent airway, so that immediate invasive airway intervention is not required?
options: Inability to speak or make sounds
originalOptions: Inability to speak or make sounds
allQuestions.explanation: Vocalization requires airflow through the airway, whereas the other findings indicate obstruction or respiratory failure. Ongoing reassessment is still required, since stridor, fatigue, or deterioration can develop.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are true regarding confirmation of endotracheal tube position, EXCEPT:
options: Auscultation of the chest and epigastrium
Visualizing the tube passing through the esophagus
Direct visualization of the tube passing between the vocal cords
originalOptions: Auscultation of the chest and epigastrium
Visualizing the tube passing through the esophagus
Direct visualization of the tube passing between the vocal cords
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Visualizing the tube passing through the esophagus
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Visualizing the tube passing through the esophagus
allQuestions.explanation: A tube passing into the esophagus is a misplacement, not a confirmation. Correct placement is through the vocal cords into the trachea, confirmed by waveform capnography and clinical checks.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are true regarding retropharyngeal abscess, EXCEPT:
options: It presents with fever, neck pain, drooling, and torticollis
The prevertebral soft-tissue space is widened on a lateral neck X-ray
It may obstruct the airway or extend into the mediastinum
It is most common between ages 5 and 7 years
originalOptions: It presents with fever, neck pain, drooling, and torticollis
The prevertebral soft-tissue space is widened on a lateral neck X-ray
It may obstruct the airway or extend into the mediastinum
It is most common between ages 5 and 7 years
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It is most common between ages 5 and 7 years
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is most common between ages 5 and 7 years
allQuestions.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess is more common in young children, and the stated age range is not the typical peak. The other statements are true, and the condition is potentially life-threatening.

allQuestions.text: Apnea is defined as a respiratory pause lasting at least:
allQuestions.explanation: Apnea is a pause of at least 20 seconds, or a shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia, desaturation, cyanosis, or pallor. The same definition applies to apnea of prematurity in a preterm infant.

allQuestions.text: An unresponsive adult has no pulse, and the rescuer is unable or unwilling to give breaths. What should the rescuer do?
options: Start hands-only chest compressions immediately and use an AED as soon as available
Wait for EMS to arrive before any intervention
Recheck the pulse repeatedly until help arrives
Place the patient in the recovery position
originalOptions: Start hands-only chest compressions immediately and use an AED as soon as available
Wait for EMS to arrive before any intervention
Recheck the pulse repeatedly until help arrives
Place the patient in the recovery position
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Start hands-only chest compressions immediately and use an AED as soon as available
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Start hands-only chest compressions immediately and use an AED as soon as available
allQuestions.explanation: Compressions and early defibrillation are the priority in pulseless arrest, and hands-only CPR is acceptable when breaths cannot be given. Trained rescuers should add ventilation when feasible.

allQuestions.text: What is the best artery for assessing the pulse in an infant?
allQuestions.explanation: The brachial artery is the preferred pulse-check site in infants (under 1 year), because the short, fat neck makes the carotid pulse difficult to palpate.

allQuestions.text: What is the correct initial BLS sequence after finding a collapsed adult?
options: Start chest compressions, call EMS, check the pulse, assess responsiveness
Assess responsiveness, call EMS and get an AED, check breathing and pulse (≤10 seconds), start chest compressions
Assess responsiveness, open the airway, give two breaths, call EMS, start compressions
Call EMS, check the pulse for 30 seconds, give rescue breaths, start compressions
Assess responsiveness, check breathing and pulse, start compressions, then call EMS
originalOptions: Start chest compressions, call EMS, check the pulse, assess responsiveness
Assess responsiveness, call EMS and get an AED, check breathing and pulse (≤10 seconds), start chest compressions
Assess responsiveness, open the airway, give two breaths, call EMS, start compressions
Call EMS, check the pulse for 30 seconds, give rescue breaths, start compressions
Assess responsiveness, check breathing and pulse, start compressions, then call EMS
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Assess responsiveness, call EMS and get an AED, check breathing and pulse (≤10 seconds), start chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Assess responsiveness, call EMS and get an AED, check breathing and pulse (≤10 seconds), start chest compressions
allQuestions.explanation: Responsiveness is assessed first, EMS and an AED are requested early, and breathing and pulse are checked together within 10 seconds before compressions begin.

allQuestions.text: Which is the most common cause of bronchiolitis in children under 2 years of age, including many children older than 1 year?
allQuestions.explanation: RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis in this age group, although it is not the only pathogen. Parainfluenza virus is the typical cause of croup.

allQuestions.text: How often should compressors switch during two-rescuer CPR?
allQuestions.explanation: Rescuers switch about every 2 minutes (approximately 5 cycles of 30:2) to prevent fatigue and preserve compression quality, with the pause kept minimal.

allQuestions.text: Which is the earliest sign of respiratory distress or airway compromise?
allQuestions.explanation: An increased respiratory rate is the earliest change. Flaring and retractions reflect increased work of breathing, whereas cyanosis and hypotension are late signs.

allQuestions.text: A farmer presents with cyanosis, frothy oral secretions, difficulty breathing, and pinpoint pupils. What is the first step?
options: Remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin
originalOptions: Remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin
allQuestions.explanation: This is an organophosphate toxidrome with copious bronchial secretions. Airway and breathing take priority over antidotes (atropine, pralidoxime) in the ABC approach.

allQuestions.text: Which is the most commonly used first-choice intraosseous (IO) access site in pediatric patients?
allQuestions.explanation: The proximal tibia is the classic first-choice site in children. The distal tibia and proximal humerus are alternatives depending on age, equipment, and training.

allQuestions.text: Which maneuver should be used to open the airway when cervical spine injury is suspected?
options: Rolling the patient into the lateral position
Jaw thrust with manual in-line stabilization
originalOptions: Rolling the patient into the lateral position
Jaw thrust with manual in-line stabilization
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Jaw thrust with manual in-line stabilization
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Jaw thrust with manual in-line stabilization
allQuestions.explanation: Jaw thrust opens the airway without extending the neck. Head tilt–chin lift is used only if the airway cannot otherwise be opened.

allQuestions.text: In an unresponsive patient, the pulse should be checked for no more than ____ seconds.
allQuestions.explanation: The pulse check is limited to 10 seconds so that compressions are not delayed. If there is any doubt about the pulse, CPR is started.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a late sign of airway compromise?
allQuestions.explanation: Desaturation appears late, so the airway must be addressed before it develops. Agitation, tachypnea, voice change, and stridor or gurgling are early signs.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is considered a definitive airway?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Cuffed tube in the trachea
allQuestions.explanation: A definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea, which protects against aspiration and allows full ventilatory control. Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways and masks are adjuncts.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the appropriate management of peritonsillar abscess?
options: Penicillin plus clindamycin plus vancomycin for every patient
Drainage plus antibiotics covering group A streptococci and oral anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin–sulbactam)
originalOptions: Penicillin plus clindamycin plus vancomycin for every patient
Drainage plus antibiotics covering group A streptococci and oral anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin–sulbactam)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Drainage plus antibiotics covering group A streptococci and oral anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin–sulbactam)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Drainage plus antibiotics covering group A streptococci and oral anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin–sulbactam)
allQuestions.explanation: Treatment combines drainage with antibiotics directed at group A streptococci and oral anaerobes. Penicillin plus clindamycin and/or vancomycin is not a blanket regimen for every patient.

allQuestions.text: Which route is the preferred first-line route for administering drugs during cardiac arrest?
allQuestions.explanation: The peripheral IV route is first-line, with IO as the alternative when IV access fails. The endotracheal route is a last resort because absorption is poor and unpredictable.

allQuestions.text: What is the first maneuver to improve oxygenation after chest injury?
options: Ascertain the need for a chest tube
Obtain a lateral cervical spine X-ray
originalOptions: Ascertain the need for a chest tube
Obtain a lateral cervical spine X-ray
allQuestions.explanation: The simplest effective intervention comes first, and supplemental oxygen is given to all critically ill patients. Definitive airway management follows only if indicated.

allQuestions.text: Which is an appropriate first-aid measure for snake bite?
options: Keep the patient calm, remove rings and constricting items, immobilize the limb at about heart level, and arrange urgent transport for antivenom
A tight arterial tourniquet above the bite
originalOptions: Keep the patient calm, remove rings and constricting items, immobilize the limb at about heart level, and arrange urgent transport for antivenom
A tight arterial tourniquet above the bite
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Keep the patient calm, remove rings and constricting items, immobilize the limb at about heart level, and arrange urgent transport for antivenom
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Keep the patient calm, remove rings and constricting items, immobilize the limb at about heart level, and arrange urgent transport for antivenom
allQuestions.explanation: Incision, suction, ice, and tight tourniquets worsen local tissue damage and delay proper care without reliably reducing venom spread.

allQuestions.text: What approximate inspired oxygen concentration is delivered by a standard low-flow nasal cannula at 1–6 L/min?
allQuestions.explanation: A nasal cannula at 1–6 L/min delivers approximately 24–44% oxygen, varying with flow rate and the patient's inspiratory pattern.

allQuestions.text: A choking patient becomes unresponsive. What is the best method to clear the obstruction?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Start CPR with chest compressions
allQuestions.explanation: In an unresponsive choking victim, compressions double as expulsion attempts. The mouth is inspected before each set of breaths, and an object is removed only if visible, never by blind finger sweep.

allQuestions.text: What is the preferred initial peripheral vascular access for major trauma resuscitation?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Two large-bore peripheral IV lines
allQuestions.explanation: Two 14–16G cannulae allow rapid fluid and blood-product administration. IO access is used if IV access fails or is delayed.

allQuestions.text: What is the best method to confirm and continuously monitor endotracheal tube placement?
allQuestions.explanation: Waveform capnography is the most reliable objective confirmation and allows continuous monitoring. Auscultation alone is insufficient.

allQuestions.text: What is the earliest sign of ARDS?
allQuestions.explanation: An increased respiratory rate precedes hypoxemia, crackles, and radiographic changes.

allQuestions.text: A child is found pulseless and not breathing (unwitnessed), and the rescuer is alone. What is the initial management?
options: Start CPR immediately for 2 minutes, then call EMS
originalOptions: Start CPR immediately for 2 minutes, then call EMS
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Start CPR immediately for 2 minutes, then call EMS
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Start CPR immediately for 2 minutes, then call EMS
allQuestions.explanation: In a child, paediatric arrest is usually respiratory in origin, so CPR is started first and EMS is called after 2 minutes if the rescuer is alone. This differs from a witnessed adult collapse, where EMS is called first.

allQuestions.text: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse in an adult?
allQuestions.explanation: Atropine is first-line, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. Pacing or dopamine/epinephrine infusion follows if atropine is ineffective.

allQuestions.text: When can a laryngeal mask airway be used after an attempted endotracheal intubation?
options: To replace the tube after successful intubation
Only when the patient is fully conscious
As a definitive airway that fully protects against aspiration
As a rescue airway when intubation fails and ventilation is required
originalOptions: To replace the tube after successful intubation
Only when the patient is fully conscious
As a definitive airway that fully protects against aspiration
As a rescue airway when intubation fails and ventilation is required
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) As a rescue airway when intubation fails and ventilation is required
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: As a rescue airway when intubation fails and ventilation is required
allQuestions.explanation: A supraglottic airway is quicker to place and serves as a rescue device in failed or delayed intubation. It does not fully protect against aspiration and is not a definitive airway.

allQuestions.text: When giving rescue breaths to an apneic patient who has a pulse, how often should the pulse be rechecked?
allQuestions.explanation: The pulse is rechecked about every 2 minutes. CPR is started if the pulse is lost.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the LEAST likely, by itself, to justify unusually prolonged resuscitation?
allQuestions.explanation: Prolonged resuscitation is justified when a potentially reversible cause exists, such as hypothermia, toxins, electrical injury, or pregnancy near term. Arrest from catastrophic SAH carries a poor prognosis and does not justify extension.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an indication for admission in an asthma exacerbation?
options: Persistent symptoms despite initial bronchodilator therapy
Frequent MDI use over the previous months
originalOptions: Persistent symptoms despite initial bronchodilator therapy
Frequent MDI use over the previous months
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Frequent MDI use over the previous months
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Frequent MDI use over the previous months
allQuestions.explanation: Admission is determined by the severity and response of the current episode. Chronic frequent inhaler use does not by itself mandate admission.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about high-quality adult CPR is WRONG?
options: Compress at least 5 cm (2 in) while avoiding excessive depth
Use 30:2 before an advanced airway is placed
originalOptions: Compress at least 5 cm (2 in) while avoiding excessive depth
Use 30:2 before an advanced airway is placed
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Allow only partial chest recoil
allQuestions.explanation: Full chest recoil must be allowed after every compression to permit cardiac refilling. Incomplete recoil reduces coronary and cerebral perfusion.

allQuestions.text: While performing CPR on an infant, a second rescuer arrives and EMS has already been activated. What is the next step?
options: Ask the second rescuer to repeat the call to EMS
Have the second rescuer give ventilations only at a 30:2 ratio
Have the second rescuer join for two-rescuer CPR (15:2) and switch compressor roles about every 2 minutes
originalOptions: Ask the second rescuer to repeat the call to EMS
Have the second rescuer give ventilations only at a 30:2 ratio
Have the second rescuer join for two-rescuer CPR (15:2) and switch compressor roles about every 2 minutes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Have the second rescuer join for two-rescuer CPR (15:2) and switch compressor roles about every 2 minutes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Have the second rescuer join for two-rescuer CPR (15:2) and switch compressor roles about every 2 minutes
allQuestions.explanation: Two-rescuer pediatric CPR uses 15:2, and switching roles about every 2 minutes minimizes fatigue and preserves compression quality. EMS activation has already been completed.

allQuestions.text: A rescuer is uncomfortable giving mouth-to-mouth breaths to an unresponsive person with no pulse. What should be done?
options: Attempt head tilt and jaw thrust, then give a breath
Wait for EMS before any intervention
Place the patient in the recovery position
originalOptions: Attempt head tilt and jaw thrust, then give a breath
Wait for EMS before any intervention
Place the patient in the recovery position
allQuestions.explanation: Hands-only compressions are the priority in pulseless arrest and are acceptable when the rescuer is unable or unwilling to give breaths.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following lists the correct steps of basic life support (BLS)?
options: Assess the victim, activate EMS and bring an AED, perform chest compressions, give rescue breaths
Assess the victim, perform chest compressions, give rescue breaths, defibrillate before calling EMS
Call EMS, intubate, perform chest compressions
Give rescue breaths, assess the victim, perform chest compressions
originalOptions: Assess the victim, activate EMS and bring an AED, perform chest compressions, give rescue breaths
Assess the victim, perform chest compressions, give rescue breaths, defibrillate before calling EMS
Call EMS, intubate, perform chest compressions
Give rescue breaths, assess the victim, perform chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Assess the victim, activate EMS and bring an AED, perform chest compressions, give rescue breaths
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Assess the victim, activate EMS and bring an AED, perform chest compressions, give rescue breaths
allQuestions.explanation: BLS begins with assessment and activation of the emergency response with AED retrieval, followed by compressions and breaths. Early defibrillation follows when an AED is available.

allQuestions.text: A choking patient is unresponsive but still has a pulse, and EMS has been activated. What is the next step?
options: Place the patient in the recovery position
originalOptions: Place the patient in the recovery position
allQuestions.explanation: A pulse is present, so compressions and an AED are not indicated. The airway obstruction must be addressed first by opening the airway.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is WRONG regarding basic life support?
options: Scene safety must be ensured first
For a child, the compression-to-breath ratio is 15:2 when only one rescuer is present
For a child, two-rescuer CPR uses 15:2
The brachial artery is used for the pulse check in infants
Compression depth is about one-third of the chest depth in children
originalOptions: Scene safety must be ensured first
For a child, the compression-to-breath ratio is 15:2 when only one rescuer is present
For a child, two-rescuer CPR uses 15:2
The brachial artery is used for the pulse check in infants
Compression depth is about one-third of the chest depth in children
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) For a child, the compression-to-breath ratio is 15:2 when only one rescuer is present
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: For a child, the compression-to-breath ratio is 15:2 when only one rescuer is present
allQuestions.explanation: Single-rescuer pediatric CPR uses 30:2, while 15:2 applies only when two rescuers are present.

allQuestions.text: After a failed attempt at peripheral IV access, what is the next step?
options: Central venous catheter via the femoral vein
Central venous catheter via the internal jugular vein
Central venous catheter via the subclavian vein
originalOptions: Central venous catheter via the femoral vein
Central venous catheter via the internal jugular vein
Central venous catheter via the subclavian vein
allQuestions.explanation: IO access is the rapid, reliable alternative when peripheral IV access fails or is delayed, and it works even in shock. Central lines are slower and carry more complications.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to intraosseous line insertion (before placement)?
options: Previous IO attempt in the same bone
originalOptions: Previous IO attempt in the same bone
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Fluid leakage from the line
allQuestions.explanation: Leakage is a post-insertion sign of extravasation or malposition, after which the line should be abandoned. Fracture, local infection, and a prior attempt in the same bone are pre-insertion contraindications.

allQuestions.text: What is the target oxygen saturation range in a COPD patient with hypercapnia?
allQuestions.explanation: Controlled oxygen therapy targets 88–92% in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, to avoid worsening CO₂ retention. The 94–98% target applies to patients without this risk.

allQuestions.text: A conscious child older than 1 year shows the universal sign of choking. Which maneuver is used for severe foreign-body airway obstruction?
options: Alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
originalOptions: Alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
allQuestions.explanation: Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts are continued until the object clears or the child becomes unresponsive. At that point CPR is started.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are indications for admission of a pediatric patient with croup, EXCEPT:
options: Persistent moderate–severe symptoms despite corticosteroid and nebulized epinephrine
originalOptions: Persistent moderate–severe symptoms despite corticosteroid and nebulized epinephrine
allQuestions.explanation: Admission depends on severity, response to treatment, and risk of deterioration, not on an age of 24 months. Admission or PICU escalation is required for persistent symptoms despite treatment, repeated epinephrine need, failure to maintain oxygenation or hydration, or impending respiratory failure.

allQuestions.text: Which is NOT a component of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
allQuestions.explanation: The triangle comprises Appearance, Work of breathing, and Circulation to skin. Airway is assessed separately in the hands-on primary survey.

allQuestions.text: All of the following cause acute stridor in children, EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Bronchiolitis is a lower-airway disease presenting with wheeze and crackles, not stridor. The other conditions are upper-airway causes of acute stridor.

allQuestions.text: Which statement regarding epiglottitis is correct?
options: Hib vaccination has markedly reduced Hib epiglottitis, but other organisms such as streptococci and staphylococci can also cause it
It is always caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b
The diagnosis should be confirmed by throat examination with a tongue depressor
The child should be laid flat to obtain a lateral neck X-ray
The thumbprint sign is seen on an AP neck X-ray
originalOptions: Hib vaccination has markedly reduced Hib epiglottitis, but other organisms such as streptococci and staphylococci can also cause it
It is always caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b
The diagnosis should be confirmed by throat examination with a tongue depressor
The child should be laid flat to obtain a lateral neck X-ray
The thumbprint sign is seen on an AP neck X-ray
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Hib vaccination has markedly reduced Hib epiglottitis, but other organisms such as streptococci and staphylococci can also cause it
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hib vaccination has markedly reduced Hib epiglottitis, but other organisms such as streptococci and staphylococci can also cause it
allQuestions.explanation: Epiglottitis is not always Hib-related. Throat examination or laying the child flat can precipitate complete obstruction, and the thumbprint sign is seen on the lateral neck film.

allQuestions.text: Which finding indicates total or near-total airway obstruction due to a foreign body in a child?
options: Weak or absent cough with inability to speak or make sounds
Intermittent wheezing with good air movement
originalOptions: Weak or absent cough with inability to speak or make sounds
Intermittent wheezing with good air movement
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Weak or absent cough with inability to speak or make sounds
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Weak or absent cough with inability to speak or make sounds
allQuestions.explanation: Total obstruction is also associated with cyanosis, altered mental status, apnea, and poor or absent air movement. An effective cough indicates mild obstruction.

allQuestions.text: Which combination constitutes the "croup triangle"?
options: Toxic appearance, thick purulent secretions, high fever
originalOptions: Toxic appearance, thick purulent secretions, high fever
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness
allQuestions.explanation: These three features characterize croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). The other options describe epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess, bronchiolitis, and bacterial tracheitis respectively.

allQuestions.text: What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used for pediatric CPR with one rescuer?
