allQuestions.text: A 25-year-old man opens his eyes to pain, moans periodically, and has the left arm reach toward the painful stimulus. The right arm does not respond and the legs are stiffly extended. What is the GCS?
allQuestions.explanation: Eye opening to pain scores 2 and moaning (incomprehensible sounds) scores 2. The best motor response is localization, which scores 5, giving 2 + 2 + 5 = 9.

allQuestions.text: A patient opens his eyes to command, moves his arms and legs on command, and is disoriented in conversation. What is the GCS?
allQuestions.explanation: Eye opening to command scores 3, obeying commands scores 6, and confused conversation scores 4, giving 3 + 6 + 4 = 13.

allQuestions.text: A patient's eyes open to voice, speech consists of inappropriate words, and he localizes pain. What is the GCS?
allQuestions.explanation: Eye opening to voice is 3, inappropriate words is 3, and localizing pain is 5, giving a total GCS of 11. Withdrawal rather than localization would score M4 and give 10.

allQuestions.text: A 40-year-old motorcyclist with isolated head injury has unequal dilated pupils, eye opening to pain, incomprehensible sounds, and abnormal flexion. BP is 130/80 mmHg with noisy breathing. What are the GCS and the immediate management?
options: GCS 9; observe and repeat the examination
GCS 7; mannitol and CT before addressing the airway
GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
GCS 5; burr-hole decompression in the emergency department
originalOptions: GCS 9; observe and repeat the examination
GCS 7; mannitol and CT before addressing the airway
GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
GCS 5; burr-hole decompression in the emergency department
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: GCS 7; secure the airway with cervical protection, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give hyperosmolar therapy, and obtain urgent CT and neurosurgical review
allQuestions.explanation: E2 + V2 + M3 = 7, and unequal dilated pupils with falling consciousness indicate impending herniation. Airway control comes first, and hyperventilation is only a brief rescue measure.

allQuestions.text: A 21-year-old man thrown from a horse has a facial injury and a GCS of 9. Despite suction and an oropharyngeal airway, he continues to snore. What is the next step?
options: CT of the head before airway intervention
originalOptions: CT of the head before airway intervention
allQuestions.explanation: Persistent obstruction despite basic maneuvers shows the airway cannot be maintained, so a definitive airway is required. Pre-intubation GCS components are documented, and CT follows once the patient is stable.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about moderate brain injury is correct?
options: CT is indicated only if a neurological deficit is present
If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
Discharge depends on clinical examination alone
originalOptions: CT is indicated only if a neurological deficit is present
If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
Discharge depends on clinical examination alone
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: If the patient deteriorates, he should be managed as a severe head injury
allQuestions.explanation: Moderate injury is GCS 9–13, all patients need CT, and serial neurological examination is mandatory. Deterioration prompts the severe-injury pathway of airway control, ICP management, and neurosurgical consultation.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an indication for CT of the brain after minor head injury?
options: Two or more episodes of vomiting
GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
originalOptions: Two or more episodes of vomiting
GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) A single episode of vomiting
allQuestions.explanation: By the Canadian CT Head Rule, vomiting becomes an indication only with two or more episodes. A single episode is not sufficient on its own.

allQuestions.text: All of the following statements about subdural hematoma are correct EXCEPT:
options: It worsens if the patient is taking anticoagulants
It carries high morbidity and mortality because of the underlying brain injury
It needs rapid evacuation if CT shows a midline shift of more than 5 mm
It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
originalOptions: It worsens if the patient is taking anticoagulants
It carries high morbidity and mortality because of the underlying brain injury
It needs rapid evacuation if CT shows a midline shift of more than 5 mm
It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is classically caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery
allQuestions.explanation: Subdural hematoma results from torn bridging veins. Middle meningeal artery injury, usually after temporal bone fracture, causes epidural hematoma.

allQuestions.text: All of the following statements about epidural hematoma are correct EXCEPT:
options: It is associated with skull fracture
It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
It has a lenticular (biconvex) shape on CT
It is associated with a lucid interval
originalOptions: It is associated with skull fracture
It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
It has a lenticular (biconvex) shape on CT
It is associated with a lucid interval
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is classically caused by a tear of the bridging veins
allQuestions.explanation: Epidural hematoma arises from the middle meningeal artery and is lens-shaped on CT. Bridging-vein tears cause subdural hematoma, which is crescent-shaped.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a definitive airway?
allQuestions.explanation: A definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea that protects against aspiration. A laryngeal mask is a supraglottic device and does not fully protect the airway.

allQuestions.text: A patient with head trauma, a depressed skull fracture, gurgling respirations, and vomitus on the face has a low GCS. After supplemental oxygen and jaw elevation, what is the next step?
options: Obtain a lateral cervical spine X-ray
originalOptions: Obtain a lateral cervical spine X-ray
allQuestions.explanation: Gurgling indicates fluid in the airway, and it must be cleared before ventilation can be effective. Failure to suction prevents airway management and risks aspiration.

allQuestions.text: A 17-year-old helmeted motorcyclist has GCS 7, BP 140/92 mmHg, HR 88/min, and RR 18/min. Appropriate immobilization should include a semirigid cervical collar and:
options: Soft collar in place of the rigid collar
originalOptions: Soft collar in place of the rigid collar
allQuestions.explanation: A rigid collar with a long board and head blocks is standard for transport of a patient with possible spinal injury. The patient should be removed from the board as soon as practical to limit pressure and respiratory complications.

allQuestions.text: Cervical spine injury should be assumed in all of the following EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated chest pain is not a criterion for presuming cervical injury. Multisystem trauma, altered consciousness, neurological deficit, and significant blunt injury above the clavicles are.

allQuestions.text: Which finding precludes clinical clearance of the cervical spine without imaging?
options: Absence of a painful distracting injury
originalOptions: Absence of a painful distracting injury
allQuestions.explanation: NEXUS and Canadian C-spine criteria require a normal level of alertness for clinical clearance. An obtunded patient cannot be cleared clinically and requires imaging.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following alone is NOT sufficient to clear the cervical spine and remove the collar?
options: Absence of pain with voluntary movement
originalOptions: Absence of pain with voluntary movement
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) A negative cervical spine X-ray
allQuestions.explanation: Plain films miss a substantial proportion of cervical injuries. Clearance requires clinical criteria, with CT or MRI when indicated.

allQuestions.text: Which statement is correct regarding rigid cervical collars in isolated penetrating neck trauma?
options: They are mandatory in all cases
They must be applied before airway assessment
They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
They are indicated only when an anterior neck hematoma is present
originalOptions: They are mandatory in all cases
They must be applied before airway assessment
They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
They are indicated only when an anterior neck hematoma is present
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They should be avoided because they can obscure bleeding, impede airway inspection, and delay surgery
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated penetrating neck trauma rarely causes unstable spinal injury. A collar can hide expanding hematoma and hinder airway management.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT generally used in acute traumatic brain-injury care?
allQuestions.explanation: Anticoagulation worsens intracranial hemorrhage and requires reversal in head injury. Hyperosmolar agents, anticonvulsants, sedation, and isotonic fluids are part of acute management.

allQuestions.text: In a trauma patient with cerebral edema, why should hypercarbia be avoided?
options: It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
originalOptions: It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood flow and ICP
allQuestions.explanation: CO₂ is a potent cerebral vasodilator, so hypercarbia raises intracranial pressure. The target PaCO₂ is 35–40 mmHg, with brief hyperventilation reserved for herniation.

allQuestions.text: In managing a head-injured patient, what is the most important initial step?
allQuestions.explanation: Airway comes first in the ABCDE sequence. Hypoxia and hypotension are the most damaging secondary insults to an injured brain.

allQuestions.text: A 73-year-old man falls down stairs. He is hypotensive and tachycardic, opens his eyes to voice, is confused, and has clear fluid dripping from the ear with mastoid ecchymosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Otorrhea of cerebrospinal fluid with mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign) is the classic sign of basilar skull fracture. Hypotension, however, should still prompt a search for hemorrhage elsewhere.

allQuestions.text: A motorcyclist with severe facial fractures and GCS 6 arrives in the emergency department. What is the immediate management?
options: CT of the head and face before airway management
Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
Maxillofacial reduction before any airway intervention
originalOptions: CT of the head and face before airway management
Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
Maxillofacial reduction before any airway intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Early definitive airway with cervical-spine protection by the most experienced operator, with a rescue surgical-airway plan, treating the patient as severe TBI
allQuestions.explanation: Facial fractures with GCS 6 imply a difficult airway and an unprotected airway. Traumatic brain injury and cervical spine injury must be presumed.

allQuestions.text: A facial-trauma patient with initial hypoxemia and GCS 10 is intubated with cervical-spine protection and becomes physiologically stable. What should be done next?
options: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
originalOptions: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine, with facial imaging as indicated
allQuestions.explanation: Once the patient is stabilized, CT is the investigation of choice for acute intracranial and cervical injury. Neurosurgical and maxillofacial teams are involved early.

allQuestions.text: A trauma patient has BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 125/min, SpO₂ 89%, and is unresponsive to voice. A foot is deformed and the opposite arm has a large laceration. What is the best next step?
options: Apply a tourniquet to the deformed foot
Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
originalOptions: Apply a tourniquet to the deformed foot
Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Airway control with cervical-spine protection while controlling the external hemorrhage and resuscitating shock
allQuestions.explanation: The unresponsive, hypoxic patient needs airway control, while the bleeding arm laceration needs direct control simultaneously. The deformed foot is a closed injury and does not require a tourniquet.

allQuestions.text: A hemodynamically unstable patient has a narrow-complex tachycardia of 180/min. What is the next step?
allQuestions.explanation: Instability from a tachyarrhythmia mandates immediate synchronized cardioversion. Adenosine and vagal maneuvers are reserved for stable patients.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are adjuncts to the primary survey of a trauma patient EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: CT requires transport and a relatively stable patient, so it belongs to the secondary survey. ECG, ABG, FAST, and portable radiographs are primary-survey adjuncts.

allQuestions.text: As the first doctor receiving a trauma patient in the emergency room, what is the most important task?
options: Write the specific details of the injury
Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
originalOptions: Write the specific details of the injury
Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Perform the ABCDE primary survey and treat life-threatening problems
allQuestions.explanation: The first clinical priority is identification and treatment of immediate life threats. History and documentation follow stabilization.

allQuestions.text: What is the appropriate initial volume of crystalloid for a pediatric trauma patient in shock?
allQuestions.explanation: The traditional initial pediatric bolus is 20 mL/kg of warmed isotonic crystalloid, followed by reassessment. In hemorrhagic shock, blood products are started early rather than repeating large crystalloid volumes.

allQuestions.text: Which screening radiographs are traditionally obtained in the initial assessment of a multiply injured patient?
allQuestions.explanation: The classic trauma series comprises a lateral cervical spine, an AP chest, and an AP pelvis. Current practice is selective and relies on CT according to stability and local protocol.

allQuestions.text: In the initial assessment of trauma patients, which of the following does NOT affect circulation?
options: Second-degree burn of 20% body surface area
originalOptions: Second-degree burn of 20% body surface area
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated brain injury does not cause hypotension, so shock should prompt a search for hemorrhage or another cause. Spinal cord injury causes neurogenic shock, and the other options reduce effective circulating volume or cardiac output.

allQuestions.text: In the initial assessment of trauma patients, which of the following does NOT affect ventilation?
allQuestions.explanation: Tamponade impairs circulation by restricting cardiac filling, not ventilation. The other options directly impair air entry or lung expansion.

allQuestions.text: Maintaining a target systolic blood pressure of 80–90 mmHg in active hemorrhage without traumatic brain injury, until surgical hemostasis is achieved, is known as:
allQuestions.explanation: Permissive hypotension is a component of damage-control resuscitation. It avoids disrupting early clot, and it is not used in traumatic brain injury, where cerebral perfusion pressure must be maintained.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an immediately life-threatening thoracic injury identified and treated during the primary survey?
allQuestions.explanation: Esophageal rupture is serious but is usually identified in the secondary survey. Airway obstruction, tension and open pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, and tamponade are the immediate threats.

allQuestions.text: Which statement best distinguishes a mass-casualty incident from a multiple-casualty incident?
options: A multiple-casualty incident exceeds the facility's resources
A mass-casualty incident can be handled with the usual resources
In a mass-casualty incident, only the most severely injured are treated, regardless of survivability
A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
originalOptions: A multiple-casualty incident exceeds the facility's resources
A mass-casualty incident can be handled with the usual resources
In a mass-casualty incident, only the most severely injured are treated, regardless of survivability
A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A mass-casualty incident exceeds the available resources and requires disaster triage
allQuestions.explanation: In a multiple-casualty incident, resources are adequate and the most seriously injured are treated first. A mass-casualty incident overwhelms capacity.

allQuestions.text: Which principle applies to triage in a mass-casualty incident?
options: Allocate the most time and equipment to the most severely injured, including those with unsurvivable injuries
Treat patients in order of arrival
Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
Treat children before all other patients
originalOptions: Allocate the most time and equipment to the most severely injured, including those with unsurvivable injuries
Treat patients in order of arrival
Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
Treat children before all other patients
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Use limited resources for the greatest overall benefit, with unsurvivable injuries classified as expectant
allQuestions.explanation: The goal shifts from the best outcome for one patient to the best outcome for the greatest number. Committing disproportionate resources to one patient reduces total lives saved.

allQuestions.text: A patient with multiple stab wounds has BP 89/40 mmHg and is irritable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypotension with altered behavior after multiple stab wounds indicates major blood loss. Tamponade and tension pneumothorax must still be actively excluded during the Breathing and Circulation steps.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT included in the primary survey?
allQuestions.explanation: The primary survey is limited to identifying and treating immediate life threats. A detailed history (AMPLE) belongs to the secondary survey.

allQuestions.text: A patient with diabetes and hypertension has fever, hypotension, and turbid urine draining from a Foley catheter. Which shock state is most likely?
allQuestions.explanation: Fever and hypotension with a urinary catheter and turbid urine point to a urinary source of sepsis. Treatment is cultures, early antimicrobials, resuscitation, and source control.

allQuestions.text: A patient has dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hemoptysis, and pulmonary embolism is strongly suspected. What is the imaging study of choice?
allQuestions.explanation: CTPA is the first-line confirmatory test in a stable patient with a high pre-test probability. V/Q scanning is preferred in pregnancy, renal impairment, or contrast allergy.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is essential before passing a urinary catheter in a male trauma patient?
options: Perform a retrograde urethrogram in every patient
originalOptions: Perform a retrograde urethrogram in every patient
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Examine the rectum and perineum
allQuestions.explanation: Rectal and perineal examination excludes signs of urethral injury, namely a high-riding prostate, perineal bruising, and a scrotal hematoma. Blood at the meatus likewise warrants a retrograde urethrogram before catheterization.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to Foley catheter insertion in a trauma patient?
allQuestions.explanation: Urinary retention is an indication for catheterization. The other findings suggest urethral disruption and require a urethrogram first.

allQuestions.text: What does the AMPLE history mnemonic stand for in the trauma secondary survey?
options: Airway, Medications, Pain, Last meal, Events
Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
Age, Medications, Previous surgery, Labs, Environment
originalOptions: Airway, Medications, Pain, Last meal, Events
Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
Age, Medications, Previous surgery, Labs, Environment
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events surrounding the injury
allQuestions.explanation: AMPLE is the focused history obtained in the secondary survey. Pregnancy is included under past medical history, and the event history covers the environment and mechanism.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common type of shock in trauma patients?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypotension after trauma is hemorrhagic until proven otherwise. Tension pneumothorax and tamponade must still be excluded during the primary survey.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolytic therapy?
options: Ischemic stroke more than 3 months earlier
originalOptions: Ischemic stroke more than 3 months earlier
allQuestions.explanation: Any prior intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication because of the risk of recurrent intracranial bleeding. The other options are relative contraindications or are not contraindications.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an indication for intubation?
options: GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
Severe maxillofacial injury with impending airway obstruction
originalOptions: GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
Severe maxillofacial injury with impending airway obstruction
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: GCS of 10 with a protected airway and adequate oxygenation
allQuestions.explanation: A GCS of 8 or less is the threshold for intubation. A patient with a higher GCS needs intubation only if the airway is unprotected or deterioration is anticipated.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an objective sign of airway obstruction?
options: Use of accessory muscles of respiration
originalOptions: Use of accessory muscles of respiration
allQuestions.explanation: Neck vein distention reflects a circulatory problem such as tamponade or tension pneumothorax. Stridor, accessory-muscle use, paradoxical movement, and cyanosis are objective signs of airway obstruction.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about trauma patients with comorbidities is false?
options: In elderly patients, normal vital signs may mask significant shock
They warrant a lower threshold for imaging and admission
They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
originalOptions: In elderly patients, normal vital signs may mask significant shock
They warrant a lower threshold for imaging and admission
They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They should not be transferred to a higher-level facility
allQuestions.explanation: Patients with comorbidities have poor reserve and benefit from care at a higher-level trauma center. Transfer is appropriate when their needs exceed local capability.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about the emergency management of trauma patients is correct?
options: The specific injury must be identified before management begins
The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
A detailed history must precede resuscitation
Diagnosis must be established before treatment
Unstable patients should undergo CT first
originalOptions: The specific injury must be identified before management begins
The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
A detailed history must precede resuscitation
Diagnosis must be established before treatment
Unstable patients should undergo CT first
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The priorities are the same for all trauma patients
allQuestions.explanation: Management follows the same ABCDE sequence of treating the greatest threat to life first. It does not depend on knowing the specific injury.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about the classes of hemorrhagic shock is false?
options: Class IV: more than 40% blood loss
Class I: normal heart rate and blood pressure
Class I: less than 5% blood loss
originalOptions: Class IV: more than 40% blood loss
Class I: normal heart rate and blood pressure
Class I: less than 5% blood loss
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Class I: less than 5% blood loss
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Class I: less than 5% blood loss
allQuestions.explanation: Class I corresponds to a loss of less than 15% of blood volume, which the body absorbs with little physiological change.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about airway management in trauma is false?
options: Endotracheal intubation helps protect the airway
Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
Endotracheal intubation allows control of ventilation
originalOptions: Endotracheal intubation helps protect the airway
Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
Endotracheal intubation allows control of ventilation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Endotracheal intubation is always required in trauma
allQuestions.explanation: Intubation is indicated when airway protection, oxygenation, ventilation, or severe neurological compromise requires it, not simply because trauma occurred.

allQuestions.text: How should the airway be opened in a trauma patient with possible cervical spine injury?
options: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway in every patient
Flexing the neck over a pillow
originalOptions: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway in every patient
Flexing the neck over a pillow
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilization
allQuestions.explanation: Jaw thrust opens the airway without extending the neck. Head-tilt/chin-lift is avoided when cervical injury is suspected.

allQuestions.text: Which rapid adjuncts help identify occult hemorrhage in an unstable trauma patient?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
originalOptions: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: eFAST with portable chest and pelvic radiographs
allQuestions.explanation: These bedside studies identify the main hidden sources of bleeding without leaving the resuscitation area. A baseline hemoglobin cannot exclude acute hemorrhage, and unstable patients should not go to CT.

allQuestions.text: How is hemorrhage from an unstable pelvic fracture managed?
options: Repeated rocking of the pelvis to assess stability
Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
Urinary catheter insertion in all patients
originalOptions: Repeated rocking of the pelvis to assess stability
Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
Urinary catheter insertion in all patients
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, and early hemorrhage control
allQuestions.explanation: Circumferential compression reduces pelvic volume and tamponades venous and bony bleeding. Definitive control is by pelvic packing, angioembolization, or surgery according to physiology and resources.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about traumatic diaphragmatic injury is FALSE?
options: Blunt trauma can produce a large diaphragmatic tear
It may be misinterpreted as hemothorax on chest radiograph
Even small tears require surgical repair
A nasogastric tube coiled in the chest is a diagnostic clue
The right diaphragm is injured more often than the left
originalOptions: Blunt trauma can produce a large diaphragmatic tear
It may be misinterpreted as hemothorax on chest radiograph
Even small tears require surgical repair
A nasogastric tube coiled in the chest is a diagnostic clue
The right diaphragm is injured more often than the left
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) The right diaphragm is injured more often than the left
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The right diaphragm is injured more often than the left
allQuestions.explanation: Left-sided injury is more common because the liver protects the right hemidiaphragm. The injury can be missed initially and later present as herniation of bowel or stomach into the thorax.

allQuestions.text: An unresponsive patient regains a pulse after defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation, and the post-shock ECG shows third-degree AV block with a slow ventricular rate. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
allQuestions.explanation: With a pulse present, symptomatic complete heart block is treated with transcutaneous pacing (± dopamine/epinephrine infusion) rather than defibrillation or chest compressions, which are reserved for pulseless rhythms.
allQuestions.note: Without a pulse, this is PEA: resume CPR and give epinephrine; routine pacing during established arrest is not recommended.

allQuestions.text: The recovered ECG shows P waves marching out independently from QRS complexes at a faster rate than the ventricular rate, with no fixed relationship between P and QRS. What is the diagnosis? [img: ERArrhythmia1.png ]
options: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
originalOptions: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
allQuestions.explanation: Complete AV dissociation — P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular escape rate — defines third-degree AV block, unlike Mobitz I/II where some P waves still conduct.

allQuestions.text: Which statement correctly differentiates Mobitz type I from Mobitz type II second-degree AV block?
options: Mobitz I has a constant PR interval with sudden dropped beats; Mobitz II shows progressive PR prolongation
Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
originalOptions: Mobitz I has a constant PR interval with sudden dropped beats; Mobitz II shows progressive PR prolongation
Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
allQuestions.explanation: Mobitz I reflects reversible AV-nodal delay with progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat; Mobitz II is an infranodal block with fixed PR intervals and a higher risk of progressing to complete heart block.

allQuestions.text: A 12-lead ECG shows a constant PR interval of 240 ms with every P wave followed by a QRS complex. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A fixed PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction (no dropped beats) defines first-degree AV block, a partial delay rather than an interruption of conduction.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia2.png ] The ECG shows constant PR intervals with intermittent nonconducted P waves in a patient with an acute anterior wall MI. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
originalOptions: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
allQuestions.explanation: Mobitz II or high-grade AV block complicating anterior MI reflects extensive infranodal conduction system damage and can progress abruptly to complete block/asystole, so urgent pacing readiness and cardiology evaluation are required rather than observation or AV-nodal blocking drugs.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia3.png ] An asymptomatic 29-year-old has first-degree AV block on this ECG with no other conduction disease. What is the best next step?
options: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
originalOptions: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic first-degree AV block requires no acute intervention beyond identifying reversible causes (e.g., AV-nodal blocking drugs); cardioversion and defibrillation are irrelevant since this is not a tachyarrhythma

allQuestions.text: What are the defining ECG features of complete (third-degree) AV block?
options: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
originalOptions: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
allQuestions.explanation: In third-degree block, P waves and QRS complexes occur completely independently (AV dissociation), with the atrial rate faster than the escape ventricular rate; the escape QRS is narrow if junctional, wide if ventricular/infranodal.

allQuestions.text: What ECG finding is diagnostic of complete (third-degree) heart block?
options: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
originalOptions: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
allQuestions.explanation: The hallmark of complete heart block is total dissociation of atrial and ventricular activity — P waves and QRS complexes occur independently at their own rates.

allQuestions.text: A patient develops Mobitz II AV block complicating an acute anterior wall MI. When is a permanent pacemaker indicated?
options: Only if the patient develops asystole
Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves
If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
originalOptions: Only if the patient develops asystole
Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves
If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression

allQuestions.text: A patient has atrial fibrillation of unknown duration and is hemodynamically stable. What anticoagulation strategy should precede elective cardioversion?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
No anticoagulation needed if cardioversion restores sinus rhythm
Anticoagulation is only needed after cardioversion, not before

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia4.png] A hemodynamically stable patient has atrial flutter with a ventricular rate around 130/min and no heart-failure symptoms. What is the best initial treatment?

allQuestions.text: Which arrhythmia is most commonly associated with thyrotoxicosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis sensitizes atrial myocardium and is a classic reversible cause of atrial fibrillation; thyroid function should be checked in all new-onset AF.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] A patient has had palpitations for 1 week due to atrial fibrillation, with no syncope, heart failure, or chest pain. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
allQuestions.explanation: In stable AF with preserved LVEF, IV diltiazem provides acute ventricular rate control; cardioversion is not first-line without addressing anticoagulation given the AF duration is ≥48 hours, and defibrillation is inappropriate for a non-shockable rhythm with a pulse.

allQuestions.text: Which finding alone is NOT considered an ACLS sign of hemodynamic instability in a patient with atrial flutter?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) A high ventricular rate alone

allQuestions.text: In a patient with atrial fibrillation, which factor determines whether rate control or rhythm control is prioritized, and how should ventricular rate be managed if AF is hemodynamically stable?
options: If AF causes instability, perform immediate synchronized cardioversion; if stable, choose rate or rhythm control based on symptoms/comorbidities, using a beta-blocker as an acute rate-control option (diltiazem/verapamil reserved for LVEF >40%)
All stable AF patients require immediate cardioversion regardless of duration

allQuestions.text: A hemodynamically stable patient with atrial fibrillation has an LVEF of 30%. Which agent should be avoided for ventricular rate control?
allQuestions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers have negative inotropic effects and should be avoided when LVEF is below 40%; beta-blockers (if compensated), digoxin, or amiodarone in decompensated states are preferred alternatives.

allQuestions.text: A patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Which class of drugs must be avoided?

allQuestions.text: What is the primary indication for emergency electrical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation?
options: AF diagnosed incidentally on a routine ECG

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] What rhythm is shown on this 12-lead ECG?
allQuestions.explanation: The tracing shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm without discrete P waves, replaced by fine fibrillatory baseline oscillations — diagnostic of atrial fibrillation.

allQuestions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a heart rate of 32/min and a palpable pulse. Which of the following are acceptable therapeutic options if the initial drug is ineffective?
options: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion

Observation only, since bradycardia is never treated pharmacologically

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] An adult patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse and poor perfusion. What is the correct approach to management?

allQuestions.text: What is the first-line medication to treat symptomatic bradycardia?
allQuestions.explanation: Atropine is the first drug given in the adult symptomatic bradycardia algorithm because it reverses excessive vagal tone at the SA/AV node; beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers would worsen bradycardia.

allQuestions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise. What is the correct atropine dosing and next step if ineffective?

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an EXTRINSIC (reversible) cause of bradycardia rather than intrinsic SA-node disease?

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a pathological, intrinsic cause of bradycardia rather than a normal physiological variant?
options: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
originalOptions: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia6.png] A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presents with palpitations. and she is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step for management?

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia19.png] A 73-year-old ICU patient becomes unresponsive with a tachyarrhythmia on ECG and a blood pressure of 70/40. What is the best next step for management?

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia7.png] A patient becomes unresponsive and the ECG shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate next step?

allQuestions.text: How is adult asystolic cardiac arrest managed?

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] A young athlete collapses and the his ECG. What is the rhythm?
allQuestions.explanation: The twisting QRS axis around the isoelectric baseline is characteristic of torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT associated with QT prolongation (e.g., congenital long-QT syndrome in a young patient).

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia9.png] An 85-year-old previously healthy woman presents with recurrent syncope, the last episode an hour ago. Her ECG shows a fixed PR interval with intermittently nonconducted P waves. What type of block does she have?
allQuestions.explanation: A constant PR interval with sudden, unpredicted dropped QRS complexes (no progressive lengthening) defines Mobitz type II, an infranodal block with a high risk of progression to complete heart block — consistent with her syncope.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] An ICU patient becomes unresponsive with no pulse and is not breathing. What is the best next step?
allQuestions.explanation: Pulseless polymorphic VT (torsades) is treated as a shockable rhythm; immediate defibrillation takes priority over airway management or drug administration.

allQuestions.text: Which intervention provides the greatest immediate survival benefit in ventricular fibrillation?

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia11.png] An athletic patient presents with a racing heart sensation and stable vitals. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. What do you give?

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia12.png] A patient has normal vital signs with a heart rate of 170/min. The ECG shows a regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia. What do you give?

allQuestions.text: What are the symptoms/signs of tachycardia (HR >150 bpm) that indicate urgent treatment?

allQuestions.text: A patient has a tachyarrhythmia with a rate above 150 bpm but is asymptomatic with normal blood pressure and mentation. How should this be classified?

allQuestions.text: A patient is found pulseless with an organized rhythm on the monitor. What is the most appropriate management?

allQuestions.text: How is an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse treated?

allQuestions.text: A patient treated for SVT develops transient flushing, chest pressure, and dyspnea immediately after a rapid IV drug push. Which drug most likely caused these effects?
allQuestions.explanation: Adenosine causes brief, self-limited flushing, chest pressure, and dyspnea due to its very short half-life and transient AV-nodal/vasodilatory effects, which resolve within seconds.

allQuestions.text: A conscious, hemodynamically stable patient has regular monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. What is the next treatment?

allQuestions.text: A person with alcohol use disorder collapses and is found to be in torsades de pointes. What intervention is most likely to correct the underlying problem?

allQuestions.text: What is ventricular bigeminy?

Two consecutive PVCs followed by a compensatory pause

allQuestions.explanation: Bigeminy describes the fixed alternating pattern of one sinus beat followed by one PVC, repeating throughout the rhythm strip.

allQuestions.text: What is the underlying etiology of torsades de pointes?

allQuestions.text: What is the first-line treatment for a drug-resistant, stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse that persists despite antiarrhythmic therapy?

allQuestions.text: Which drugs must be avoided in a patient with WPW syndrome who develops atrial fibrillation?

allQuestions.text: What is a delta wave on ECG?
options: A notched, tall R wave in the inferior leads

allQuestions.explanation: The delta wave reflects pre-excitation — early ventricular depolarization via an accessory pathway bypassing the AV node's normal conduction delay — and, with a short PR interval, is diagnostic of WPW.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia18.png ] What is the diagnostic ECG triad of Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation?

options: Assess duration, stroke risk, heart failure/LVEF, blood pressure, and pre-excitation; use appropriate ventricular rate control and an anticoagulation/rhythm strategy as indicated

allQuestions.text: What are the ECG characteristics of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?

allQuestions.text: A 55-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolaemia, and known stable angina, presents with chest pain radiating to both arms. What ECG finding is most likely?
allQuestions.explanation: Stable angina is demand ischaemia on a fixed plaque without myocardial infarction, so the ECG and troponin are typically normal. Persistent ST depression suggests NSTE-ACS, ST elevation suggests STEMI or vasospasm, and Q waves indicate an old infarct.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognised life-threatening complication of acute coronary syndrome?
options: Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VF or pulseless VT)
Papillary-muscle rupture with acute severe mitral regurgitation
Ventricular free-wall rupture with cardiac tamponade

allQuestions.explanation: ACS complications are electrical (VF, pulseless VT, high-grade AV block), pump failure (acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock), and mechanical (papillary-muscle rupture, septal rupture, free-wall rupture). Tension pneumothorax is not a complication of MI.

allQuestions.text: What is the most clinically important adverse effect of nitroglycerin?
allQuestions.explanation: Dose-related vasodilation causes hypotension, which is the most clinically important effect and can lead to syncope. Headache is very common but not dangerous, and reflex tachycardia is a secondary response.

allQuestions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with chest pain. She has a history of previous deep vein thrombosis and is not pregnant. Pulmonary embolism is suspected. What is the investigation of choice?
allQuestions.explanation: CTPA is the first-line confirmatory test for suspected PE in a non-pregnant patient with no contrast contraindication. V/Q scanning is preferred only in pregnancy, significant renal impairment, or contrast allergy, and CXR, ECG, and echocardiography cannot confirm PE.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with tearing chest pain and a difference in blood pressure between the two arms. What is the best initial medication?
allQuestions.explanation: Tearing chest pain with an inter-arm BP difference indicates aortic dissection, which requires IV beta-blockade first (target heart rate 60–70 bpm, systolic BP 100–120 mmHg) to reduce aortic shear stress. Antiplatelets, anticoagulants, and thrombolytics are contraindicated, and a vasodilator is added only after heart-rate control.

allQuestions.text: A diabetic patient presents with dyspnoea but no chest pain. Which diagnosis must NOT be missed?
allQuestions.explanation: Diabetic patients, especially those with autonomic neuropathy, often present with silent or atypical ACS in which dyspnoea is the anginal equivalent. The other options are pain-predominant conditions and are not the critical diagnosis to exclude.

allQuestions.text: An older farmer develops central chest pain while working. The pain subsides after a 10-minute rest and returns when he resumes work. His ECG and troponin are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Predictable exertional pain that is relieved by rest, with normal ECG and troponin, indicates stable angina (demand ischaemia on a fixed plaque with no infarction). Unstable angina presents with new, crescendo, or rest pain, and NSTEMI requires a troponin rise.

allQuestions.text: A patient with confirmed STEMI is in an ambulance. A non-PCI hospital and a PCI-capable hospital are each about 15 minutes away. What is the best management?

Take him to the nearest emergency department and wait for serial troponins
Transfer him directly to the PCI-capable hospital for primary PCI
Give fibrinolytics in the ambulance, then take him to the non-PCI hospital

allQuestions.explanation: Primary PCI is preferred when the anticipated first-medical-contact-to-device delay is 120 minutes or less, and the patient should not be detoured to a non-PCI hospital. Fibrinolysis is reserved for when the delay to PCI exceeds 120 minutes.

allQuestions.text: What is the definitive reperfusion treatment for an eligible STEMI patient at a PCI-capable centre?
allQuestions.explanation: In STEMI the goal is reperfusion, and primary PCI within 90 minutes of arrival is the preferred strategy at a PCI-capable centre. Fibrinolysis is used only when timely PCI is not available.

allQuestions.text: An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. The most likely location of the myocardial infarction is: [img: ERChestInferiorMI.jpg ]
allQuestions.explanation: ST elevation in II, III and aVF localises the infarct to the inferior wall (usually RCA), with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. Lateral infarcts involve I, aVL, V5–V6, anterior or septal infarcts involve V1–V4, and posterior MI shows reciprocal ST depression in V1–V2.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following medications used in coronary artery disease relieves symptoms but has no proven effect on mortality or morbidity?
allQuestions.explanation: Nitrates relieve angina through vasodilation but have not been shown to improve survival. Aspirin and statins reduce cardiovascular events in established CAD, and beta-blockers improve prognosis after MI.

allQuestions.text: A patient has ischaemic chest pain. The ECG shows no ST-segment elevation (normal, ST depression, or T-wave inversion) and the troponin level is elevated. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: NSTEMI is myocardial injury with a troponin rise without ST elevation. Unstable angina has a normal troponin, and STEMI requires ST elevation or hyperacute T waves.

allQuestions.text: Chest pain radiating to the jaw and relieved by sitting forward is most likely due to:
allQuestions.explanation: Pericarditis pain is classically worse when lying supine and relieved by sitting forward, and may radiate to the neck, back, or jaw. Stable angina is exertional and relieved by rest or GTN, not by posture.

allQuestions.text: Chest pain that is reproducible on palpation of the chest wall most likely indicates:
allQuestions.explanation: Pain reproduced by chest-wall palpation points to a musculoskeletal cause and lowers the probability of ACS (LR ≈ 0.3). It does not exclude ACS on its own, since about 15% of ACS patients also have chest-wall tenderness.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are life-threatening causes of chest pain EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Costochondritis is a benign musculoskeletal cause of chest pain. Aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, PE, and oesophageal rupture are all immediately life-threatening.

allQuestions.text: In a patient with suspected acute myocardial infarction, which of the following statements is FALSE?

allQuestions.text: A patient with a previous history of myocardial infarction attends the cardiology clinic for a routine check-up. He is asymptomatic, and his ECG is shown. What is the most appropriate management? [img: ERChestnoacutetherapy.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: A fixed PR interval above 200 ms with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV block, which is benign and needs no treatment when asymptomatic. Pacing is reserved for symptomatic bradycardia, asymptomatic Mobitz II, or complete heart block.

allQuestions.text: What is abdominal angina, and what is its classic presentation?

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with sudden-onset tearing chest pain radiating to the back. This is classically associated with:
allQuestions.explanation: Aortic dissection typically causes abrupt, severe tearing pain that is maximal at onset and radiates to the back. Myocardial infarction causes pressure-like pain that builds more gradually, and pericarditis pain is positional.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common initiating event of acute coronary syndrome?

allQuestions.text: A patient with a tachyarrhythmia (ECG shown) has hypotension and ischaemic chest discomfort. What is the immediate treatment? [img: ERChestisc.png ]

allQuestions.text: An ECG shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment? [img: ERChestacutepericarditis.png ]

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional 8 D's of stroke care?

originalOptions: Tadalafil use within the past 48 hours
Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with normal blood pressure and no other contraindication
allQuestions.explanation: Nitrates are indicated for ongoing angina when blood pressure permits. They cause severe hypotension in preload-dependent states (RV infarction, severe aortic stenosis), in baseline hypotension, and after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours).

allQuestions.text: A patient with STEMI has been referred for primary PCI and the catheterisation laboratory is activated. Which medication regimen should be started while preparing for PCI?
options: Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
originalOptions: Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g. clopidogrel), and an anticoagulant (UFH or LMWH)
allQuestions.explanation: Aspirin is given immediately, with clopidogrel whenever PCI is planned and initial anticoagulation with heparin or LMWH, along with a high-intensity statin. Warfarin is not an acute anticoagulant in ACS, and nitrates, morphine, and oxygen are given only for specific indications.

allQuestions.text: Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression is seen in:
allQuestions.explanation: Pericarditis causes diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression (and PR elevation in aVR). Tamponade shows low-voltage QRS and electrical alternans, and benign early repolarisation lacks PR depression and is stable on serial ECGs.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the most common ECG finding in acute pulmonary embolism?
allQuestions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. S1Q3T3 is classic but rare, and RBBB, right axis deviation, and P pulmonale are less common, non-specific findings.

allQuestions.text: What is the key chest X-ray finding in acute aortic dissection?
options: Visceral pleural line with absent lung markings
originalOptions: Visceral pleural line with absent lung markings
allQuestions.explanation: A widened mediastinum with an abnormal aortic contour is the classic radiographic finding in aortic dissection, although a normal CXR never excludes it and CT aortography is the diagnostic study. A water-bottle silhouette indicates a large pericardial effusion.

allQuestions.text: A patient with diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolaemia presents with ischaemic chest pain, and the ECG shows lateral T-wave inversions. What is the best next step?
options: Discharge with an outpatient stress test
Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
originalOptions: Discharge with an outpatient stress test
Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Cardiac monitoring with aspirin and anti-ischaemic therapy while completing ACS risk stratification
allQuestions.explanation: T-wave inversion without ST elevation suggests NSTE-ACS, which is managed with monitoring, aspirin, anti-ischaemic therapy, and serial ECG and troponin with risk stratification (e.g. HEART or TIMI score). Fibrinolysis is indicated only for STEMI, and the timing of invasive management depends on risk.

allQuestions.text: Which leads primarily represent the anterior wall of the left ventricle?
allQuestions.explanation: V3–V4 overlie the anterior wall (LAD territory), V1–V2 the septum, and V5–V6 and I/aVL the lateral wall. V1–V4 together are often described as the anteroseptal/anterior territory.

allQuestions.text: Which myocardial territory is involved when ST elevation is seen in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5 and V6)? [img: ERChestlateralwall.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 face the lateral wall (circumflex or diagonal/LAD territory), and extension of the changes through V3–V6 is described as anterolateral. The inferior wall is represented by II, III and aVF, and posterior infarction appears as reciprocal ST depression in V1–V2.

allQuestions.text: Which medication should be avoided in inferior myocardial infarction because of possible right ventricular infarction and preload dependence?
allQuestions.explanation: Nitrates reduce preload, which can cause severe hypotension and even arrest in a preload-dependent RV infarction (confirmed by ST elevation in V4R) and after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use. Aspirin and antiplatelet therapy remain indicated, and oxygen is given only when SpO₂ is below 95%.

allQuestions.text: How is a posterior myocardial infarction recognised on the standard 12-lead ECG, and how is it best confirmed?
options: ST elevation in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
ST elevation in II, III and aVF, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
Pathological Q waves in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V3R–V4R)
ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6, confirmed by posterior leads V7–V9
originalOptions: ST elevation in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
ST elevation in II, III and aVF, confirmed by right-sided leads (V4R)
Pathological Q waves in V1–V3, confirmed by right-sided leads (V3R–V4R)
ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6, confirmed by posterior leads V7–V9
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall broad R waves, confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9
allQuestions.explanation: Posterior MI appears on the standard ECG only as reciprocal changes in V1–V3, and ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9 gives direct confirmation. Right-sided leads (V4R) are used to confirm right ventricular infarction.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolytic therapy in ACS?
options: Ischaemic stroke more than 3 months ago
originalOptions: Ischaemic stroke more than 3 months ago
allQuestions.explanation: Fibrinolysis can precipitate catastrophic bleeding in suspected aortic dissection, so it is an absolute contraindication. Pregnancy, current anticoagulant use, and an ischaemic stroke more than 3 months ago are relative contraindications.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following patients meets the criteria for fibrinolytic therapy?
options: A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
A patient with STEMI who presents directly to a PCI-capable centre with an expected door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes
originalOptions: A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
A patient with STEMI who presents directly to a PCI-capable centre with an expected door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A patient with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, no contraindication, and an anticipated first-medical-contact-to-PCI delay greater than 120 minutes
allQuestions.explanation: Fibrinolysis is indicated for STEMI (≥1 mm ST elevation in two contiguous leads) within the time window when timely PCI is not available. It is not used for NSTEMI or unstable angina, and primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered promptly.

allQuestions.text: A patient with STEMI arrived at a non-PCI hospital 30 minutes ago. The nearest PCI-capable centre is 45 minutes away, and the decision is made to transfer him for PCI. What is the maximum acceptable time from first medical contact to PCI?
allQuestions.explanation: When the patient presents to a non-PCI hospital, transfer for primary PCI is appropriate if the first-medical-contact-to-device time is 120 minutes or less; beyond that, fibrinolysis should be given. The 90-minute target applies only to direct presentation to a PCI-capable hospital.

allQuestions.text: What is the target door-to-balloon time for a patient presenting directly to a PCI-capable hospital?
allQuestions.explanation: The door-to-balloon target for primary PCI is within 90 minutes of arrival. Thirty minutes is the door-to-needle target for fibrinolysis, and 120 minutes is the first-medical-contact-to-device threshold used in transfer decisions.

allQuestions.text: A haemodynamically stable asthmatic patient has atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response and no heart failure (ECG shown). What is the most appropriate first treatment? [img: ERChestdiltiazem.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Stable AF is managed with rate control, and a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is preferred in asthma because beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm. Cardioversion is for unstable patients, adenosine is for regular narrow-complex SVT, and amiodarone is reserved for AF with reduced ejection fraction (EF < 40%).

allQuestions.text: Which leads are used for rapid ECG-axis determination?
allQuestions.explanation: Leads I and aVF divide the frontal plane into quadrants (I positive and aVF positive = normal axis; I positive and aVF negative = leftward axis; I negative and aVF positive = right axis). Lead II is used to resolve borderline left axis deviation.

allQuestions.text: How many large squares are there in 1 second of an ECG tracing at the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s?
allQuestions.explanation: One large square equals 0.20 s, so 1 second contains 5 large squares (25 mm). A small square equals 0.04 s.

allQuestions.text: What is the heart rate on the regular ECG strip shown, in which each R–R interval spans two large squares? [img: ERECG150beats.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Heart rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares between consecutive R waves = 300 ÷ 2 = 150 beats/min.

allQuestions.text: How many large squares are there in 1 minute of ECG tracing?
allQuestions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, 1 second contains 5 large squares, so 1 minute contains 5 × 60 = 300. This is the basis of the 300 rule for heart rate.

allQuestions.text: How many small squares are there in 1 minute of ECG tracing?
allQuestions.explanation: One small square equals 0.04 s, so 60 ÷ 0.04 = 1500. This is the basis of the 1500 rule for precise rate calculation.

allQuestions.text: How many small squares correspond to 1 mV of amplitude on a standard ECG?
allQuestions.explanation: The standard calibration is 10 mm/mV, and each small square (1 mm) equals 0.1 mV, so 10 small squares equal 1 mV.

allQuestions.text: Which method is used to calculate the heart rate from a regular rhythm on an ECG?
options: 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
1500 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
300 divided by the number of small squares between consecutive R waves
The number of QRS complexes in one large square multiplied by 300
The R–R interval in seconds multiplied by 60
originalOptions: 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
1500 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
300 divided by the number of small squares between consecutive R waves
The number of QRS complexes in one large square multiplied by 300
The R–R interval in seconds multiplied by 60
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: 300 divided by the number of large squares between consecutive R waves
allQuestions.explanation: The 300 rule applies to regular rhythms. The 1500 rule requires small squares (1500 ÷ small squares), and the heart rate is 60 divided by the R–R interval in seconds, not multiplied by it.

allQuestions.text: Calculate the ventricular rate on the regular ECG strip shown. [img: ERECG180beats.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: An R–R interval of about 1.7 large squares gives 300 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 180 beats/min using the 300 rule.

allQuestions.text: What ECG findings define right bundle branch block? [img: ERECGRBBB.png ]
options: QRS ≥120 ms with broad notched R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6 and a deep S wave in V1
QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with an rSR′ pattern in V1 and normal terminal forces
Short PR interval with a delta wave and a widened QRS
Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves
originalOptions: QRS ≥120 ms with broad notched R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6 and a deep S wave in V1
QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with an rSR′ pattern in V1 and normal terminal forces
Short PR interval with a delta wave and a widened QRS
Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: QRS ≥120 ms with an rsR′ (M-shaped) pattern in V1–V2 and a broad terminal S wave in I and V6
allQuestions.explanation: RBBB requires a QRS ≥120 ms with late right-ventricular forces (rsR′ in V1–V2) and a broad terminal S wave in the left-sided leads. Option C describes incomplete RBBB, and option A describes LBBB.

allQuestions.text: What diagnostic difficulties can arise when a patient has LBBB on the ECG?
options: It abolishes P waves, preventing rhythm interpretation
It shortens the PR interval and mimics pre-excitation
It produces diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, mimicking pericarditis
It produces a dominant R wave in V1, mimicking posterior MI
It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
originalOptions: It abolishes P waves, preventing rhythm interpretation
It shortens the PR interval and mimics pre-excitation
It produces diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, mimicking pericarditis
It produces a dominant R wave in V1, mimicking posterior MI
It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It causes secondary ST–T changes that can obscure or mimic acute ST elevation, making MI diagnosis and localisation difficult
allQuestions.explanation: LBBB alters ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation, so ischaemic ST changes are hard to interpret. Clinical context, serial biomarkers, and validated criteria such as modified Sgarbossa are used, and a new LBBB with chest pain is managed as a STEMI equivalent.

allQuestions.text: Which set of ECG findings supports the diagnosis of right ventricular hypertrophy?
options: Sokolow-Lyon voltage ≥35 mm with left axis deviation and lateral strain pattern
Left axis deviation with deep S waves in V1 and tall R waves in V5–V6
Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
Tall R wave in aVL with ST depression and T-wave inversion in I and aVL
Pathological Q waves in V1–V4 with ST elevation
originalOptions: Sokolow-Lyon voltage ≥35 mm with left axis deviation and lateral strain pattern
Left axis deviation with deep S waves in V1 and tall R waves in V5–V6
Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
Tall R wave in aVL with ST depression and T-wave inversion in I and aVL
Pathological Q waves in V1–V4 with ST elevation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio >1), with or without ST depression and T-wave inversion in V1–V3
allQuestions.explanation: RVH is recognised by right axis deviation and a dominant R wave in V1 (R/S >1), often with a right ventricular strain pattern. Option A describes LVH.

allQuestions.text: What are the ECG characteristics of left bundle branch block?
options: QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
QRS ≥120 ms; rSR′ pattern in V1; broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with a delta wave and short PR interval
QRS ≥120 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm
Narrow QRS with a tall R wave in V1 and ST depression in V1–V3
originalOptions: QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
QRS ≥120 ms; rSR′ pattern in V1; broad terminal S wave in I and V6
QRS <120 ms with a delta wave and short PR interval
QRS ≥120 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm
Narrow QRS with a tall R wave in V1 and ST depression in V1–V3
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: QRS ≥120 ms; broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL, and V5–V6; absent septal q waves; deep S waves in V1–V3; secondary ST–T discordance
allQuestions.explanation: LBBB shows a broad monophasic or notched R wave in the lateral leads and a deep QS or rS in V1–V3, with ST–T changes opposite to the QRS direction. Option B describes RBBB, and option D describes TCA toxicity.

allQuestions.text: A patient with chest pain has a normal ECG and elevated cardiac troponin. This most likely suggests:
allQuestions.explanation: NSTEMI is myocardial infarction with a raised troponin and no ST elevation (the ECG may be normal, or show T inversion or ST depression). Unstable angina is the closest alternative, but its troponin is normal.

allQuestions.text: A patient with suspected inferior MI has ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF and in lead V4R. Which drug is contraindicated?
allQuestions.explanation: ST elevation in V4R indicates right ventricular infarction, which is preload-dependent, so nitrates can cause profound hypotension. Nitrates are also contraindicated after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.

allQuestions.text: A patient has an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse. What is the immediate treatment?
allQuestions.explanation: An unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse requires immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if feasible. Adenosine is for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, and unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless VT or VF.

allQuestions.text: What rhythm is shown on the ECG strip? [img: ERECGMAT.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: MAT is an irregular tachycardia with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and variable PR intervals. Atrial fibrillation is the closest alternative, but it has no discernible P waves.

allQuestions.text: The ECG shows constant PR intervals with intermittent non-conducted P waves and dropped QRS complexes. What is the diagnosis? [img: ERECGsecAVblockM2.png ]
options: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
originalOptions: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
allQuestions.explanation: A constant PR interval before a suddenly dropped QRS defines Mobitz II. Mobitz I shows progressive PR lengthening before the dropped beat.

allQuestions.text: An ECG shows diffuse concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation in all leads. What is the diagnosis and treatment? [img: ERECGpericarditis.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression that does not follow a coronary territory indicates pericarditis, treated with an NSAID plus colchicine. STEMI shows convex elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal depression.

allQuestions.text: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF indicates infarction of which wall?
allQuestions.explanation: Leads II, III, and aVF face the inferior wall of the left ventricle, typically supplied by the right coronary artery.

allQuestions.text: A haemodynamically stable patient has a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia (ventricular tachycardia). Which treatment is most appropriate? [img: ERECGamiodarone.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Stable monomorphic VT is treated with IV antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, procainamide, lidocaine, or sotalol). Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for unstable VT, and defibrillation for pulseless VT.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following describes the ECG characteristics of sinus arrhythmia?
options: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves
Inverted P waves before every QRS with a shortened PR interval
