Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
Progressive PR lengthening with intermittently dropped QRS complexes
Regular P–P intervals with variable QRS morphology
originalOptions: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves
Inverted P waves before every QRS with a shortened PR interval
Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
Progressive PR lengthening with intermittently dropped QRS complexes
Regular P–P intervals with variable QRS morphology
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Normal P waves before every QRS with a constant PR interval and P–P variation of at least 120 ms, classically respiratory
allQuestions.explanation: In sinus arrhythmia the P, QRS, and T morphology is normal and only the R–R timing varies, rising with inspiration and falling with expiration. Non-respiratory variation suggests pathology.

allQuestions.text: Which characteristic ST-segment morphology is seen with digoxin effect?
options: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Osborn waves at the J point
Peaked T waves with a widened QRS
originalOptions: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Osborn waves at the J point
Peaked T waves with a widened QRS
allQuestions.explanation: Digoxin effect produces a scooped ST depression ("reverse tick") with a shortened QT, and is a benign finding at therapeutic levels. Digoxin toxicity instead causes arrhythmias.

allQuestions.text: A report states "possible left axis deviation" (lead I positive, aVF negative). Which finding confirms true left axis deviation?
allQuestions.explanation: When lead I is positive and aVF is negative, a negative lead II confirms true left axis deviation (about −30° to −90°). A positive lead II means the axis is borderline and may still be normal.

allQuestions.text: Which ECG findings suggest an early repolarization pattern?
options: Convex ST elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression and evolving Q waves
J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a pseudo-RBBB pattern
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Scooped ST depression with a shortened QT interval
originalOptions: Convex ST elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal ST depression and evolving Q waves
J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a pseudo-RBBB pattern
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Scooped ST depression with a shortened QT interval
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: J-point elevation ≥1 mm in at least two contiguous leads with concave ST elevation and a notched or slurred QRS downstroke
allQuestions.explanation: Early repolarization is a benign pattern, most common in young males and athletes, that is stable on serial ECGs. Pericarditis is the closest alternative, but it shows PR depression and diffuse changes.

allQuestions.text: A patient has first-degree heart block on ECG (PR >200 ms, all P waves conducted). What is the immediate management?
allQuestions.explanation: First-degree AV block is a benign finding in which every impulse is conducted, so no treatment is needed unless it is symptomatic or drug-induced.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a pathological Q wave?
options: Depth >25% of the following R-wave amplitude
originalOptions: Depth >25% of the following R-wave amplitude
allQuestions.explanation: A pathological Q wave is ≥40 ms wide and deeper than 25% of the R wave. A Q wave narrower than 40 ms is physiological, and any Q wave in V1–V4 is considered pathological.

allQuestions.text: All of the following shorten the QT interval EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Hypothyroidism prolongs the QT interval (via bradycardia). Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, and increased sympathetic tone (fever, hyperthyroidism) shorten it.

allQuestions.text: An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: AF shows chaotic atrial activity with no P waves, a fibrillatory baseline, and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. MAT is also irregular, but it has at least three distinct P-wave morphologies.

allQuestions.text: Which option correctly defines a pathological Q wave and lists conditions that can produce pseudoinfarction Q waves?
options: Width <40 ms and depth <25% of the R wave; causes: MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms only; causes: hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, digoxin effect, cardiac tamponade
Depth ≥2 mm in leads III and aVR only; causes: PE, pericarditis, early repolarization, Brugada syndrome
Width <40 ms and depth >50% of the R wave; causes: hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, TCA toxicity
originalOptions: Width <40 ms and depth <25% of the R wave; causes: MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
Width ≥40 ms only; causes: hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, digoxin effect, cardiac tamponade
Depth ≥2 mm in leads III and aVR only; causes: PE, pericarditis, early repolarization, Brugada syndrome
Width <40 ms and depth >50% of the R wave; causes: hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, TCA toxicity
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Width ≥40 ms and depth >25% of the R wave; causes: prior MI, WPW, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB
allQuestions.explanation: Pathological Q waves represent myocardial scar. Pseudoinfarction Q waves occur in WPW (negative delta wave), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, LBBB, severe LVH, and acute myocarditis.

allQuestions.text: Which group of conditions causes shortening of the QT interval?
options: Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics, ondansetron
Hypothyroidism, bradycardia, raised ICP, myocardial ischaemia
Congenital long QT syndrome, hypomagnesaemia, tricyclic antidepressants
Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
originalOptions: Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics, ondansetron
Hypothyroidism, bradycardia, raised ICP, myocardial ischaemia
Congenital long QT syndrome, hypomagnesaemia, tricyclic antidepressants
Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, digoxin effect, congenital short QT syndrome
allQuestions.explanation: These conditions shorten repolarisation. The other options list classic causes of QT prolongation (electrolyte depletion, drugs, and bradycardic states).

allQuestions.text: P mitrale (a broad, notched P wave >0.12 s in lead II) is most commonly associated with:
allQuestions.explanation: P mitrale reflects left atrial enlargement, as in mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, or left heart failure. COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension cause the tall peaked P pulmonale instead.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognised cause of poor R-wave progression across the precordial leads?
allQuestions.explanation: Loss of anterior forces from anteroseptal infarction (also LVH, LBBB, COPD, and lead misplacement) impairs R-wave progression. Posterior MI, left-sided WPW, RBBB, and the paediatric variant produce tall R waves in V1.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognised cause of a tall R wave in V1?
allQuestions.explanation: Posterior infarction produces a tall R wave in V1–V2 as the mirror image of posterior Q waves. Other causes are RVH, RBBB, left-sided WPW, and dextrocardia. The other options cause poor R-wave progression or deep S waves in V1.

allQuestions.text: An ECG shows both a tall peaked P wave and a broad notched P wave. Which chamber-enlargement pattern does this suggest?
allQuestions.explanation: The tall peaked component reflects right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale) and the broad notched component reflects left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), so both atria are enlarged.

allQuestions.text: What are the normal duration and amplitude of the P wave on ECG?
options: <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
originalOptions: <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: <120 ms (3 small squares) and <2.5 mm in limb leads
allQuestions.explanation: A normal P wave is shorter than 120 ms and lower than 2.5 mm in the limb leads. A longer P wave suggests left atrial enlargement, and a taller one suggests right atrial enlargement.

allQuestions.text: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, what defines a narrow and a wide QRS complex?
options: Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
originalOptions: Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Narrow <120 ms (<3 small squares); wide ≥120 ms (≥3 small squares)
allQuestions.explanation: A QRS of 120 ms or more is wide, suggesting a ventricular origin, bundle branch block, or pre-excitation.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of QT prolongation?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT interval. Hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and hypothermia prolong it, as do many drugs.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognised cause of left axis deviation?
allQuestions.explanation: Left axis deviation (lead I positive, aVF negative) occurs with left anterior fascicular block, LVH, inferior MI, and ventricular pacing. The other options cause right axis deviation.

allQuestions.text: In which limb lead are the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave normally predominantly negative?
allQuestions.explanation: Lead aVR looks at the heart from the right shoulder, opposite to the normal direction of depolarisation, so all its waves are normally negative.

allQuestions.text: When can the normally negative complexes in lead aVR become predominantly positive?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Dextrocardia or right-arm/left-arm limb-lead reversal
allQuestions.explanation: Both conditions invert the normal limb-lead vectors. They are distinguished by precordial R-wave progression, which is lost in dextrocardia and normal in limb-lead reversal.

allQuestions.text: Which is NOT a component of the FAST stroke recognition tool?
allQuestions.explanation: FAST consists of Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call emergency services. Seizures can accompany stroke but are not a recognition sign in this tool.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with acute dysarthria suggestive of stroke, with no available medical history. Which immediate bedside test must not be missed?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia can mimic acute stroke and is rapidly correctable, so glucose is checked first. The stroke pathway (last-known-well time, urgent brain imaging) proceeds in parallel.

allQuestions.text: A stroke patient presents with intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus, ataxia, and a contralateral motor deficit. Which arterial territory is affected?
allQuestions.explanation: Cerebellar and brainstem signs (intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus, ataxia) with a contralateral motor deficit localise to the posterior circulation. MCA strokes produce contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia or neglect, not cerebellar signs.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to IV thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke?
options: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
originalOptions: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ischaemic stroke within the last 3 months
allQuestions.explanation: Ischaemic stroke or serious head trauma within the last 3 months is an absolute exclusion. Recent major surgery, pregnancy, seizure at onset, and minor or rapidly improving symptoms are relative considerations.

allQuestions.text: Which standardized tool is used for the clinical neurological assessment of stroke severity in the Emergency Department?
allQuestions.explanation: The NIHSS quantifies stroke deficits and is the standard severity assessment in the stroke team pathway. The Cincinnati scale is a prehospital recognition tool (face, arm, speech), and the GCS and AVPU assess conscious level only.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are relative exclusion criteria for IV thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke EXCEPT:
options: Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
originalOptions: Seizure at onset with post-ictal residual deficits
allQuestions.explanation: Platelets < 100,000/µL (like INR > 1.7 and therapeutic anticoagulation) is an absolute exclusion. The other options are relative exclusions.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) therapy in acute ischaemic stroke?
allQuestions.explanation: Severe uncontrolled hypertension (classically ≥ 185/110 mmHg despite treatment) is an exclusion. The other options are within the treatment window or are normal findings.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are contraindications to thrombolysis in acute stroke EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: The platelet exclusion threshold is < 100,000/µL, so a count between 100,000 and 150,000 is not a contraindication. Onset 5 hours ago is outside the standard window, INR > 1.7 and active bleeding are exclusions, and a stroke within 3 months is an absolute exclusion.

allQuestions.text: A patient with acute stroke has a large established multilobar infarct on brain imaging. How does this finding affect eligibility for IV thrombolysis?
options: It is an absolute contraindication in all cases
It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
It is an indication to give a double dose of the thrombolytic
It has no effect on thrombolysis decisions
It mandates repeat CT at 24 hours before any treatment
originalOptions: It is an absolute contraindication in all cases
It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
It is an indication to give a double dose of the thrombolytic
It has no effect on thrombolysis decisions
It mandates repeat CT at 24 hours before any treatment
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is a relative caution, weighed against time window, clinical severity, and bleeding risk
allQuestions.explanation: A large established infarct increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation. In current practice it is treated as a relative caution rather than a fixed stand-alone exclusion.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the "D"s of stroke care?
allQuestions.explanation: The 8 D's are Detection, Dispatch, Delivery, Door, Data, Decision, Drug (or device), and Disposition. Defibrillation belongs to arrest management, not the stroke chain.

allQuestions.text: A patient has isolated left-hand weakness with pronator drift and no sensory loss. Where is the lesion?
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated contralateral weakness with pronator drift and intact sensation indicates a lesion of the motor cortex or corticospinal pathway, here on the right. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia and incoordination rather than weakness, and parietal lesions cause sensory deficits.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following arteries is NOT part of the circle of Willis?
allQuestions.explanation: The vertebral arteries unite to form the basilar artery and supply the circle only indirectly, so they are feeding vessels rather than components of the ring. The ring is formed by the internal carotid, anterior and posterior cerebral, and the anterior and posterior communicating arteries.

allQuestions.text: A patient with diabetes and hypertension presents with vertigo, double vision, and difficulty speaking. The symptoms resolve within 1–2 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis and affected vessel?
allQuestions.explanation: Vertigo, diplopia, and dysarthria point to posterior-circulation ischaemia, and complete resolution within a short window defines a TIA. MCA events cause contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia, or neglect.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with thunderclap headache, photophobia, vomiting, neck stiffness, and blood pressure 190/110 mmHg. Subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected and urgent non-contrast CT head is arranged. Which listed IV agent is appropriate if controlled blood-pressure reduction is required?
allQuestions.explanation: Nicardipine is the preferred titratable IV antihypertensive in SAH, allowing controlled reduction while avoiding hypotension. Ceftriaxone treats meningitis, and ketorolac, platelets, and vitamin K have no role in blood-pressure control.

allQuestions.text: A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presents with sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and nausea. What is the most important immediate step in the Emergency Department?
allQuestions.explanation: Connective tissue disease raises the risk of aneurysmal rupture and arterial dissection, so sudden severe headache is treated as SAH until proven otherwise. After ABC stabilisation, urgent non-contrast CT is highly sensitive in the first 6 hours, and LP is reserved for a negative CT with persistent suspicion.

allQuestions.text: A woman presents with headache. Which of the following is the correct match?
options: Unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation – Tension-type headache
originalOptions: Unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation – Tension-type headache
allQuestions.explanation: Meningism from blood irritating the meninges accompanies SAH, usually with thunderclap onset. Band-like pain is tension-type, periorbital pain with lacrimation is cluster, and early-morning headache suggests raised intracranial pressure.

allQuestions.text: Can severe hyperglycaemia (above 300 mg/dL) cause a decreased level of consciousness?
options: Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
No, only hypoglycaemia lowers the level of consciousness
No, it affects consciousness only in non-diabetic patients
Yes, but only through direct neuronal toxicity of glucose
No, unless the glucose exceeds 1,000 mg/dL
originalOptions: Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
No, only hypoglycaemia lowers the level of consciousness
No, it affects consciousness only in non-diabetic patients
Yes, but only through direct neuronal toxicity of glucose
No, unless the glucose exceeds 1,000 mg/dL
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Yes, through hyperosmolarity, dehydration, or diabetic ketoacidosis
allQuestions.explanation: Severe hyperglycaemia impairs consciousness through hyperosmolar dehydration or DKA, where acidosis disrupts neuronal metabolism. Hyperglycaemia is therefore a recognised cause of altered mental status.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following diseases is NOT among those that must be reported immediately to health authorities?
allQuestions.explanation: Cholera, plague, poliomyelitis, and yellow fever are the classic immediately reportable diseases. Meningitis is not part of this group (national notification lists may vary).

allQuestions.text: A patient has a brief, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by complete spontaneous recovery without a persistent neurological deficit. What is this event called?
allQuestions.explanation: TLOC is a spontaneous, self-limited loss of awareness and postural tone with prompt, complete recovery. It is termed syncope when caused by transient global cerebral hypoperfusion. Coma is prolonged unarousable unresponsiveness, typically more than 1 hour.

allQuestions.text: A person collapses after prolonged standing in a hot, crowded environment. What is the likely diagnosis and initial management?
options: Drug-induced orthostatic hypotension – IV vasopressor infusion
Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
originalOptions: Drug-induced orthostatic hypotension – IV vasopressor infusion
Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Vasovagal syncope – supine position with leg elevation, assessment of ABCs and glucose, and exclusion of dangerous causes
allQuestions.explanation: Prolonged standing and a hot, crowded setting are typical orthostatic triggers of reflex (vasovagal) syncope. Management is supportive: lay the patient supine, elevate the legs, assess ABCs and glucose, and exclude dangerous causes.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best defines a Stokes-Adams attack?
options: A gradual faint after prolonged standing, preceded by pallor and nausea
Exertional syncope from fixed outflow obstruction in severe aortic stenosis
Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
Loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic movements and prolonged post-ictal confusion
Fainting during or immediately after micturition
originalOptions: A gradual faint after prolonged standing, preceded by pallor and nausea
Exertional syncope from fixed outflow obstruction in severe aortic stenosis
Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
Loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic movements and prolonged post-ictal confusion
Fainting during or immediately after micturition
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Sudden syncope from transient complete heart block or a long sinus pause, often without prodrome
allQuestions.explanation: A transient, severe bradyarrhythmia causes abrupt cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid recovery, and the lack of a prodrome distinguishes it from vasovagal syncope. A gradual faint with pallor and nausea is vasovagal, and prolonged post-ictal confusion indicates seizure.

allQuestions.text: A patient faints during or immediately after urination. What is the likely diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
Orthostatic hypotension – inadequate preload from volume depletion
originalOptions: Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
Orthostatic hypotension – inadequate preload from volume depletion
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Micturition syncope – situational reflex syncope from vagal activation with reduced vascular resistance and venous return
allQuestions.explanation: Fainting that is temporally linked to voiding is a situational reflex syncope. Vagal activation lowers vascular resistance and venous return, producing cerebral hypoperfusion.

allQuestions.text: What is reflex (neurally mediated) syncope, and what are its main subtypes?
options: Syncope from an arrhythmia; subtypes are bradyarrhythmic and tachyarrhythmic
Syncope from volume depletion, drugs, or autonomic failure on standing
Syncope from brainstem ischaemia; subtypes are vertebral and basilar
Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
Syncope from mechanical obstruction such as massive PE or aortic dissection
originalOptions: Syncope from an arrhythmia; subtypes are bradyarrhythmic and tachyarrhythmic
Syncope from volume depletion, drugs, or autonomic failure on standing
Syncope from brainstem ischaemia; subtypes are vertebral and basilar
Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
Syncope from mechanical obstruction such as massive PE or aortic dissection
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Syncope from an involuntary autonomic reflex causing vasodilation and/or bradycardia; subtypes are vasovagal, situational, and carotid-sinus
allQuestions.explanation: Reflex syncope results from a sudden rise in parasympathetic tone and sympathetic withdrawal, causing bradycardia and/or hypotension. The other options describe cardiac, orthostatic, neurological, and obstructive causes.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of appendicitis?
allQuestions.explanation: Grey Turner sign is flank discolouration from retroperitoneal/pancreatic haemorrhage. Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs are the appendicitis signs.

allQuestions.text: Which sign is elicited by passive extension of the right hip while the patient lies on his left side, and suggests a retrocecal appendix?
allQuestions.explanation: A retrocecal appendix irritates the psoas muscle, so hip extension causes RLQ pain. The obturator sign is pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip. Rovsing sign is RLQ pain on palpation of the LLQ.

allQuestions.text: What proportion of patients with appendicitis present with the full classic picture of fever, nausea/vomiting, RLQ pain, and leukocytosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Only about 20% have the full classic combination. Atypical or muted presentations are common, especially in the elderly.

allQuestions.text: How should a patient with an Alvarado score of 6 be managed?
options: Observation with further imaging and serial examination
originalOptions: Observation with further imaging and serial examination
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Observation with further imaging and serial examination
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Observation with further imaging and serial examination
allQuestions.explanation: A score of 5–6 means possible appendicitis (about 66%), so observe and image. Surgery is reserved for 7–10, and a score of ≤ 4 makes appendicitis unlikely.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with acute right lower quadrant pain and tenderness at McBurney's point. What is the most likely diagnosis and the appropriate initial management?
options: Acute diverticulitis; oral co-amoxiclav and clear liquids
Renal colic; parenteral NSAIDs and discharge
Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
originalOptions: Acute diverticulitis; oral co-amoxiclav and clear liquids
Renal colic; parenteral NSAIDs and discharge
Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Acute appendicitis; imaging (CT in adults, ultrasound in children/pregnancy), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
allQuestions.explanation: McBurney's point tenderness is the classic finding of appendicitis, which needs imaging and early surgical review. Methotrexate would be used only for a stable ectopic pregnancy.

allQuestions.text: Murphy's sign is characteristic of:
allQuestions.explanation: Murphy's sign is inspiratory arrest on deep palpation of the RUQ. Appendicitis is assessed with psoas/Rovsing signs instead.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with afebrile right upper quadrant pain. There is no Murphy sign or jaundice, and ultrasound shows gallstones with acoustic shadowing. The pain has resolved after analgesia and the laboratory results are reassuring. What is the best next step?
options: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent cholecystectomy
originalOptions: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent cholecystectomy
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and surgical follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
allQuestions.explanation: This is uncomplicated biliary colic. Fever, Murphy sign, jaundice, cholestatic labs, or duct dilation would call for admission and a different pathway.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about biliary colic pain is correct?
options: It is specifically triggered by protein
It always begins exactly 15 minutes after eating
It is typically relieved by food intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
It is typically accompanied by high fever and jaundice
originalOptions: It is specifically triggered by protein
It always begins exactly 15 minutes after eating
It is typically relieved by food intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
It is typically accompanied by high fever and jaundice
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It may radiate to the right shoulder or infrascapular region
allQuestions.explanation: Biliary pain is referred to the right infrascapular region. It is commonly precipitated by a fatty meal, but timing and triggers vary. Relief by food suggests peptic ulcer disease, and fever with jaundice suggests cholangitis.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about choledocholithiasis is correct?
options: It is defined by common bile duct dilatation below 5–7 mm
It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
It refers to stones confined to the gallbladder
It is infection of the bile duct diagnosed by Charcot's triad
It is inflammation of the gallbladder wall from cystic duct obstruction
originalOptions: It is defined by common bile duct dilatation below 5–7 mm
It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
It refers to stones confined to the gallbladder
It is infection of the bile duct diagnosed by Charcot's triad
It is inflammation of the gallbladder wall from cystic duct obstruction
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
allQuestions.explanation: Choledocholithiasis is defined by the stone, not by a duct diameter cut-off. Stones in the gallbladder are cholelithiasis, gallbladder inflammation is cholecystitis, and bile-duct infection is cholangitis.

allQuestions.text: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain form the diagnostic triad of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: This is Charcot's triad of cholangitis, which is infection behind an obstructed bile duct. Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status, and signals suppurative cholangitis needing urgent ERCP decompression. Cholecystitis does not classically cause jaundice.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are true regarding Meckel's diverticulum EXCEPT:
options: It occurs in about 2% of the population
It is located about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve
It is more common in females
It may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue
originalOptions: It occurs in about 2% of the population
It is located about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve
It is more common in females
It may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) It is more common in females
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is more common in females
allQuestions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is about twice as common in males, and complications are also more common in males. This is the rule-of-2s trap.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an independent predictor of adverse outcome in upper GI bleeding?
allQuestions.explanation: The adverse threshold is an initial hematocrit < 30%, and even that often underestimates true acute blood loss. A hematocrit < 45% is not a recognised predictor.

allQuestions.text: What does red blood in the nasogastric aspirate of a patient with GI bleeding suggest?
options: A lower GI source such as diverticular bleeding
An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
originalOptions: A lower GI source such as diverticular bleeding
An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: An upper GI source with higher-risk bleeding
allQuestions.explanation: Red blood in NG lavage localises the bleed to the upper GI tract and predicts an adverse outcome. A negative aspirate does not exclude an upper GI bleed.

allQuestions.text: A patient with known cirrhosis presents with haematemesis. Which source must be treated as the cause until proven otherwise?
allQuestions.explanation: In cirrhosis, haematemesis is variceal until proven otherwise. It needs a vasoactive drug (octreotide), prophylactic antibiotics, restrictive transfusion, and urgent endoscopy.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes angiodysplasia?
options: Healthy new blood vessels that do not bleed
Mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction after vomiting
Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
originalOptions: Healthy new blood vessels that do not bleed
Mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction after vomiting
Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Fragile, dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that cause intermittent bleeding
allQuestions.explanation: Angiodysplasia is a common cause of lower GI bleeding, most often in the right colon of older adults. It is associated with chronic kidney disease and aortic stenosis (Heyde's syndrome).

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of non-specific abdominal pain?
options: It is a diagnosis of exclusion
There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
Symptoms are improving and the patient tolerates oral fluids
originalOptions: It is a diagnosis of exclusion
There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
Symptoms are improving and the patient tolerates oral fluids
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: There is marked localised tenderness with guarding
allQuestions.explanation: Tenderness, if present, is mild and non-localising. Guarding, rigidity, rebound, or a toxic appearance requires a search for a specific serious cause.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common cause of abdominal pain in the emergency department?
allQuestions.explanation: Non-specific abdominal pain accounts for about 34% of ED abdominal pain, followed by appendicitis (28%) and biliary disease (10%).

allQuestions.text: Which is the least typical cause of acute pancreatitis?
allQuestions.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes. Hypertriglyceridaemia and idiopathic disease are established causes. The "I GET SMASHED" mnemonic lists scorpion sting, not snake bite.

allQuestions.text: Stroking the skin of the upper medial thigh in a normal cremasteric reflex causes:
options: Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
Contraction of the scrotal skin only, with no testicular movement
originalOptions: Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
Contraction of the scrotal skin only, with no testicular movement
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ipsilateral testicular elevation from cremaster muscle contraction
allQuestions.explanation: The reflex is ipsilateral. Its absence supports testicular torsion, although a present reflex does not exclude torsion.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about testicular torsion is FALSE?
options: It presents with a swollen, high-riding testis with a transverse lie
Duplex ultrasound shows absent blood flow
Salvage is 80–100% if detorsion occurs within 6 hours
It is most common at 20–30 years of age
originalOptions: It presents with a swollen, high-riding testis with a transverse lie
Duplex ultrasound shows absent blood flow
Salvage is 80–100% if detorsion occurs within 6 hours
It is most common at 20–30 years of age
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It is most common at 20–30 years of age
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is most common at 20–30 years of age
allQuestions.explanation: The peak age is 12–16 years, and only about 10% of cases occur after age 20. Salvage falls to about 50% at 12 hours and 0% at 24 hours.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of retroperitoneal haemorrhage?
allQuestions.explanation: Battle sign is mastoid ecchymosis, which indicates a basilar skull fracture. Cullen (periumbilical), Grey Turner (flank), and Fox (inguinal) signs suggest retroperitoneal or pancreatic haemorrhage.

allQuestions.text: Which is NOT a major compartment for occult blood loss causing haemorrhagic shock in an adult?
allQuestions.explanation: The sites of hidden blood loss are "blood on the floor and four more": chest, abdomen/retroperitoneum, pelvis, and long bones. Intracranial bleeding cannot account for profound systemic blood loss in an adult.

allQuestions.text: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
allQuestions.explanation: Smoking is the single strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA, and it also accelerates aneurysm growth. Hypertension and atherosclerosis are contributory only.

allQuestions.text: Which is the most important predictor of abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture?
allQuestions.explanation: Maximum diameter is the strongest predictor, and risk rises sharply above 5.5 cm. Smoking and hypertension raise risk mainly by increasing growth rate.

allQuestions.text: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is typically described by the patient as:
options: Colicky right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder
Burning epigastric pain relieved by food
Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
Postprandial pain with fear of eating
The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
originalOptions: Colicky right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder
Burning epigastric pain relieved by food
Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
Postprandial pain with fear of eating
The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The worst pain of their life: sudden, severe, tearing abdominal, flank, or back pain
allQuestions.explanation: Rupture classically causes sudden excruciating pain with hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass. The full triad is present in only about half of patients.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about lactate in suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is correct?
options: A normal lactate reliably excludes the diagnosis
Lactate is highly sensitive, so CTA is unnecessary when it is normal
Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
An elevated lactate is required to make the diagnosis
Lactate rises only in chronic mesenteric ischaemia
originalOptions: A normal lactate reliably excludes the diagnosis
Lactate is highly sensitive, so CTA is unnecessary when it is normal
Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
An elevated lactate is required to make the diagnosis
Lactate rises only in chronic mesenteric ischaemia
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Lactate is not sensitive enough; a normal level does not exclude ischaemia and must not delay CT angiography
allQuestions.explanation: Lactate can be normal early, before enough bowel is ischaemic to raise it. A high lactate supports severe ischaemia, but a normal value never rules it out.

allQuestions.text: Which best describes the pain of early acute mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
Mild pain with marked rigidity and rebound tenderness
Postprandial pain starting 15–30 minutes after eating and lasting 1–3 hours
Pain relieved promptly by standard analgesia
Localised RLQ pain with periumbilical migration
originalOptions: Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
Mild pain with marked rigidity and rebound tenderness
Postprandial pain starting 15–30 minutes after eating and lasting 1–3 hours
Pain relieved promptly by standard analgesia
Localised RLQ pain with periumbilical migration
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Severe pain out of proportion to the examination findings, with a soft abdomen and poor response to analgesia
allQuestions.explanation: Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen is the early clue. Rigidity and peritonitis appear late with bowel necrosis, and option C describes chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

allQuestions.text: What is the classic symptom triad of chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
Hypotension, back pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass
Jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension
Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
Pain out of proportion, a soft abdomen, and lactic acidosis
originalOptions: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
Hypotension, back pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass
Jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension
Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
Pain out of proportion, a soft abdomen, and lactic acidosis
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss
allQuestions.explanation: This is "abdominal angina", from a fixed mesenteric stenosis that cannot meet post-meal demand. Acute ischaemia instead causes sudden severe constant pain out of proportion to the examination.

allQuestions.text: What is the preferred initial imaging test when acute mesenteric ischaemia is suspected?
allQuestions.explanation: CT angiography is the rapid diagnostic study of choice. It shows vessel occlusion, pneumatosis intestinalis, and absent bowel-wall enhancement.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements is WRONG?
options: Bowel strangulation classically causes a lactic metabolic acidosis
Vomiting may independently cause a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
A high lactate supports the diagnosis of mesenteric ischaemia
Pain out of proportion to examination findings is an early feature of acute mesenteric ischaemia
Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
originalOptions: Bowel strangulation classically causes a lactic metabolic acidosis
Vomiting may independently cause a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
A high lactate supports the diagnosis of mesenteric ischaemia
Pain out of proportion to examination findings is an early feature of acute mesenteric ischaemia
Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Bowel strangulation causes metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
allQuestions.explanation: Ischaemia produces lactic metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. Any alkalosis in these patients comes from a separate cause, usually vomiting.

allQuestions.text: What is required to establish a diagnosis of shock?
options: Documented hypotension with low cardiac output
Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
originalOptions: Documented hypotension with low cardiac output
Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Evidence of inadequate perfusion of the body's organs
allQuestions.explanation: Shock is defined by inadequate end-organ perfusion, so no single parameter is required. Hypotension, acidosis and hypoxia may all be absent in compensated shock, and vascular resistance is low in distributive shock.

allQuestions.text: The shock index is calculated as:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Heart rate ÷ systolic blood pressure
allQuestions.explanation: Shock index = HR ÷ SBP (normal 0.5–0.7). A value ≥ 0.9–1.0 suggests occult shock even when the systolic pressure appears normal.

allQuestions.text: A patient who was stabbed multiple times presents with heart rate 130/min, blood pressure 95/70 mmHg and SpO₂ 93%. Which class of haemorrhagic shock does this represent?
allQuestions.explanation: Heart rate > 120 with a falling blood pressure and a narrowed pulse pressure (25 mmHg) indicates Class III (31–40% blood loss), which requires blood transfusion. Class IV shows heart rate > 140 and a markedly low blood pressure.

allQuestions.text: A previously healthy 70-kg man has an estimated acute blood loss of 2 litres. Which statement applies?
options: His urinary output will be at the lower limit of normal
His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
He will have tachycardia with no change in systolic blood pressure
His pulse pressure will be widened
He will have a normal respiratory rate and mental state
originalOptions: His urinary output will be at the lower limit of normal
His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
He will have tachycardia with no change in systolic blood pressure
His pulse pressure will be widened
He will have a normal respiratory rate and mental state
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: His systolic blood pressure will be decreased, with a narrowed pulse pressure
allQuestions.explanation: A loss of about 2 L (~30% of blood volume) corresponds to Class III, in which systolic pressure falls and pulse pressure narrows, with tachycardia > 120, tachypnoea, confusion and reduced urine output. Tachycardia with a preserved systolic pressure describes Class II.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following describes Class I haemorrhagic shock?
options: Blood loss of 15–30% with a narrowed pulse pressure
Heart rate > 140/min with negligible urine output
Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
originalOptions: Blood loss of 15–30% with a narrowed pulse pressure
Heart rate > 140/min with negligible urine output
Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Blood loss of less than 15% with normal heart rate and blood pressure, and at most mild anxiety
allQuestions.explanation: Class I (< 750 mL) is absorbed with essentially normal vital signs. Tachycardia and a narrowed pulse pressure begin in Class II, and hypotension appears in Class III.

allQuestions.text: A trauma patient has Class III haemorrhagic shock. Which of the following findings is NOT expected?
allQuestions.explanation: Urine output is reduced in Class III but becomes negligible only in Class IV (> 40% blood loss). The other findings are all characteristic of Class III.

allQuestions.text: A 34-year-old man pinned by a cement truck has deformities and marked swelling of both thighs. His shock:
options: Cannot be explained without a major arterial injury
Will likely reverse with traction splints
Cannot be explained without a concomitant intra-abdominal injury
Cannot be explained without a concomitant pelvic fracture
Is most likely neurogenic in origin
originalOptions: Cannot be explained without a major arterial injury
Will likely reverse with traction splints
Cannot be explained without a concomitant intra-abdominal injury
Cannot be explained without a concomitant pelvic fracture
Is most likely neurogenic in origin
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Will likely reverse with traction splints
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Will likely reverse with traction splints
allQuestions.explanation: Each femoral fracture can cause 1–2 L of blood loss, so bilateral femoral fractures alone can account for Class III–IV haemorrhage; the long bones are one of the "blood on the floor and four more" sites. Shock of this kind requires blood resuscitation.

allQuestions.text: The "physiologic hypervolaemia" of pregnancy is clinically significant because it:
options: Increases the risk of pulmonary oedema
Reduces the need for blood transfusion
Reduces the crystalloid volume required for resuscitation
Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
Complicates the management of closed head injury
originalOptions: Increases the risk of pulmonary oedema
Reduces the need for blood transfusion
Reduces the crystalloid volume required for resuscitation
Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
Complicates the management of closed head injury
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Increases the volume of blood loss required to produce hypotension
allQuestions.explanation: Blood volume expands by about 40–50% in pregnancy, so a pregnant patient can lose considerably more blood before tachycardia or hypotension appear. This masks the severity of haemorrhage while the fetus may already be compromised.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about crystalloid resuscitation in haemorrhagic shock is correct?
options: Large volumes are preferred to restore oxygen delivery
Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
Crystalloid restores oxygen-carrying capacity as effectively as blood
It should be continued until blood pressure is normal, regardless of bleeding control
It is preferred over blood products once haemoglobin falls below 9 g/dL
originalOptions: Large volumes are preferred to restore oxygen delivery
Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
Crystalloid restores oxygen-carrying capacity as effectively as blood
It should be continued until blood pressure is normal, regardless of bleeding control
It is preferred over blood products once haemoglobin falls below 9 g/dL
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Excessive volumes can worsen oedema, dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia, increasing morbidity and mortality
allQuestions.explanation: Crystalloid carries no oxygen and dilutes haemoglobin and clotting factors. In haemorrhagic shock, blood products and definitive haemorrhage control are prioritised, with permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled.

allQuestions.text: Which packed red cells : plasma : platelets ratio is commonly used in massive transfusion for severe haemorrhage?
allQuestions.explanation: Massive transfusion protocols use balanced resuscitation with packed red cells, plasma and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio, which replaces volume and clotting factors together.

allQuestions.text: A patient in shock is not responding to initial fluid resuscitation. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?
options: Repeat crystalloid boluses until the blood pressure normalises
Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
Continue observation, as response is expected to be delayed
Defer resuscitation until CT imaging is completed
originalOptions: Repeat crystalloid boluses until the blood pressure normalises
Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
Continue observation, as response is expected to be delayed
Defer resuscitation until CT imaging is completed
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Reassess using ABCDE, search for hidden causes, and start vasopressors or blood products as indicated
allQuestions.explanation: Fluid refractoriness calls for immediate ABCDE reassessment and a search for ongoing haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax or tamponade. Noradrenaline is started for vasodilatory shock, and blood products for haemorrhagic shock.

allQuestions.text: Shortly after urinary catheterisation, a patient develops fever, tachycardia, altered mental status and hypotension. Which type of shock should be suspected?
allQuestions.explanation: Fever with haemodynamic instability in a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter indicates urosepsis. Management is cultures and lactate, antibiotics within the hour, fluids, and noradrenaline to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg if shock persists.

allQuestions.text: A patient with poor oral intake and dehydration is hypotensive, with no fever and no documented source of infection. Which type of shock best fits this presentation?
allQuestions.explanation: Volume depletion from poor intake explains the hypotension, and there is neither fever nor an infective source to suggest sepsis. If fever or an infective source appears, reassess urgently for septic shock.

allQuestions.text: A tachycardic patient with fever remains hypotensive despite initial fluid resuscitation. Which type of shock is most likely?
allQuestions.explanation: Fever with persistent hypoperfusion despite fluids indicates infection-driven vasodilation, which is septic shock. Dehydration alone would be expected to respond to fluid replacement.

allQuestions.text: A child develops a skin reaction, hoarseness and shortness of breath after receiving an antibiotic. After stopping the drug, what is the best next step?
options: IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
originalOptions: IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh
allQuestions.explanation: This is anaphylaxis with airway involvement, and IM adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving treatment. Corticosteroids, antihistamines and bronchodilators are adjuncts and must not delay it; repeat dosing depends on response and the local protocol.

allQuestions.text: A patient has hypotension, distended neck veins and absent breath sounds on one side. Which type of shock is this?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypotension with raised JVP and unilateral absent breath sounds indicates tension pneumothorax, a mechanical cause of obstructive shock. Cardiogenic shock can also raise the JVP but would not explain the unilateral absent breath sounds.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following constitutes Beck's triad in cardiac tamponade?
options: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
Hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry skin
Hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent unilateral breath sounds
Hypotension, widened pulse pressure and bounding pulse
originalOptions: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
Hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry skin
Hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent unilateral breath sounds
Hypotension, widened pulse pressure and bounding pulse
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds
allQuestions.explanation: Beck's triad is hypotension, jugular venous distension and muffled heart sounds. The complete triad is often absent, so eFAST should be used to confirm tamponade.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes milrinone?
options: A β-adrenergic agonist producing inotropy with vasoconstriction
An α₁-agonist that raises systemic vascular resistance
A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
A calcium channel blocker with negative inotropic effect
originalOptions: A β-adrenergic agonist producing inotropy with vasoconstriction
An α₁-agonist that raises systemic vascular resistance
A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
A calcium channel blocker with negative inotropic effect
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilator effects, whose main risks are hypotension and arrhythmia
allQuestions.explanation: Milrinone raises cAMP independently of β-receptors, so it remains effective in patients taking β-blockers, and it is an "inodilator". Its vasodilation explains the hypotension.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognised complication of central venous catheter insertion?
allQuestions.explanation: Recognised complications include arterial puncture, pneumothorax or haemothorax, malposition with arrhythmia, air embolism, infection and thrombosis. Hypercalcaemia is not related to catheter insertion.

questions.text: Which plain radiograph is the most sensitive for detecting free air under the diaphragm?

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologyacalcifiedfibroid.jpg ]
questions.explanation: A coarse, popcorn-like calcification in the pelvis in the uterine region is the classic appearance of a calcified leiomyoma. A phlebolith is small and round with a central lucency, and a bladder stone is a rounded intravesical density.
questions.note: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are the most common benign solid uterine tumors of myometrial origin, commonly found incidentally. They can be evaluated via US, MRI, CT, and classically present as "popcorn calcification" on X-ray when calcified.

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologyarenalstonehydronephrosis.png ]
questions.correctAnswer: A) Obstructing renal stone with hydronephrosis
questions.explanation: The CT shows a calculus with upstream dilatation of the collecting system, consistent with an obstructing stone causing hydronephrosis.

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologyasmallbowelobstruction.png ]
questions.explanation: The supine film shows multiple centrally located dilated loops with valvulae conniventes crossing the full lumen width, typical of small (not large) bowel obstruction.

questions.text: Which statement is wrong about pyloric stenosis?
options: A longitudinal measurement > 7 mm alone is the defining diagnostic criterion
Pyloric canal length is usually 15–17 mm
Single pyloric wall thickness > 3 mm is diagnostic
originalOptions: A longitudinal measurement > 7 mm alone is the defining diagnostic criterion
Pyloric canal length is usually 15–17 mm
Single pyloric wall thickness > 3 mm is diagnostic
questions.correctAnswer: A) A longitudinal measurement > 7 mm alone is the defining diagnostic criterion
questions.correctAnswerText: A longitudinal measurement > 7 mm alone is the defining diagnostic criterion
questions.explanation: The accepted diagnostic criteria are muscle wall thickness > 3 mm and canal length > 15–17 mm; a "> 7 mm" longitudinal measurement is not the recognized standalone criterion.

questions.text: Which statement is wrong about colonic intussusception?
options: About 95% of cases occur in children
Most commonly due to a benign tumor in adults
Ileocolic type is the most common location
originalOptions: About 95% of cases occur in children
Most commonly due to a benign tumor in adults
Ileocolic type is the most common location
questions.correctAnswer: B) Most commonly due to a benign tumor in adults
questions.correctAnswerText: Most commonly due to a benign tumor in adults
questions.explanation: In adult colonic intussusception, a malignant tumor (such as primary adenocarcinoma) is the most common lead point rather than a benign lesion, making this statement false.
questions.note: This question is not covered in the course slides. || In adults, over 80% of cases have a clear structural cause, which is mostly benign (85–90%) in the small bowel but mainly malignant (50–65%) in the colon and large intestine. || In children, up to 90% of cases are idiopathic, meaning they have no clear cause and are usually triggered by swollen lymph tissue from a viral infection.

questions.text: Which artery is most likely shown? [img: Radiologyasuperiormesentericartery.png ]
questions.explanation: The arrow points to a single anterior aortic branch arising at approximately the L1 level, just below the celiac trunk, the typical origin of the SMA.

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologyagallstonexray.png ]
questions.explanation: The abdominal x-ray shows rounded, faintly calcified opacities in the right upper quadrant overlying the expected gallbladder location, consistent with radiopaque gallstones.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a typical radiologic feature of acute pancreatitis?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Smooth outline of the pancreas
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis causes irregular, fuzzy pancreatic borders due to inflammation and edema, not a smooth outline.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding abdominal vasculature is false?
options: Renal arteries are paired vessels that arise superior to the gonadal arteries
The IVC passes through the diaphragm at the T8 level
The hindgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery
The IVC has a retroperitoneal course within the abdomen
originalOptions: Renal arteries are paired vessels that arise superior to the gonadal arteries
The IVC passes through the diaphragm at the T8 level
The hindgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery
The IVC has a retroperitoneal course within the abdomen
questions.correctAnswer: C) The hindgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery
questions.correctAnswerText: The hindgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery
questions.explanation: The hindgut is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, not the SMA (which supplies the midgut); the other statements are correct.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about pneumobilia is false?
options: Pneumobilia refers to the presence of gas in the biliary tree
Most commonly seen after endoscopic procedures
originalOptions: Pneumobilia refers to the presence of gas in the biliary tree
Most commonly seen after endoscopic procedures
questions.correctAnswer: D) It appears peripherally on CT
questions.explanation: Pneumobilia is centrally distributed near the porta hepatis on CT; it is portal venous gas that characteristically extends peripherally to the liver capsule.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about hiatal hernias is false?
options: Rolling hernias are more common than sliding hernias
Sliding hernias are often associated with gastroesophageal reflux
Rolling hernias increase the risk of volvulus
In sliding hernias, the gastroesophageal junction moves above the diaphragm
originalOptions: Rolling hernias are more common than sliding hernias
Sliding hernias are often associated with gastroesophageal reflux
Rolling hernias increase the risk of volvulus
In sliding hernias, the gastroesophageal junction moves above the diaphragm
questions.correctAnswer: A) Rolling hernias are more common than sliding hernias
questions.correctAnswerText: Rolling hernias are more common than sliding hernias
questions.explanation: Sliding hernias account for over 90% of cases and are far more common than rolling (paraesophageal) hernias, making this statement false.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about CT findings in acute appendicitis is false?
options: Dilated appendix with a distended lumen (> 6 mm)
An appendicolith is always present, and its absence excludes the diagnosis
originalOptions: Dilated appendix with a distended lumen (> 6 mm)
An appendicolith is always present, and its absence excludes the diagnosis
questions.correctAnswer: B) An appendicolith is always present, and its absence excludes the diagnosis
questions.correctAnswerText: An appendicolith is always present, and its absence excludes the diagnosis
questions.explanation: An appendicolith may be identified in some cases but is not required, so its absence does not exclude appendicitis. A dilated lumen, thickened enhancing wall, cecal apex thickening, and fat stranding are the recognized CT findings.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the small intestine is incorrect?
options: Jejunum shows more prominent folds than ileum
Valvulae conniventes span the entire lumen of the small intestine
Functional ileus can present with a discrete transition point
originalOptions: Jejunum shows more prominent folds than ileum
Valvulae conniventes span the entire lumen of the small intestine
Functional ileus can present with a discrete transition point
questions.correctAnswer: C) Functional ileus can present with a discrete transition point
questions.correctAnswerText: Functional ileus can present with a discrete transition point
questions.explanation: Functional (adynamic) ileus shows diffuse bowel dilatation without a discrete transition point, unlike mechanical obstruction; a discrete transition point argues against ileus.

questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding cecal volvulus?
options: Colonic haustral pattern is generally maintained
Extends towards the right upper quadrant
One air-fluid level may be seen
Distal colon is usually collapsed and the small bowel is distended
Arises in the right lower quadrant
originalOptions: Colonic haustral pattern is generally maintained
Extends towards the right upper quadrant
One air-fluid level may be seen
Distal colon is usually collapsed and the small bowel is distended
Arises in the right lower quadrant
questions.correctAnswer: B) Extends towards the right upper quadrant
questions.correctAnswerText: Extends towards the right upper quadrant
questions.explanation: Cecal volvulus classically extends toward the epigastrium or left upper quadrant, not the right upper quadrant, distinguishing it from the expected distension pattern.

questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding achalasia?
options: Anterior displacement and bowing of the trachea
originalOptions: Anterior displacement and bowing of the trachea
questions.explanation: Achalasia produces marked esophageal dilatation, not a normal-caliber esophagus, making this the false statement.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding acute cholecystitis?
options: Seen on ultrasound as hyperechoic foci with acoustic shadowing
originalOptions: Seen on ultrasound as hyperechoic foci with acoustic shadowing
questions.correctAnswer: D) Seen on ultrasound as hyperechoic foci with acoustic shadowing
questions.correctAnswerText: Seen on ultrasound as hyperechoic foci with acoustic shadowing
questions.explanation: Gallstones are hyperechoic with posterior shadowing on ultrasound; stones are actually hypointense (dark) on MRI, and cholecystitis typically shows gallbladder distension with pericholecystic edema, making the other options false.

questions.text: Wrong about appendicitis?
options: Most common cause of acute abdomen in young patients
Can present with periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant
A fecalith may be seen as an appendicolith
Less common in the pediatric age group
originalOptions: Most common cause of acute abdomen in young patients
Can present with periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant
A fecalith may be seen as an appendicolith
Less common in the pediatric age group
questions.correctAnswer: D) Less common in the pediatric age group
questions.correctAnswerText: Less common in the pediatric age group
questions.explanation: Appendicitis is actually common in children and young adults, not less common in this age group, making this statement false.

questions.text: False about volvulus?
options: Midgut volvulus shows a whirlpool sign
Sigmoid volvulus shows a coffee bean sign
Volvulus is twisting of the bowel around its mesentery
originalOptions: Midgut volvulus shows a whirlpool sign

Volvulus is twisting of the bowel around its mesentery
questions.correctAnswer: B) Cecal volvulus has no haustration
questions.explanation: Cecal volvulus generally maintains a haustral pattern, unlike sigmoid volvulus which is typically ahaustral, making this statement false.
