options: The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
The hippocampus lies anterosuperior to the amygdala
The uncus forms the lateral border of the temporal lobe
The claustrum lies medial to the putamen, separated by the internal capsule
originalOptions: The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
The hippocampus lies anterosuperior to the amygdala
The uncus forms the lateral border of the temporal lobe
The claustrum lies medial to the putamen, separated by the internal capsule
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
allQuestions.explanation: The claustrum is a thin sheet of grey matter lateral to the insula (separated by the extreme capsule); the hippocampus lies posteroinferior (not anterosuperior) to the amygdala, and the uncus is the medial (not lateral) temporal border.

allQuestions.text: On T1-weighted MRI, which of the following statements about basal ganglia signal is TRUE?
options: The putamen is hyperintense relative to the globus pallidus
The caudate is hyperintense relative to the thalamus
The globus pallidus is isointense to the putamen
The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
originalOptions: The putamen is hyperintense relative to the globus pallidus
The caudate is hyperintense relative to the thalamus
The globus pallidus is isointense to the putamen
The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
allQuestions.explanation: On T1-weighted MRI, the globus pallidus normally appears relatively hyperintense compared with the putamen — a useful anatomical landmark.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following locations is NOT typical for hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypertensive ICH classically occurs in deep structures (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) supplied by small penetrating vessels; a lobar location like the frontal lobe instead suggests another etiology (e.g., amyloid angiopathy, AVM, tumor).

allQuestions.text: Which stage of hemorrhage is classically hyperintense on both T1 and T2-weighted MRI due to extracellular methemoglobin?
allQuestions.explanation: Late subacute hemorrhage (extracellular methemoglobin) is T1 and T2 hyperintense; early subacute (intracellular methemoglobin) is T1 hyperintense but T2 hypointense, and acute/chronic stages are T2 hypointense.

allQuestions.text: Regarding cerebral sinus thrombosis, which of the following is TRUE?
options: Sinus thrombosis is an occlusion of arterial channels in the cranial cavity
The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
The dura typically does not enhance
A hypodense sinus is seen on non-contrast CT
originalOptions: Sinus thrombosis is an occlusion of arterial channels in the cranial cavity
The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
The dura typically does not enhance
A hypodense sinus is seen on non-contrast CT
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
allQuestions.explanation: The empty delta sign — a triangular filling defect surrounded by enhancing dura — is classically seen on contrast-enhanced imaging; sinus thrombosis is a venous (not arterial) occlusion, acute thrombus typically does NOT enhance, the dura DOES enhance, and non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense (not hypodense) sinus.

allQuestions.text: Regarding subdural hematoma, which of the following is TRUE?
options: It does not cross the falx cerebri
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
originalOptions: It does not cross the falx cerebri
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.explanation: Subdural hematoma is confined by the falx cerebri and tentorium but CAN cross suture lines (opposite epidural hematoma); it is typically caused by bridging vein tears (not the middle meningeal artery) and has a crescentic (not lenticular) shape.

allQuestions.text: Regarding extradural (epidural) hematoma, which of the following is FALSE?
options: It does not cross the falx cerebri
There is a history of trauma
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
originalOptions: It does not cross the falx cerebri
There is a history of trauma
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.explanation: Epidural hematoma CAN cross the falx cerebri but does NOT cross cranial sutures (opposite the pattern of subdural hematoma); the other listed features are true.

allQuestions.text: Which one of the following is a common radiologic feature of diffuse brain edema?
allQuestions.explanation: Diffuse cerebral edema effaces the sulci and narrows the ventricles/basal cisterns; the brain typically appears diffusely hypodense (not hyperdense) except for the relatively dense-appearing cerebellum.

allQuestions.text: Identify the labeled structure. [img: Radiologynanatomyuncusbrain.png ]
options: Anterior Horn of the Lateral Ventricle
originalOptions: Anterior Horn of the Lateral Ventricle
allQuestions.explanation: I don't know what to write; there's no explanation :)

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a part of the corpus callosum?
allQuestions.explanation: The thalamus is a deep grey matter nucleus located centrally in the brain, distinct from the components of the corpus callosum which is a major white matter tract anatomically divided into the rostrum, genu, body, and splenium.

questions.text: Under Jordanian law, abortion is permitted under which of the following circumstances?
options: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
originalOptions: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
questions.correctAnswer: B) When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
questions.correctAnswerText: When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
questions.explanation: Jordanian law criminalizes abortion except when continuing the pregnancy would seriously endanger the mother's life or health; it is not permitted on demand, for socioeconomic reasons, or for fetal anomaly alone.

questions.text: Abortion in Jordanian law is allowed:
options: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
originalOptions: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
questions.correctAnswer: E) To save the mother's life
questions.explanation: Under the Jordan Penal Code, abortion is a criminal offense except when continuation of pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life.

questions.text: Burking involves which combination of asphyxial mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Burking (the Burke and Hare method) combines simultaneous chest compression (traumatic asphyxia) with covering the mouth/nose (smothering), causing rapid death from combined asphyxial mechanisms without leaving obvious external marks.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of inward (central) hyoid bone fracture?
questions.explanation: Throttling involves direct manual compression of the neck, characteristically producing an inward/central hyoid bone fracture, distinguishing it from hanging or ligature strangulation.

questions.text: Which method of asphyxia shows the MOST severe internal neck damage?
questions.explanation: In throttling, the hands directly grip and compress the neck with intense, sustained pressure, causing tears in the sternomastoid muscle, hyoid fracture, thyroid cartilage fractures, and even cervical spine injury — more severe than the mechanisms in hanging or ligature strangulation.

questions.text: The neck shows extensive laceration, tears in the sternomastoid, and fracture-dislocation of C2-C3 vertebrae. These findings are most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Judicial (long-drop) hanging involves a measured drop generating massive kinetic energy, producing a hangman's fracture (C2-C3 fracture-dislocation) and sternomastoid tearing from cervical spinal cord disruption — findings not typically seen in the shorter drops of suicidal or accidental hanging.

questions.text: What are the characteristic features of a ligature mark in strangulation?
questions.explanation: Ligature strangulation produces a horizontal (level), low (below the thyroid cartilage), and complete (fully encircling) mark, in contrast to hanging's characteristically oblique, high, and incomplete mark.

questions.text: Which features characterize ligature marks in strangulation?
options: Associated with multiple lines on the neck at varying heights
Marks positioned high on the neck
originalOptions: Associated with multiple lines on the neck at varying heights
Marks positioned high on the neck
questions.explanation: Ligature strangulation produces transverse (horizontal), complete, low-neck marks, distinct from the oblique, high, often incomplete marks of hanging.

questions.text: Abrasions found on the neck are always considered what until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Neck abrasions (from fingernails or a ligature) are presumed indicative of strangulation until proven otherwise — a key medicolegal principle guiding initial death investigation.

questions.text: What are the characteristics of the frothy secretions seen in drowning?
questions.explanation: Drowning froth is classically white, fine, persistent, leathery, and tenacious — not bloody or turbid unless there is additional injury.

questions.text: In drowning, which finding is most indicative of the time passed since death (time in water)?
questions.explanation: Washerwoman skin (macerated, wrinkled skin from prolonged water immersion) progresses in a time-dependent manner, making it the most reliable indicator of how long a body has been submerged.

questions.text: What finding is characteristic of traumatic asphyxia?
questions.explanation: In traumatic asphyxia, chest compression prevents venous return from the head, producing cyanosis above the compression site and pallor below it, creating a sharp line of demarcation.

questions.text: A clear line of demarcation on the body is always seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Traumatic (compressive) asphyxia produces a sharp line of demarcation between the congested, cyanotic upper body and the relatively normal-appearing lower body, a finding not characteristic of hanging, gagging, or drowning.

questions.text: Petechial hemorrhages are typically seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots) are a hallmark of asphyxia, especially traumatic/crush asphyxia, resulting from increased venous pressure rupturing capillaries in the face, conjunctivae, and skin above the compression site.

questions.text: What are the mechanisms of death in mechanical asphyxia?
options: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
originalOptions: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
questions.correctAnswer: B) Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
questions.correctAnswerText: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
questions.explanation: Mechanical asphyxia causes death through multiple overlapping mechanisms: oxygen deprivation, pulmonary edema, vagal reflex cardiac arrest (especially relevant in hanging/strangulation), and cerebral hypoxia.

questions.text: Mechanical asphyxia is a type of:
questions.explanation: Mechanical asphyxia (hanging, drowning, smothering) prevents oxygen from entering the lungs, representing anoxic anoxia — failure of oxygen to reach the blood — rather than a defect in oxygen transport or cellular utilization.

questions.text: Death in an environment with decreased atmospheric oxygen levels (e.g., high altitude, enclosed spaces) results in what type of anoxia?
questions.explanation: Decreased inspired oxygen concentration directly causes anoxic (hypoxic) anoxia, since insufficient oxygen is available in the air to be taken up by the blood.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT part of the classic triad features of asphyxia?
options: Fluid in the left side of the heart
Petechial hemorrhages in skin of face and eyes
originalOptions: Fluid in the left side of the heart
Petechial hemorrhages in skin of face and eyes
questions.correctAnswer: B) Fluid in the left side of the heart
questions.correctAnswerText: Fluid in the left side of the heart
questions.explanation: The asphyxia triad consists of cyanosis, congestion, and petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots); fluid accumulation in the left heart is not a recognized feature — right heart dilatation is more typically associated with asphyxial death.

questions.text: How are antemortem hangings diagnosed?
options: By the presence of cadaveric spasm
By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
originalOptions: By the presence of cadaveric spasm
By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
questions.correctAnswer: B) By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
questions.correctAnswerText: By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
questions.explanation: Antemortem hanging is confirmed by vital reactions in the ligature mark — hemorrhage, WBC infiltration, and early tissue repair — which are absent when the ligature is applied postmortem.

questions.text: What is a sign of antemortem hanging?
questions.explanation: Dripping or dribbling of saliva from the angle of the mouth toward the shoulder is a vital sign requiring intact salivary gland function, confirming the person was alive during the hanging (antemortem).

questions.text: Hypostasis (livor mortis) in the lower limbs is a sign of which condition?
questions.explanation: In complete hanging, the body is fully suspended, causing blood to gravitate and pool in the lower limbs, producing lower-limb hypostasis.

questions.text: Abrasions around the mouth indicate which mechanism of asphyxia?
questions.explanation: Perioral abrasions from hand or pillow pressure applied to obstruct the airway are characteristic of smothering, distinguishing it from neck-focused mechanisms like throttling or hanging.

questions.text: What is the most common manner of death in choking?
questions.explanation: Choking from foreign body airway obstruction (food, small objects) is most commonly accidental; homicidal choking (e.g., forced feeding) is rare.

questions.text: Histotoxic anoxia is caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), preventing cells from utilizing oxygen even when it is available in the blood — defining histotoxic (cellular) anoxia, unlike CO (which impairs oxygen transport) or CNS depressants.

questions.text: Complete hanging (as opposed to incomplete) is defined by which factor?
questions.explanation: Complete versus incomplete hanging is distinguished by whether the body is fully suspended off the ground or partially supported/touching a surface, not by the victim's physical characteristics.

questions.text: A 65-year-old found dead in seawater shows goose skin appearance, easily removable hair, and the right hand forcefully grasping grass weeds. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Forceful grasping of an object (weeds) at the instant of death represents cadaveric spasm — instantaneous muscle locking that proves the person was alive and gripping at the moment they entered the water, distinct from the gradual onset of ordinary rigor mortis.

questions.text: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) causes death via what type of anoxia?
options: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
originalOptions: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
questions.correctAnswer: A) Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
questions.correctAnswerText: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
questions.explanation: GBS causes ascending paralysis leading to respiratory muscle failure, preventing adequate ventilation so oxygen cannot enter the lungs — anoxic anoxia, despite normal oxygen availability in the environment.

questions.text: What type of anoxia is caused by cyanide (HCN) poisoning?
questions.explanation: HCN inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), blocking cellular oxygen utilization despite normal oxygen delivery — defining histotoxic (cellular) anoxia.

questions.text: The vagus nerve shares the same anatomical root and exit point with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and CN X (vagus) both arise from the medulla oblongata and exit the skull together through the jugular foramen, making their close anatomical relationship medicolegally relevant to vagal reflex death in asphyxia

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism of carbon monoxide toxicity?
options: Decreases oxygen delivery to the tissues
Binds reversibly to haemoglobin with an affinity 200–230 times that of oxygen
Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
Shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left
Binds to cytochrome oxidase and impairs oxidative metabolism
originalOptions: Decreases oxygen delivery to the tissues
Binds reversibly to haemoglobin with an affinity 200–230 times that of oxygen
Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
Shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left
Binds to cytochrome oxidase and impairs oxidative metabolism
questions.correctAnswer: C) Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
questions.correctAnswerText: Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
questions.explanation: CO forms carboxyhaemoglobin, which lowers oxygen-carrying capacity and left-shifts the curve, so oxygen transport and release both fall. It never increases them.

questions.text: All of the following are NOT true regarding CO poisoning in pregnancy EXCEPT, which statement is true? Which statement is NOT true regarding CO poisoning in pregnancy?
options: Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
Fetal haemoglobin binds CO with a higher affinity than adult haemoglobin
The fetus is more susceptible to CO than the mother
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but eventually reaches a higher level than the mother's
originalOptions: Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
Fetal haemoglobin binds CO with a higher affinity than adult haemoglobin
The fetus is more susceptible to CO than the mother
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but eventually reaches a higher level than the mother's
questions.correctAnswer: A) Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
questions.correctAnswerText: Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
questions.explanation: CO is eliminated from the fetus much more slowly than from the mother, which is why the fetus ends up with higher COHb and is more susceptible to hypoxia even when the mother survives.

questions.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning affects the fetus in all of the following ways EXCEPT:
options: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide is eliminated slowly from the fetal circulation
Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but ends higher than the maternal level
originalOptions: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide is eliminated slowly from the fetal circulation
Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but ends higher than the maternal level
questions.correctAnswer: D) Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
questions.correctAnswerText: Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
questions.explanation: Elimination from the fetus is slow, not rapid. Combined with the higher affinity of fetal Hb for CO, this prolongs fetal hypoxia.

questions.text: Which of the following is the WRONG mechanism regarding carbon monoxide poisoning?
options: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with high affinity
It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
It left-shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
It decreases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
originalOptions: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with high affinity
It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
It left-shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
It decreases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
questions.correctAnswer: B) It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
questions.correctAnswerText: It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
questions.explanation: CO increases the affinity of the remaining haem sites for oxygen (left shift), so oxygen release to the tissues decreases, not increases.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of carbon monoxide?
options: Oxidation of ferrous iron in haemoglobin to form methaemoglobin
Right shift of the dissociation curve with increased oxygen release
Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
originalOptions: Oxidation of ferrous iron in haemoglobin to form methaemoglobin
Right shift of the dissociation curve with increased oxygen release
Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.correctAnswer: E) Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.correctAnswerText: Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.explanation: CO competes with O₂ at the haem site and forms COHb, which lowers carrying capacity and left-shifts the curve, causing tissue hypoxia. AChE inhibition is the organophosphate mechanism, and methaemoglobin is formed by oxidation, not by CO.

questions.text: All of the following can cause CO poisoning EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CO comes only from incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels. An electrical heater involves no combustion and produces no CO.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a source of carbon monoxide?
questions.explanation: An electrical heater has no combustion, so it produces no CO. Firearm discharge gases contain CO, and methylene chloride is metabolised by the liver to CO.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for CO poisoning?
questions.explanation: Increased ambient temperature, not decreased, raises the rate of CO uptake. Cold is not a risk factor.

questions.text: All of the following are features of carbon monoxide gas and its poisoning EXCEPT:
options: The most common type of fatal poisoning in many countries
Produced by incomplete combustion of fuels
originalOptions: The most common type of fatal poisoning in many countries
Produced by incomplete combustion of fuels
questions.correctAnswer: B) Causes irritative symptoms on inhalation
questions.explanation: CO is non-irritant, so there are no warning symptoms, which is why it is called the "silent killer".

questions.text: CO poisoning is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Sinus tachycardia and ST-segment changes on ECG
originalOptions: Sinus tachycardia and ST-segment changes on ECG
questions.explanation: Despite asphyxiation, cyanosis does not occur in CO poisoning because COHb is bright red; the skin is pink or pale and the lips are bright red.

questions.text: Cherry-red discoloration after CO poisoning is located in:
options: Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
originalOptions: Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
questions.correctAnswer: C) Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
questions.correctAnswerText: Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
questions.explanation: Carboxyhaemoglobin and carboxymyoglobin colour the blood, skin, lividity, mucous membranes, muscles and internal organs, so no single site is the answer.

questions.text: What is the normal COHb level in the blood of a resting healthy non-smoker?
questions.explanation: Background COHb from endogenous haem catabolism is the lowest option, about 1–3% (0.4–0.7% in the lecture). Smokers reach about 5–10%, and symptoms usually begin around 10–20%.

questions.text: In a death from CO poisoning, the cherry-pink colour is absent. This implies that:
options: The cause of death was not CO poisoning
The death was caused by hanging
The patient died too quickly for any COHb to form
originalOptions: The cause of death was not CO poisoning
The death was caused by hanging
The patient died too quickly for any COHb to form
questions.explanation: Resuscitation and oxygen administration lower the COHb level, so the cherry-pink colour fades. Its absence does not exclude CO, and a blood COHb level confirms the diagnosis.

questions.text: What is the mainstay of management of CO poisoning?
questions.explanation: High-flow 100% O₂ shortens the half-life of CO from 3–4 hours on room air to 30–90 minutes, and hyperbaric O₂ shortens it further. Pralidoxime and atropine are for organophosphate poisoning, and naloxone is for opioids.

questions.text: All of the following cause a LEFT shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acidosis and increased CO₂ cause a RIGHT shift (Bohr effect), which lowers Hb affinity and increases O₂ release. The other four increase affinity and shift the curve to the left.

questions.text: All of the following are risk factors for a LEFT shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Respiratory acidosis (high CO₂, low pH) right-shifts the curve through the Bohr effect, which favours O₂ release. All the other options left-shift it.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause or indicator of child abuse?
questions.explanation: MS is a neurological autoimmune disease unrelated to abuse; multiple bruises, shaken baby syndrome, and Munchausen by proxy are classic abuse indicators.

questions.text: Bruising in which of the following areas is NOT considered a suspicious sign of child abuse?
questions.explanation: Knee bruising is a common, normal childhood injury from falls and play; abuse-related bruising is characteristically found on protected areas such as the torso, back, abdomen, and chest.

questions.text: Regarding Munchausen syndrome by proxy, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
Parents readily admit to causing the illness
originalOptions: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
Parents readily admit to causing the illness
questions.correctAnswer: D) Parents readily admit to causing the illness
questions.correctAnswerText: Parents readily admit to causing the illness
questions.explanation: Munchausen by proxy is characterized by unexplained illness that improves when the child is separated from the caregiver, a lack of clear diagnosis, and negative workup; perpetrators rarely confess to causing the illness.

questions.text: A 31-year-old woman claims sexual assault 4 days ago. Examination shows a recent hymenal tear at the 5 o'clock position. Which statement is TRUE?
options: No informed consent is required before examination
Delay in reporting confirms a fabricated story
Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
Rupture of the hymen is an absolute sign confirming rape
The findings determine the exact time of the assault
originalOptions: No informed consent is required before examination
Delay in reporting confirms a fabricated story
Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
Rupture of the hymen is an absolute sign confirming rape
The findings determine the exact time of the assault
questions.correctAnswer: C) Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
questions.correctAnswerText: Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
questions.explanation: A recent hymenal tear is corroborative evidence supporting the allegation, but it alone cannot confirm rape; consent is required before examination, and delayed reporting is common even in genuine cases.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true concerning sexual assault victims?
options: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
Post-assault forensic sampling is vital for evaluation
Victims should be assessed for genitourinary health, contraception needs, and counseling
Emergency contraception may include oral contraceptives
originalOptions: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
Post-assault forensic sampling is vital for evaluation
Victims should be assessed for genitourinary health, contraception needs, and counseling
Emergency contraception may include oral contraceptives
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
questions.correctAnswerText: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
questions.explanation: This statistic is false — paedophilia and bestiality are not common practices in any population; the other statements reflect appropriate sexual assault management.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized type of hymen?
questions.explanation: Cribriform hymen (with multiple small openings) is a recognized anatomical variant; notches at 3 or 9 o'clock are considered normal artefacts rather than named types, and "elastic" is not a recognized hymen type.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of erectile dysfunction (impotence) in young men?
questions.explanation: In young men, erectile dysfunction is most commonly psychogenic in origin, whereas vascular causes become more predominant with advancing age.

questions.text: Which of the following cases is considered a medico-legal case?
options: Death at home from a known chronic natural disease
Death in hospital from a known disease under medical care
Death of a person in prison
Expected death of a terminally ill patient under palliative care
Death of an elderly patient from known heart failure attended by his physician
originalOptions: Death at home from a known chronic natural disease
Death in hospital from a known disease under medical care
Death of a person in prison
Expected death of a terminally ill patient under palliative care
Death of an elderly patient from known heart failure attended by his physician
questions.correctAnswer: C) Death of a person in prison
questions.correctAnswerText: Death of a person in prison
questions.explanation: Any death in custody (prison, police, juvenile home) is a medico-legal case regardless of its apparent cause, to exclude foul play and establish accountability. The other options are expected natural deaths under medical care.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of myocardial infarction without atheroma?
questions.explanation: Intense emotional stress causes coronary spasm through a catecholamine surge and can produce infarction in the absence of atheroma. Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and diabetes act through atheroma formation.

questions.text: A prisoner dies from bronchospasm. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A standard death certificate is sufficient
An autopsy is not required because the cause of death is natural
Family consent is required before an autopsy can be performed
The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
The prison physician may release the body for burial without notification
originalOptions: A standard death certificate is sufficient
An autopsy is not required because the cause of death is natural
Family consent is required before an autopsy can be performed
The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
The prison physician may release the body for burial without notification
questions.correctAnswer: D) The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
questions.correctAnswerText: The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
questions.explanation: A death in custody is a mandatory medico-legal case, so it must be reported to the public prosecutor and followed by a medico-legal autopsy. Neither a death certificate alone nor family consent is applicable, even if the apparent cause is natural.

questions.text: Which of the following causes of death is NOT considered medico-legal?
options: Pulmonary embolism following a hip fracture in a hospitalized patient
Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
Pneumonia in a 16-year-old male in a juvenile home
A 30-year-old brought in dead following a head injury
A 60-year-old man who died suddenly while waiting for an X-ray
originalOptions: Pulmonary embolism following a hip fracture in a hospitalized patient
Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
Pneumonia in a 16-year-old male in a juvenile home
A 30-year-old brought in dead following a head injury
A 60-year-old man who died suddenly while waiting for an X-ray
questions.correctAnswer: B) Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
questions.correctAnswerText: Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
questions.explanation: Death from a diagnosed disease under active medical care is an expected natural death. The other options involve trauma or its complications, custody, a "brought in dead" case, or sudden unexpected death.

questions.text: When a forensic physician is called to the scene by the public prosecutor, the primary purposes are:
options: Only to confirm that death has occurred
To clean and document the scene
To perform a complete autopsy at the scene
To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
originalOptions: Only to confirm that death has occurred
To clean and document the scene
To perform a complete autopsy at the scene
To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
questions.correctAnswer: E) To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
questions.correctAnswerText: To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
questions.explanation: The forensic physician identifies the deceased, determines the time, cause and manner of death, and helps reconstruct the events for the prosecutor. Confirming death or collecting samples are only parts of this role.

questions.text: Which stage of lobar pneumonia is most likely to cause death in children?
questions.explanation: Children most often die in the first stage, from overwhelming toxaemia, before consolidation develops. Red and grey hepatization are later stages, and resolution is the recovery stage.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of sudden unexpected death?
questions.explanation: Coronary artery disease with myocardial infarction, together with hypertensive heart disease, accounts for most sudden unexpected deaths in adults. Respiratory, CNS, metabolic and gastrointestinal causes are far less frequent.

questions.text: Molecular (cellular) death occurs in relation to somatic death:
options: Only after rigor mortis is fully established
Only after the onset of putrefaction
originalOptions: Only after rigor mortis is fully established
Only after the onset of putrefaction
questions.explanation: Molecular death follows somatic death (about 1–2 hours after vital functions stop) and occurs piecemeal, cell by cell. This lag is the basis of the organ-donation window.

questions.text: Which statement about second-degree burns is NOT correct?
options: It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
It is less severe than a full-thickness burn
originalOptions: It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
It is less severe than a full-thickness burn
questions.correctAnswer: A) It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
questions.correctAnswerText: It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
questions.explanation: A second-degree burn does not suppress the vital signs, so it cannot simulate death. Its features are dermal involvement, blisters and marked pain, because the nerve endings are intact, unlike third-degree burns.

questions.text: A dead body is found in a flat. Rectal temperature is 26.4°C, ambient temperature 18°C, and body weight 90 kg. The approximate time since death is:
questions.explanation: (37.2 − 26.4) = 10.8°C ÷ 1–1.5°C/hour gives about 7–11 hours. A heavy 90 kg body cools more slowly, so the interval is, if anything, longer (Henssge nomogram corrects for weight and ambient temperature).

questions.text: A body is found in an apartment with a rectal temperature of 32°C and rigor mortis not yet complete. The most likely time since death is:
questions.explanation: (37.2 − 32) = 5.2°C ÷ 1–1.5°C/hour gives about 3.5–5 hours. Incomplete rigor, which begins at 2–3 hours and is established by 9–12 hours, fits a recent death.

questions.text: The estimated time since death of a body found cold AND stiff is:
questions.explanation: Cold with rigor present means 8–36 hours. Warm and flaccid is under 3 hours, warm and stiff is 3–8 hours, and cold and flaccid (secondary flaccidity) is over 36 hours.

questions.text: A full stomach with undigested meal at autopsy indicates that the last meal was taken:
options: More than four hours before death
More than six hours before death
Less than two hours before death
More than twelve hours before death
originalOptions: More than four hours before death
More than six hours before death
Less than two hours before death
More than twelve hours before death
questions.correctAnswer: C) Less than two hours before death
questions.correctAnswerText: Less than two hours before death
questions.explanation: A full stomach with undigested food suggests death within about 2 hours of the meal, whereas an empty stomach suggests at least 4–6 hours. It is only a rough guide, since fear, injury and coma delay gastric emptying.

questions.text: Which of the following post-mortem changes begins immediately after death?
questions.explanation: Livor starts as soon as circulation stops and blood is governed by gravity (apparent at about 2 hours, fixed at about 6–8 hours). Rigor appears at 2–3 hours and putrefaction becomes visible at 48–72 hours. Cooling (algor) is a gradual process.

questions.text: Which of the following appears immediately after death in a person who died under intense emotion?
questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm is instantaneous rigidity at the moment of death, linked to violent death with intense emotion. Ordinary rigor mortis is delayed by 2–3 hours.

questions.text: Rigor mortis is first evident in:
questions.explanation: Rigor is first detected in the small muscles of the eyelids, then face and jaw, neck, upper limbs, trunk and lower limbs (head to foot). The myocardium stiffens early but this is not evident on examination.

questions.text: The fundamental cause of rigor mortis is:
options: Active contraction triggered by calcium channel activation
Breakdown of the muscle cell wall by autolytic enzymes
Coagulation of muscle proteins by heat
Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
originalOptions: Active contraction triggered by calcium channel activation
Breakdown of the muscle cell wall by autolytic enzymes
Coagulation of muscle proteins by heat
Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
questions.correctAnswer: E) Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
questions.correctAnswerText: Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
questions.explanation: Rigor is a passive stiffening, not an active contraction: with low ATP and rising acidity the actin–myosin bonds cannot dissociate. Heat coagulation causes heat stiffness, and muscle turns alkaline again only in secondary flaccidity.

questions.text: The best site for recording body temperature to estimate the time of death is:
questions.explanation: The rectum (8–10 cm above the anus) gives the true core temperature and is the standard site for the cooling formula. The external ear is a recognised site but is not the ideal one.

questions.text: In practice, the most accurate way of estimating the time of death is:
options: Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
originalOptions: Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
questions.correctAnswer: A) Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
questions.correctAnswerText: Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
questions.explanation: All biological methods are imprecise, and scene markers are often more accurate. Core temperature is the best scientific method, but it does not outperform circumstantial evidence.

questions.text: "Livor" in livor mortis (hypostasis) means:
questions.explanation: Livor means livid (purple), reflecting blood pooling in dependent parts. Blue is the colour of cyanosis, not of livor.

questions.text: The normal colour of post-mortem lividity is:
questions.explanation: Normal hypostasis is bluish or purplish-red. Cherry pink indicates CO, cyanide or cold, brown indicates methaemoglobinaemia, pale indicates anaemia or haemorrhage, and greenish-black is a putrefactive change.

questions.text: What is the colour of livor mortis in methaemoglobinaemia?
questions.explanation: Methaemoglobin gives brown lividity. Deep bluish violet is seen in asphyxia, and cherry pink in CO poisoning, cold and cyanide.

questions.text: The colour of hypostasis in mummified bodies is:
questions.explanation: In mummified bodies, lividity appears brown to black due to desiccation. Deep bluish violet is characteristic of asphyxia.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT related to colour?
questions.explanation: Congestion means excess blood in the vessels and is not defined by a colour. Cyanosis denotes blueness, vibices are streaks of hypostasis, and livor means livid (purple).

questions.text: Hypostasis in the lower limbs is a sign of:
questions.explanation: In complete hanging the body is vertical and fully suspended, so lividity collects distally in the legs, feet and hands. In incomplete hanging it follows the part touching the ground.

questions.text: Hypostasis in drowning is most commonly seen on:
options: A site that depends on the water current and body posture
Always the front of the body
originalOptions: A site that depends on the water current and body posture
Always the front of the body
questions.correctAnswer: B) A site that depends on the water current and body posture
questions.correctAnswerText: A site that depends on the water current and body posture
questions.explanation: Moving water keeps turning the body, so hypostasis is often faint and its site is variable. A floating body usually lies face-down, giving lividity of the face, upper chest and upper limbs, but this is not constant.

questions.text: Which of the following produces MARKED hypostasis after death?
questions.explanation: Congestive heart failure (like asphyxia and polycythaemia) leaves more blood available to pool, so hypostasis is marked. Anaemia and haemorrhage reduce circulating blood and give faint or absent lividity.

questions.text: All of the following cause faint, late or absent hypostasis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Polycythaemia increases the red-cell mass and gives marked lividity. Anaemia, haemorrhage, cholera and the extremes of age tend to produce pale, late or absent lividity.

questions.text: Absence of hypostasis after death is most likely in:
options: Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
originalOptions: Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
questions.correctAnswer: A) Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
questions.correctAnswerText: Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
questions.explanation: Lividity needs enough blood to pool in dependent vessels, and anaemia or massive blood loss leaves too little. Polycythaemia, CHF and asphyxia give marked lividity.

questions.text: Which post-mortem change is related to the red blood cell count?
questions.explanation: The intensity of livor depends on red-cell mass and blood fluidity: marked in polycythaemia and faint in anaemia. The other changes are muscular, thermal or bacterial.

questions.text: Extensive muscular exercise immediately before death:
options: Delays the onset of rigor mortis
Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
Has no effect on rigor mortis
Prolongs the duration of rigor mortis
originalOptions: Delays the onset of rigor mortis
Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
Has no effect on rigor mortis
Prolongs the duration of rigor mortis
questions.correctAnswer: B) Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
questions.correctAnswerText: Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
questions.explanation: Fatigued or exhausted muscles, and increased activity just before death, give rapid onset and short duration of rigor because of rapid ATP depletion. Rested, healthy muscles develop rigor slowly and keep it longer.

questions.text: All of the following are early signs of death EXCEPT:
options: Skin loses its elasticity with facial pallor
Muscles rapidly become flaccid (primary flaccidity) with loss of tone
The eyes lose their intraocular tension
The retinal vessels show fragmentation ("trucking") of the blood columns
The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
originalOptions: Skin loses its elasticity with facial pallor
Muscles rapidly become flaccid (primary flaccidity) with loss of tone
The eyes lose their intraocular tension
The retinal vessels show fragmentation ("trucking") of the blood columns
The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
questions.correctAnswer: E) The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
questions.correctAnswerText: The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
questions.explanation: After death muscles may still twitch focally and respond to touch or stimulation for some hours, because cellular death is progressive. Options A–D are recognised early changes.

questions.text: All of the following are early signs of death EXCEPT:
questions.correctAnswer: C) Rigor mortis (2–3 hours after death)
questions.explanation: Rigor needs 2–3 hours to appear, so it is the odd one out among the immediate changes. Primary flaccidity, loss of corneal reflex and the start of cooling occur at once.

questions.text: A 55-year-old man, apparently dead, is brought to the casualty department. The earliest post-mortem change to appear is:
options: Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
originalOptions: Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
questions.correctAnswer: A) Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
questions.correctAnswerText: Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
questions.explanation: Pallor and loss of skin elasticity appear within minutes of circulatory arrest. Lividity, corneal clouding, cooling and rigor take hours.

questions.text: All of the following are post-mortem changes in the eyes EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: After death the cornea becomes opaque (earlier if the lids are open, within about 10–12 hours if closed), so a persistently clear cornea is not a post-mortem change. The other findings are all described after death.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a post-mortem change in the eyes?
questions.explanation: A clear cornea is a feature of life or of very early death. Corneal opacity, tache noire, anisocoria and falling intraocular tension all develop after death.

questions.text: After death, body temperature may be higher than expected in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature is lower than expected after haemorrhage, cholera, CHF and hypothermia. It is higher after infections, asphyxia, pontine haemorrhage, coronary thrombosis, struggle and heat stroke.

questions.text: Which of the following is a POSITIVE sign of death?
questions.explanation: Putrefaction, adipocere, mummification, rigor and fixed hypostasis are certain signs of death. Flat EEG and absent heart or breath sounds also occur in suspended animation, and corneal reflex loss is unreliable.

questions.text: The diagnosis of brainstem death depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Apnoea after disconnection from the ventilator
originalOptions: Apnoea after disconnection from the ventilator
questions.correctAnswer: A) Presence of the gag reflex
questions.explanation: Brainstem death requires coma, absence of ALL brainstem reflexes (including gag and cough) and apnoea. A present gag reflex means brainstem function persists.

questions.text: Which of the following organs is MOST resistant to putrefaction?
questions.explanation: The prostate (and non-gravid uterus) are among the last organs to putrefy. The brain, stomach, spleen and liver putrefy early.

questions.text: Which of the following is the last organ to putrefy?
questions.explanation: The non-gravid uterus and prostate are late-putrefying organs, whereas the stomach and intestines are early. The gravid uterus is also an early-putrefying organ.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs are signs of putrefaction?
options: Waxy, soap-like fat and brittle bones
Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
originalOptions: Waxy, soap-like fat and brittle bones
Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
questions.correctAnswer: E) Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
questions.correctAnswerText: Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
questions.explanation: The first visible sign of putrefaction is greenish discoloration over the right iliac fossa (near the bacteria-rich caecum), followed by gas formation and bloating. The other pairs describe rigor, adipocere, lividity and eye changes.

questions.text: Which of the following are two other types of decomposition besides putrefaction?
questions.explanation: Mummification (desiccation in dry, warm conditions) and adipocere (fat saponification in moist conditions) are the special routes of decomposition. The other options are early post-mortem changes or part of putrefaction itself.

questions.text: Which of the following sets contains only signs of LATE putrefaction?
options: Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, rigor mortis
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, tache noire
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, early lividity
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, cadaveric spasm
originalOptions: Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, rigor mortis
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, tache noire
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, early lividity
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, cadaveric spasm
questions.correctAnswer: A) Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
questions.correctAnswerText: Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
questions.explanation: Late putrefaction progresses through bloating and blistering with skin slippage to liquefaction and eventually skeleton exposure. Rigor, tache noire, early lividity and cadaveric spasm are early or non-putrefactive changes.

questions.text: Adipocere is chiefly composed of which acid?
questions.explanation: Adipocere is mainly saturated fatty acids, chiefly palmitic acid, formed by hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fat. Stearic and hydroxy-stearic acids are minor components and little oleic acid remains.

questions.text: Adipocere formation is associated with which organism?
questions.explanation: Bacterial enzymes of Clostridium perfringens hydrolyse and hydrogenate body fat in warm, moist conditions. Moisture is essential.

questions.text: Adipocere occurs first in:
questions.explanation: Adipocere forms first in subcutaneous fat (cheeks, breasts, buttocks). Internal organs such as the liver, kidney and heart may be affected later.

questions.text: Mummification involves:
questions.explanation: Mummification needs dry, warm conditions that dry out the tissues, preventing bacterial growth. Humidity and bacterial action favour putrefaction or adipocere.

questions.text: Mummification is:
questions.explanation: Mummification is drying and shrivelling of tissues with no microbial growth. Saponification is adipocere, and liquefaction occurs in putrefaction.

questions.text: The most common source of putrefactive organisms is the:
questions.explanation: Most putrefactive bacteria come from the bowel, with Clostridium predominating. This is why discoloration starts in the right iliac fossa over the caecum.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT significantly affect putrefaction?
questions.explanation: Sex is not a major factor (only slightly faster in females, who have more fat). Temperature, moisture, clothing, age and cause of death clearly alter the rate.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT retard putrefaction?
options: Poisoning with strychnine or heavy metals
originalOptions: Poisoning with strychnine or heavy metals
questions.correctAnswer: E) Burial in a shallow grave
questions.explanation: Surface burial decomposes the body more because surface soil has more bacteria and access. Water immersion, coffins, dry sandy soil and metal poisons all delay putrefaction.

questions.text: Cadaveric spasm occurs in:
questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm affects voluntary (skeletal) muscles only, usually the hands and forearms, particularly those contracted at the moment of death.

questions.text: Suspended animation is:
options: Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
Apparent death in which the patient cannot be aroused
A state that lasts for days or weeks
A state that can never be induced voluntarily
Irreversible loss of brainstem function with preserved circulation
originalOptions: Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
Apparent death in which the patient cannot be aroused
A state that lasts for days or weeks
A state that can never be induced voluntarily
Irreversible loss of brainstem function with preserved circulation
questions.correctAnswer: A) Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
questions.correctAnswerText: Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
questions.explanation: In suspended animation vital signs are not detectable by routine methods, but the person can be resuscitated. It can even be voluntary, as in yoga practitioners.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism causes true, rapid death. Hypothermia, hypnotic or opiate overdose, electrocution and drowning can suppress vital signs reversibly.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)?
questions.explanation: A second-degree burn does not suppress the vital signs. Newborns, heat stroke, hypothermia and cholera are recognised causes of apparent death.

questions.text: All of the following may simulate death EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cyanide causes rapid true death rather than a reversible suppression of vital signs. Drowning, hypnotic or opiate overdose and electrocution can all produce apparent death.

questions.text: Maggots of a cadaver help in determining the:
questions.explanation: Forensic entomology uses the stage of maggot development (larva, pupa, adult), corrected for temperature, to give a minimum post-mortem interval.

questions.text: Maggots are most useful in forensic practice for:
options: Estimating the time of death in late stages
Estimating the time of death in early stages
originalOptions: Estimating the time of death in late stages
Estimating the time of death in early stages
questions.correctAnswer: A) Estimating the time of death in late stages
questions.correctAnswerText: Estimating the time of death in late stages
questions.explanation: Entomology is most valuable in late decomposition, when temperature, rigor and lividity no longer help. In the early hours those methods are better.

questions.text: When a tattoo has been destroyed, its former presence can be inferred from pigment in the:
questions.explanation: Macrophages carry tattoo pigment to the draining lymph nodes, so it persists there even if the skin is burnt or decomposed.

questions.text: In suspected air embolism, the body cavity to be opened first is the:
questions.explanation: The thorax is opened first so air is not introduced artefactually. The pericardial sac is filled with water and the right ventricle incised under water, where escaping bubbles confirm venous air embolism.

questions.text: "Nutmeg liver" refers to:
questions.explanation: Nutmeg liver results from chronic venous congestion, usually right-sided heart failure. It shows dark congested centrilobular zones alternating with pale periportal zones.

questions.text: Fatty change of the liver is usually and more commonly seen in:
questions.explanation: Steatosis is commonest in metabolic disorders (obesity, diabetes) and alcohol. Heart failure produces nutmeg liver (chronic venous congestion) rather than fatty change.

questions.text: Fatty change of the liver is seen in:
options: Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
originalOptions: Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
questions.correctAnswer: A) Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
questions.correctAnswerText: Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
questions.explanation: Fatty change occurs with metabolic disorders, alcohol, and poisoning by phosphorus and arsenic. Heart failure causes congestion (nutmeg liver) instead.

questions.text: A black triangular patch appears on the exposed sclera at each side of the iris in a body whose eyelids were left open for several hours. This finding is:
questions.explanation: When the lids stay open for 3–4 hours, drying of the exposed sclera forms yellow triangles that turn brown and then black. This is tache noire, not a haemorrhage or lividity.

questions.text: Which of the following is the main ethical priority of the physician when dealing with vulnerable children who are victims of violence?
options: Respect for the autonomy of the parents
originalOptions: Respect for the autonomy of the parents
questions.explanation: In suspected child abuse, the physician's primary ethical duty is early detection and protection of the child. This outranks confidentiality and parental autonomy.

questions.text: In which of the following situations is breach of confidentiality permissible?
options: Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
Request by the patient's husband or wife
Request by an insurance company representative
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
originalOptions: Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
Request by the patient's husband or wife
Request by an insurance company representative
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
questions.correctAnswer: A) Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
questions.correctAnswerText: Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
questions.explanation: Notifiable diseases must be reported to the Ministry of Health by law. Requests from a spouse, insurer, employer, or relative do not justify a breach without the patient's consent.

questions.text: All of the following are principles of bioethics EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The four principles of bioethics are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. "Reluctance" is not a bioethical principle.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT correct concerning valid consent prior to medical treatment?
options: It must be voluntary and freely given
Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
The patient must be informed of what the treatment involves
The patient must be informed of the benefits and risks
The capacity of the patient must be assessed
originalOptions: It must be voluntary and freely given
Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
The patient must be informed of what the treatment involves
The patient must be informed of the benefits and risks
The capacity of the patient must be assessed
questions.correctAnswer: B) Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
questions.correctAnswerText: Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
questions.explanation: Valid consent requires voluntariness, adequate information, and capacity. A competent adult consents for himself or herself, and requiring spousal consent would violate patient autonomy.

questions.text: A 23-year-old single adult female presents with vaginal bleeding. Which of the following statements regarding consent is correct?
options: Consent must be obtained from her father or husband
Consent of her partner is always mandatory
A court order is required before treatment
She can give her own medical consent independently
originalOptions: Consent must be obtained from her father or husband
Consent of her partner is always mandatory
A court order is required before treatment
She can give her own medical consent independently
questions.correctAnswer: E) She can give her own medical consent independently
questions.correctAnswerText: She can give her own medical consent independently
questions.explanation: Any competent adult (18 years or older) has full capacity to consent to treatment without parental, spousal, or guardian authorization.

questions.text: What is the most important rule when performing a physical examination of the intimate parts of the body?
options: The examination must be performed only after police notification
The examination must be performed by a physician of the same gender only
The examination must be photographed before it begins
The examination must be performed in the presence of a guardian
originalOptions: The examination must be performed only after police notification
The examination must be performed by a physician of the same gender only
The examination must be photographed before it begins
The examination must be performed in the presence of a guardian
questions.correctAnswer: C) A chaperone must be present
questions.explanation: A chaperone protects the dignity of the patient and the professional integrity of the physician during examination of intimate parts.

questions.text: "Respect for persons" in the ethical approach includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Respect for persons comprises autonomy, integrity, equity, and equality. Following the doctor's orders contradicts patient-centred ethics.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true concerning the duties of doctors to patients?
options: Respect the patient's right to confidentiality
Always bear in mind the obligation to respect human life
Refer the patient to another physician whenever the examination is beyond the physician's capacity
Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
Act in the patient's best interest when providing medical care
originalOptions: Respect the patient's right to confidentiality
Always bear in mind the obligation to respect human life
Refer the patient to another physician whenever the examination is beyond the physician's capacity
Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
Act in the patient's best interest when providing medical care
questions.correctAnswer: D) Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
questions.correctAnswerText: Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
questions.explanation: Informed consent is required for victims of violence as for any other patient. Only a true emergency in which delay would cause harm waives it.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT appropriate considering ethical standards?
options: Maintain professional competence throughout one's career
originalOptions: Maintain professional competence throughout one's career
questions.correctAnswer: B) Enhance intimate relationships with patients
questions.explanation: An intimate relationship between a physician and a patient is unethical because it violates professional boundaries.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a declaration of the World Medical Association related to the humanization of medical practice?
questions.explanation: The WMA declarations include Geneva, Helsinki, Oslo, Tokyo, and Sydney. There is no "Declaration of London" in medical ethics.

questions.text: The humanization of medical practice was the main theme of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Geneva (1948) is the physician's oath and defines the physician's duties. The Nuremberg Code (1947) concerns consent in research, Oslo concerns therapeutic abortion, and Tokyo concerns torture.

questions.text: The Declaration of Helsinki is related to:
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) sets the ethical standards for medical research on human subjects. Torture is addressed by Tokyo and therapeutic abortion by Oslo.

questions.text: All of the following are types of consent EXCEPT:
options: Informed consent for accepting medical treatment
Written consent by a rape victim
Request for euthanasia by the patient
Participation in a research trial authorized by an Institutional Review Board
originalOptions: Informed consent for accepting medical treatment
Written consent by a rape victim
Request for euthanasia by the patient
Participation in a research trial authorized by an Institutional Review Board
questions.correctAnswer: D) Request for euthanasia by the patient
questions.correctAnswerText: Request for euthanasia by the patient
questions.explanation: Euthanasia is illegal in Jordan and is not a type of consent. The other options are recognized forms: implied, informed, written (expressed), and research consent approved by an IRB.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT related to the World Medical Association declarations concerning the humanization of health services?
options: United Nations Development Fund for Women
originalOptions: United Nations Development Fund for Women
questions.correctAnswer: B) United Nations Development Fund for Women
questions.correctAnswerText: United Nations Development Fund for Women
questions.explanation: Helsinki, Geneva, Tokyo, and Oslo are all World Medical Association declarations. The United Nations Development Fund for Women is a United Nations agency and not a medical declaration.

questions.text: Breach of patient confidentiality is permissible in which of the following cases?
options: Request by the patient's husband or wife
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
Upon the request or consent of the patient
originalOptions: Request by the patient's husband or wife
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
Upon the request or consent of the patient
questions.correctAnswer: E) Upon the request or consent of the patient
questions.correctAnswerText: Upon the request or consent of the patient
questions.explanation: Confidentiality may be breached with the patient's own consent, for notifiable diseases, by court order, for child protection, or when there is a serious risk to others. Requests from a spouse, insurer, employer, or relative do not justify a breach.

questions.text: What type of toxicology concerns itself with medical and legal aspects, focused on detecting poisons in medicolegal investigations?
questions.explanation: Forensic toxicology represents the intersection of toxicology with the law, applying poison detection specifically to medicolegal investigations, distinguishing it from clinical (patient management), environmental, and purely analytical toxicology.

questions.text: What color is associated with methemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin (Fe³⁺ state) produces a characteristic chocolate-brown discoloration of blood and livor, and causes cyanosis that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen — distinguishing it from cherry-red (carbon monoxide) or cyanotic bluish-purple (hypoxia) presentations.

questions.text: Activated charcoal is useless in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal effectively adsorbs salicylates (along with paracetamol and tricyclics), but it is ineffective for iron, lithium, cyanide, corrosives, alcohols, and heavy metals.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is best absorbed (adsorbed) by activated charcoal?
questions.explanation: Salicylate is well adsorbed by activated charcoal, whereas iron, lithium, and cyanide are not effectively bound by it.

questions.text: Which statement about activated charcoal is TRUE?
options: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
It works by absorption into the toxin
It is contraindicated in all cases of poisoning
originalOptions: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
It works by absorption into the toxin
It is contraindicated in all cases of poisoning
questions.correctAnswer: A) It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
questions.correctAnswerText: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal works via adsorption — binding the toxin to its surface in the gut — thereby preventing systemic absorption, rather than being absorbed itself or inducing emesis.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about activated charcoal is FALSE?
options: It should be given as soon as possible after ingestion
It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
It works by adsorbing toxins in the gut
It is ineffective for metals and alcohols
originalOptions: It should be given as soon as possible after ingestion
It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
It works by adsorbing toxins in the gut
It is ineffective for metals and alcohols
questions.correctAnswer: B) It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
questions.correctAnswerText: It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal and syrup of ipecac should never be combined, since ipecac-induced vomiting would expel the charcoal from the stomach before it can adsorb the toxin.

questions.text: All of the following are true about activated charcoal EXCEPT:
options: Give with a sufficient amount of water
It is a finely arranged black powder
Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
originalOptions: Give with a sufficient amount of water
It is a finely arranged black powder
Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
questions.correctAnswer: C) Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
questions.correctAnswerText: Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
questions.explanation: Ipecac is not routinely recommended and should never be combined with activated charcoal, as it would counteract the charcoal's effect by inducing vomiting rather than improving efficacy.

questions.text: A patient arrives at the ER 2 hours after an overdose. What is the correct management?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Activated charcoal if no contraindications
questions.explanation: Within 2 hours of ingestion, activated charcoal is first-line if the airway is intact and there are no contraindications; syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended, and gastric lavage is rarely used (limited to within about 1 hour with a protected airway).

questions.text: Why are alkaline (base) burns generally MORE dangerous than acidic burns?
options: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
They cause coagulative necrosis, which limits penetration
Acids are neutralized immediately upon contact
Bases do not penetrate mucous membranes
originalOptions: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
They cause coagulative necrosis, which limits penetration
Acids are neutralized immediately upon contact
Bases do not penetrate mucous membranes
questions.correctAnswer: A) They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
questions.correctAnswerText: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
questions.explanation: Alkalis dissolve proteins and saponify fat, producing liquefactive necrosis without a limiting eschar, allowing progressively deeper tissue injury; acids instead cause coagulative necrosis, which forms a protective eschar that limits further penetration.

questions.text: Which specific enzyme is reactivated after organophosphate poisoning (before aging)?
questions.explanation: OP poisons phosphorylate AChE; before "aging" occurs (~48h), pralidoxime can remove the phosphoryl group and restore enzyme activity.

questions.text: The drug that reactivates phosphorylated AChE in organophosphate poisoning (before aging):
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime is an oxime AChE reactivator effective only before aging; atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does not reactivate the enzyme.

questions.text: Enzyme reactivated by pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning:
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime specifically reactivates AChE (not pseudocholinesterase/BuChE), and only before the phosphorylated enzyme ages.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about carbamate and organophosphate poisoning is FALSE?
options: Both cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms
Atropine is used for symptomatic treatment
Both can lead to respiratory failure
originalOptions: Both cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms
Atropine is used for symptomatic treatment
Both can lead to respiratory failure
questions.correctAnswer: D) Both are treated with pralidoxime
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime is not indicated for carbamate poisoning because carbamate-enzyme inhibition does not undergo aging (it's spontaneously reversible), unlike OP poisoning.

questions.text: Management of carbamate toxicity – all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
originalOptions: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
questions.correctAnswer: B) Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
questions.correctAnswerText: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
questions.explanation: Treatment (ABC + atropine) must never be delayed for lab confirmation in cholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning, as this is a time-critical emergency.

questions.text: Not a muscarinic sign of organophosphate poisoning:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic (SLUDGE) effects cause urinary incontinence/frequency; urinary retention instead reflects a nicotinic/sympathetic effect.

questions.text: What is the role of atropine in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning?
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist that dries secretions and reverses muscarinic toxicity; it has no effect on nicotinic weakness, which requires pralidoxime.

questions.text: Management and treatment of organophosphate poisoning – which is TRUE:
options: Atropine is antidote for nicotinic receptor
originalOptions: Atropine is antidote for nicotinic receptor
questions.explanation: Initial priority is airway management including suctioning of bronchial secretions, followed by atropine for muscarinic symptoms and then pralidoxime.

questions.text: Low dose of organophosphates is NOT associated with:
questions.explanation: Low-dose OP exposure produces muscarinic effects (bronchorrhea, miosis, salivation); paralysis is a nicotinic effect seen at high dose.

questions.text: Organophosphate-induced neuropsychiatric disorder (OPIDP) happens:
questions.correctAnswer: B) After 1-5 weeks of OP poisoning
questions.explanation: OPIDP is a delayed peripheral polyneuropathy appearing 1–5 weeks post-exposure, distinct from the immediate cholinergic crisis and the 24–96h intermediate syndrome.

questions.text: Antidote of organophosphate poisoning:
questions.explanation: Dual therapy is required — atropine blocks muscarinic toxicity while pralidoxime reactivates AChE, addressing nicotinic and central effects.

questions.text: What is the best blood sample site for forensic toxicology analysis?
questions.explanation: Femoral vein blood is preferred postmortem because it is peripheral and less affected by postmortem redistribution (PMR), unlike central sites (subclavian, jugular) that are subject to drug diffusion from nearby organs.

questions.text: Which sample site is best for QUANTITATIVE toxicology analysis?
questions.explanation: Femoral blood undergoes minimal postmortem redistribution, making it the preferred site for accurate quantitative drug measurement, whereas central blood (heart, subclavian) is prone to redistribution artifact.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of vitreous humor as a toxicology sample?
questions.correctAnswer: B) More susceptible to postmortem change
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is actually resistant to postmortem change because it is isolated behind the blood-ocular barrier, protecting it from putrefaction and postmortem redistribution — making the "more susceptible" statement false.
