questions.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding vitreous humor in forensic toxicology?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Done as a routine procedure
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is collected only in specific circumstances (decomposed bodies, suspected drug/alcohol use, or when other samples are unavailable), not as a routine procedure.

questions.text: Which of the following CANNOT be determined by analyzing vitreous fluid?
questions.explanation: Vitreous fluid can detect alcohol, glucose, electrolytes, potassium (useful for postmortem interval), and urea/creatinine (renal function), but heavy metals preferentially accumulate in hair, nails, and bone rather than vitreous humor.

questions.text: Which sample is most resistant to postmortem putrefaction, making it valuable in decomposed bodies?
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor's anatomical isolation behind the blood-ocular barrier makes it the most resistant forensic sample to putrefactive change among the options listed.

questions.text: Which statement about vitreous fluid is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is resistant to (not affected by) putrefaction due to its isolated anatomical location, making this statement false while the others are accurate.

questions.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding liver samples in forensic toxicology?
questions.explanation: The liver actually putrefies relatively quickly and is not protected from decomposition, though it remains valuable for assessing lipophilic drug concentrations and tissue distribution.

questions.text: For qualitative assessment (screening) of forensic samples, which is the preferred sample?
questions.explanation: Urine is preferred for qualitative drug screening via immunoassay, while femoral blood is used for quantitation, vitreous humor for decomposed cases, and hair for chronic exposure history.

questions.text: Which statement about urine samples in forensic toxicology is NOT correct?
options: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
Urine can detect drugs and metabolites
Urine is used for qualitative drug screening
Urine is useful for detecting drug exposure
originalOptions: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
Urine can detect drugs and metabolites
Urine is used for qualitative drug screening
Urine is useful for detecting drug exposure
questions.correctAnswer: A) Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
questions.correctAnswerText: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
questions.explanation: Urine is mainly used for qualitative detection of drug exposure, not quantitative measurement, which requires blood analysis.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT TRUE concerning sodium fluoride as a preservative in forensic blood samples?
options: Inhibits glycolysis, preventing postmortem glucose changes
Used as a preservative in blood samples for alcohol analysis
Prevents postmortem production of alcohol by microorganisms
originalOptions: Inhibits glycolysis, preventing postmortem glucose changes
Used as a preservative in blood samples for alcohol analysis
Prevents postmortem production of alcohol by microorganisms
questions.explanation: Sodium fluoride inhibits bacterial growth and glycolysis, thereby preventing fermentation (and postmortem alcohol production by microorganisms) rather than enhancing it, which is why it is used to preserve blood samples for alcohol analysis.

questions.text: Reporting and documentation of injuries include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Injury location (anatomical measurement from a fixed landmark)
Type of injury (e.g., bruise, laceration, abrasion)
Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
originalOptions: Injury location (anatomical measurement from a fixed landmark)
Type of injury (e.g., bruise, laceration, abrasion)
Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
questions.correctAnswer: C) Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
questions.correctAnswerText: Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
questions.explanation: The medico-legal report documents the victim's injuries objectively (site, type, size, age, tenderness). Assailant handedness is an investigative inference, not a clinical finding.

questions.text: According to Jordanian law, a physician is obliged to report which of the following to the Ministry of Health?
questions.explanation: The Public Health Law obliges the physician to notify the Ministry of Health of notifiable infectious diseases (e.g., cholera). It does not extend to all trauma cases or all deaths, nor is it limited to sexually transmitted diseases.

questions.text: Who is responsible for issuing the primary medico-legal report?
options: The senior physician or head of department
The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
originalOptions: The senior physician or head of department
The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
questions.correctAnswer: C) The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
questions.correctAnswerText: The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
questions.explanation: The primary report is written by the first doctor who sees the patient, usually in the emergency department, whatever his specialty. The forensic physician completes the final report later.

questions.text: The components of a medico-legal report are:
options: Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
originalOptions: Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
questions.correctAnswer: B) Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
questions.correctAnswerText: Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
questions.explanation: A complete report has three parts: the heading identifying the case and the requesting authority, the body containing the history and examination findings, and the conclusion giving the medical opinion.

questions.text: A surgeon operated while under the influence of alcohol, and the patient died. The surgeon is guilty of:
questions.explanation: Gross negligence or recklessness (operating while intoxicated) that causes death constitutes criminal negligence. Civil negligence results in compensation only, and therapeutic misadventure is an accident despite proper care.

questions.text: In Jordan, a physician is legally governed by:
options: The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
originalOptions: The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
questions.correctAnswer: D) The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
questions.correctAnswerText: The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
questions.explanation: The physician's practice is regulated by all three Jordanian laws together; international codes are not by themselves legally binding.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man underwent arthroscopy with meniscectomy and died of pulmonary embolism. Which aspect of his post-operative care was negligent?
options: He was not informed how serious a headache would be
He was not informed which analgesics to use
He was not told to stay within 2 miles of the hospital
He was not informed of the duration of work disablement
He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
originalOptions: He was not informed how serious a headache would be
He was not informed which analgesics to use
He was not told to stay within 2 miles of the hospital
He was not informed of the duration of work disablement
He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
questions.correctAnswer: E) He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
questions.correctAnswerText: He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
questions.explanation: After lower-limb surgery, shortness of breath is the warning sign of pulmonary embolism, and the patient must be told it requires urgent medical attention. The other omissions are not related to the cause of death.

questions.text: In a suicidal attempt, which finding is most characteristic?
options: Multiple deep wounds scattered over the body
Chop wounds from a heavy weapon
originalOptions: Multiple deep wounds scattered over the body
Chop wounds from a heavy weapon
questions.explanation: Hesitation marks are multiple superficial, parallel, non-lethal cuts made before the fatal cut. Defence wounds, by contrast, are found on the victim of an attack, on the dorsum of the hand and the forearm.

questions.text: Which of the following is characteristic of a suicidal cut throat in a right-handed person?
options: Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
Multiple deep, scattered wounds with defence injuries on the hands
A deep horizontal wound with no hesitation cuts
Incised wounds on the back of the neck
A wound starting on the right side of the neck and deepest at its end
originalOptions: Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
Multiple deep, scattered wounds with defence injuries on the hands
A deep horizontal wound with no hesitation cuts
Incised wounds on the back of the neck
A wound starting on the right side of the neck and deepest at its end
questions.correctAnswer: A) Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
questions.correctAnswerText: Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
questions.explanation: A suicidal cut throat is accessible, is grouped on the side opposite the dominant hand, and is accompanied by hesitation cuts. A homicidal cut is deep, often horizontal, without hesitation cuts, and may show defence wounds.

questions.text: The green colour of a bruise is due to:
questions.explanation: Green appears at about 3–5 days and is due to biliverdin. Brown (1–3 days) is haemosiderin, and yellow (5–7 days) is bilirubin.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about abrasions is FALSE?
options: They are superficial wounds involving the epidermis
Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
They may indicate the direction of the applied force
They may reproduce the pattern of the causative object
originalOptions: They are superficial wounds involving the epidermis
Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
They may indicate the direction of the applied force
They may reproduce the pattern of the causative object
questions.correctAnswer: B) Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
questions.correctAnswerText: Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
questions.explanation: Abrasions involve the epidermis only, so they heal by re-epithelialisation from the edges and hair follicles under a scab, leaving no scar.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about abrasions?
options: They always heal with a scar
They are produced only by sharp instruments
They involve the full thickness of the skin
Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
originalOptions: They always heal with a scar
They are produced only by sharp instruments
They involve the full thickness of the skin
Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
questions.correctAnswer: E) Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
questions.correctAnswerText: Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
questions.explanation: Abrasions are epidermal injuries, and even when they bleed a little from the papillary dermis they re-epithelialise without a scar. They are caused by blunt force, not sharp instruments.

questions.text: Which type of injury gives the best indication of the object or weapon used?
questions.explanation: A patterned abrasion reproduces the surface texture of the causative object (tyre tread, grille, buckle, teeth). A brush abrasion shows only the direction of sliding, and a laceration does not reflect the weapon's dimensions.

questions.text: What is the importance of Langer's lines (skin cleavage lines) in wound assessment?
options: Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
Determining the age of the wound
originalOptions: Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
Determining the age of the wound
questions.correctAnswer: A) Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
questions.correctAnswerText: Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
questions.explanation: Langer's lines follow the direction of dermal collagen and elastic fibres. A wound across the lines gapes widely, whereas a wound parallel to them gapes little and heals with a finer scar.

questions.text: Crescent-shaped (semilunar) abrasions are caused by:
options: A fall on a rough surface
originalOptions: A fall on a rough surface
questions.explanation: A fingernail pressed into the skin leaves a small crescentic abrasion, or a linear scratch if dragged. Teeth leave two opposing curved arcs (a bite mark).

questions.text: The abrasion produced by a tangential force that scrapes off the superficial layer of the skin is called:
questions.explanation: A graze is produced by tangential sliding force (e.g. road rash). Pressure and impact abrasions result from force perpendicular to the skin.

questions.text: A graze abrasion is the same as:
questions.explanation: "Graze" and "brush" are synonyms for a sliding, scraping abrasion. Crush, pressure and impact abrasions are caused by perpendicular force.

questions.text: A patterned (prominence) abrasion is seen most clearly when it occurs over the:
questions.explanation: The pattern prints best where skin lies tight over bone, as on the scalp. Padded areas such as the abdomen and buttock cushion the blow and blur the pattern.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT necessary for the formation of a patterned abrasion?
options: An object with a textured surface
originalOptions: An object with a textured surface
questions.explanation: Skin over a hard bony base is needed to reproduce the pattern. Subcutaneous fat absorbs the blow and blurs the pattern.

questions.text: Incised-like (split) lacerations can be seen in all of the following sites EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Split lacerations occur where the skin lies directly on bone and is crushed against it. They do not occur over padded areas such as the chest wall.

questions.text: Blunt trauma can simulate an incised wound most characteristically over which part of the body?
questions.explanation: The thin scalp skin is tightly stretched over the skull, so a blunt blow splits it in a clean line that looks incised. Marginal bruising, tissue bridging or crushed hair bulbs still indicate a laceration.

questions.text: One of the following statements concerning bruises is NOT true:
options: The source of bleeding is usually small-calibre vessels such as veins, venules and arterioles
Bruises are caused by leakage of blood from damaged vessels into the surrounding tissues
The size and appearance of a bruise are related to the site of the injured part
Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
originalOptions: The source of bleeding is usually small-calibre vessels such as veins, venules and arterioles
Bruises are caused by leakage of blood from damaged vessels into the surrounding tissues
The size and appearance of a bruise are related to the site of the injured part
Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
questions.correctAnswer: E) Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
questions.correctAnswerText: Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
questions.explanation: A contusion can occur anywhere in the body, for example in muscle, spleen or liver. "Bruise" usually implies a lesion visible through the skin.

questions.text: Intradermal bruising is characterized by:
options: Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
Gravitational pooling of blood in dependent areas
Migration of the blood away from the site of impact
originalOptions: Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
Gravitational pooling of blood in dependent areas
Migration of the blood away from the site of impact
questions.correctAnswer: C) Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
questions.correctAnswerText: Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
questions.explanation: Blood confined to the dermis cannot spread, so it keeps the pattern of the object. Hypostasis is a post-mortem phenomenon, and a deep bruise may migrate along tissue planes.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE concerning lacerations?
options: They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
They are always the result of intentional violence
They result from a sharp object applied to the skin
The more resilient tissues are always divided together with the weaker tissues
originalOptions: They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
They are always the result of intentional violence
They result from a sharp object applied to the skin
The more resilient tissues are always divided together with the weaker tissues
questions.correctAnswer: A) They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
questions.correctAnswerText: They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
questions.explanation: Lacerations are caused by blunt force, are not always intentional (e.g. falls), and scalp lacerations can bleed profusely. Tougher tissues such as nerves and vessels survive as bridges.

questions.text: One of the following statements regarding a lacerated wound is NOT true:
options: It is caused by blunt force
The margins show abrasion or contusion
Tissue bridging may be seen in the depth
It commonly occurs over bony prominences
originalOptions: It is caused by blunt force
The margins show abrasion or contusion
Tissue bridging may be seen in the depth
It commonly occurs over bony prominences
questions.correctAnswer: D) Its edges are always irregular
questions.explanation: Over a bony prominence (scalp, brow, shin) a laceration may have a deceptively regular, incised-looking edge. It is identified as a laceration by marginal bruising or abrasion and by tissue bridging.

questions.text: Blunt weapons can usually cause all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Clean-cut edges are the hallmark of a sharp instrument. Blunt force produces abrasions, contusions, lacerations with ragged edges, erythema and oedema.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT a characteristic of self-inflicted injuries:
options: Grouping on the side opposite the dominant hand
Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
originalOptions: Grouping on the side opposite the dominant hand
Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
questions.correctAnswer: E) Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
questions.correctAnswerText: Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
questions.explanation: Self-inflicted wounds are typically superficial, tentative, grouped and within reach of the person. Multiple deep, scattered wounds point away from self-infliction.

questions.text: Fabricated wounds are mostly:
questions.explanation: Self-made wounds produced for secondary gain are usually shallow cuts made with a sharp object on visible, reachable areas, sparing sensitive parts such as the eyes and lips.

questions.text: What is the most frequent type of wound among defence wounds in a knife attack?
questions.explanation: A victim who grasps at or deflects a blade sustains defence incisions, classically on the palm, dorsum of the hand and ulnar aspect of the forearm.

questions.text: Defence wounds are most likely to be found on the:
options: Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
originalOptions: Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
questions.correctAnswer: D) Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
questions.correctAnswerText: Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
questions.explanation: These are the sites exposed when the victim raises the arms to ward off a blade. The palm is also involved when the blade is grasped. Defence wounds are a homicide indicator.

questions.text: Regarding hesitation wounds, which of the following is NOT correct?
questions.correctAnswer: B) They are surrounded by bruises
questions.explanation: Hesitation wounds are superficial, parallel, regular-edged incisions. Surrounding bruising implies blunt force, not a sharp-edge cut.

questions.text: Yellow discoloration of a bruise is expected at approximately:
questions.explanation: Yellow is due to bilirubin at about 5–7 days. Green (biliverdin) precedes it at 3–5 days, and the bruise then fades through straw to normal colour.

questions.text: What is the usual cause of death in extradural haemorrhage?
questions.explanation: The expanding arterial clot raises intracranial pressure, causing tentorial herniation and brainstem (medullary) compression, which ends in respiratory failure. The haemorrhage is usually from the middle meningeal artery after a temporal bone fracture.

questions.text: What is the main characteristic of the wound shown in the image? [img: forensic1stabwound.jpg ]
options: Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
originalOptions: Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
questions.correctAnswer: D) Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
questions.correctAnswerText: Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
questions.explanation: A typical stab wound has clean-cut regular edges with no marginal bruising or abrasion, and its depth exceeds its length. Irregular edges, tissue bridging and marginal bruising indicate a laceration, and a wound longer than it is deep is characteristic of an incised wound.

questions.text: Concerning stab wounds, one of the following statements is NOT correct:
options: A slit-like wound usually distorts after removal of the weapon
An irregularly shaped skin wound may result if the knife is twisted
Movement of the knife may enlarge the wound
The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
One end of the wound is sharp if the weapon is single-edged
originalOptions: A slit-like wound usually distorts after removal of the weapon
An irregularly shaped skin wound may result if the knife is twisted
Movement of the knife may enlarge the wound
The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
One end of the wound is sharp if the weapon is single-edged
questions.correctAnswer: D) The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
questions.correctAnswerText: The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
questions.explanation: Skin elasticity, Langer's lines, and rocking or twisting of the blade alter the wound, so it is rarely the exact size of the blade.

questions.text: A fully conscious man sustained a head injury during a fight. Examination shows a boggy swelling of 6 × 4 cm over the right parietal area, and an X-ray shows a fracture of the parietal bone without displacement. The nature of the injury is:
questions.explanation: A linear crack without displacement is a fissure (linear) fracture, the commonest type. A depressed fracture has the fragment driven inward, a comminuted fracture has several fragments, and a complicated fracture involves injury to the underlying dura, brain or vessels.

questions.text: All of the following are types of skull fracture EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Skull fractures are classified as linear, depressed, comminuted, compound and complicated. A spiral pattern is a long-bone fracture.

questions.text: A burn that destroys the full thickness of the skin, appears white or charred and leathery, and is painless because of destruction of the nerve endings is classified as:
questions.explanation: A third-degree burn is full-thickness skin destruction and is painless. A first-degree burn involves only the epidermis, a second-degree burn extends into the dermis with blisters and severe pain, and a fourth-degree burn extends beyond the skin into fat, muscle or bone.

questions.text: During surgery on a patient with a gunshot wound, what is the correct approach regarding the bullet?
options: Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
Remove it and discard it immediately to prevent further injury
Regard it as the property of the surgeon
Hand it to the patient's family
Keep it in the hospital pathology archive without notifying the police
originalOptions: Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
Remove it and discard it immediately to prevent further injury
Regard it as the property of the surgeon
Hand it to the patient's family
Keep it in the hospital pathology archive without notifying the police
questions.correctAnswer: A) Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
questions.correctAnswerText: Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
questions.explanation: The bullet is forensic evidence belonging to the police investigation. Handle it with gloved fingers or rubber-shod forceps, because metal instruments scratch the rifling marks, and place it in a labelled, sealed container.

allQuestions.text: Under Jordanian law, abortion is permitted under which of the following circumstances?
options: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
originalOptions: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
allQuestions.explanation: Jordanian law criminalizes abortion except when continuing the pregnancy would seriously endanger the mother's life or health; it is not permitted on demand, for socioeconomic reasons, or for fetal anomaly alone.

allQuestions.text: Abortion in Jordanian law is allowed:
options: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
originalOptions: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) To save the mother's life
allQuestions.explanation: Under the Jordan Penal Code, abortion is a criminal offense except when continuation of pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life.

allQuestions.text: Burking involves which combination of asphyxial mechanisms?
allQuestions.explanation: Burking (the Burke and Hare method) combines simultaneous chest compression (traumatic asphyxia) with covering the mouth/nose (smothering), causing rapid death from combined asphyxial mechanisms without leaving obvious external marks.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common cause of inward (central) hyoid bone fracture?
allQuestions.explanation: Throttling involves direct manual compression of the neck, characteristically producing an inward/central hyoid bone fracture, distinguishing it from hanging or ligature strangulation.

allQuestions.text: Which method of asphyxia shows the MOST severe internal neck damage?
allQuestions.explanation: In throttling, the hands directly grip and compress the neck with intense, sustained pressure, causing tears in the sternomastoid muscle, hyoid fracture, thyroid cartilage fractures, and even cervical spine injury — more severe than the mechanisms in hanging or ligature strangulation.

allQuestions.text: The neck shows extensive laceration, tears in the sternomastoid, and fracture-dislocation of C2-C3 vertebrae. These findings are most consistent with:
allQuestions.explanation: Judicial (long-drop) hanging involves a measured drop generating massive kinetic energy, producing a hangman's fracture (C2-C3 fracture-dislocation) and sternomastoid tearing from cervical spinal cord disruption — findings not typically seen in the shorter drops of suicidal or accidental hanging.

allQuestions.text: What are the characteristic features of a ligature mark in strangulation?
allQuestions.explanation: Ligature strangulation produces a horizontal (level), low (below the thyroid cartilage), and complete (fully encircling) mark, in contrast to hanging's characteristically oblique, high, and incomplete mark.

allQuestions.text: Which features characterize ligature marks in strangulation?
options: Associated with multiple lines on the neck at varying heights
Marks positioned high on the neck
originalOptions: Associated with multiple lines on the neck at varying heights
Marks positioned high on the neck
allQuestions.explanation: Ligature strangulation produces transverse (horizontal), complete, low-neck marks, distinct from the oblique, high, often incomplete marks of hanging.

allQuestions.text: Abrasions found on the neck are always considered what until proven otherwise?
allQuestions.explanation: Neck abrasions (from fingernails or a ligature) are presumed indicative of strangulation until proven otherwise — a key medicolegal principle guiding initial death investigation.

allQuestions.text: What are the characteristics of the frothy secretions seen in drowning?
allQuestions.explanation: Drowning froth is classically white, fine, persistent, leathery, and tenacious — not bloody or turbid unless there is additional injury.

allQuestions.text: In drowning, which finding is most indicative of the time passed since death (time in water)?
allQuestions.explanation: Washerwoman skin (macerated, wrinkled skin from prolonged water immersion) progresses in a time-dependent manner, making it the most reliable indicator of how long a body has been submerged.

allQuestions.text: What finding is characteristic of traumatic asphyxia?
allQuestions.explanation: In traumatic asphyxia, chest compression prevents venous return from the head, producing cyanosis above the compression site and pallor below it, creating a sharp line of demarcation.

allQuestions.text: A clear line of demarcation on the body is always seen in which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Traumatic (compressive) asphyxia produces a sharp line of demarcation between the congested, cyanotic upper body and the relatively normal-appearing lower body, a finding not characteristic of hanging, gagging, or drowning.

allQuestions.text: Petechial hemorrhages are typically seen in which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots) are a hallmark of asphyxia, especially traumatic/crush asphyxia, resulting from increased venous pressure rupturing capillaries in the face, conjunctivae, and skin above the compression site.

allQuestions.text: What are the mechanisms of death in mechanical asphyxia?
options: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
originalOptions: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
allQuestions.explanation: Mechanical asphyxia causes death through multiple overlapping mechanisms: oxygen deprivation, pulmonary edema, vagal reflex cardiac arrest (especially relevant in hanging/strangulation), and cerebral hypoxia.

allQuestions.text: Mechanical asphyxia is a type of:
allQuestions.explanation: Mechanical asphyxia (hanging, drowning, smothering) prevents oxygen from entering the lungs, representing anoxic anoxia — failure of oxygen to reach the blood — rather than a defect in oxygen transport or cellular utilization.

allQuestions.text: Death in an environment with decreased atmospheric oxygen levels (e.g., high altitude, enclosed spaces) results in what type of anoxia?
allQuestions.explanation: Decreased inspired oxygen concentration directly causes anoxic (hypoxic) anoxia, since insufficient oxygen is available in the air to be taken up by the blood.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT part of the classic triad features of asphyxia?
options: Fluid in the left side of the heart
Petechial hemorrhages in skin of face and eyes
originalOptions: Fluid in the left side of the heart
Petechial hemorrhages in skin of face and eyes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Fluid in the left side of the heart
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Fluid in the left side of the heart
allQuestions.explanation: The asphyxia triad consists of cyanosis, congestion, and petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots); fluid accumulation in the left heart is not a recognized feature — right heart dilatation is more typically associated with asphyxial death.

allQuestions.text: How are antemortem hangings diagnosed?
options: By the presence of cadaveric spasm
By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
originalOptions: By the presence of cadaveric spasm
By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
allQuestions.explanation: Antemortem hanging is confirmed by vital reactions in the ligature mark — hemorrhage, WBC infiltration, and early tissue repair — which are absent when the ligature is applied postmortem.

allQuestions.text: What is a sign of antemortem hanging?
allQuestions.explanation: Dripping or dribbling of saliva from the angle of the mouth toward the shoulder is a vital sign requiring intact salivary gland function, confirming the person was alive during the hanging (antemortem).

allQuestions.text: Hypostasis (livor mortis) in the lower limbs is a sign of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: In complete hanging, the body is fully suspended, causing blood to gravitate and pool in the lower limbs, producing lower-limb hypostasis.

allQuestions.text: Abrasions around the mouth indicate which mechanism of asphyxia?
allQuestions.explanation: Perioral abrasions from hand or pillow pressure applied to obstruct the airway are characteristic of smothering, distinguishing it from neck-focused mechanisms like throttling or hanging.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common manner of death in choking?
allQuestions.explanation: Choking from foreign body airway obstruction (food, small objects) is most commonly accidental; homicidal choking (e.g., forced feeding) is rare.

allQuestions.text: Histotoxic anoxia is caused by which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), preventing cells from utilizing oxygen even when it is available in the blood — defining histotoxic (cellular) anoxia, unlike CO (which impairs oxygen transport) or CNS depressants.

allQuestions.text: Complete hanging (as opposed to incomplete) is defined by which factor?
allQuestions.explanation: Complete versus incomplete hanging is distinguished by whether the body is fully suspended off the ground or partially supported/touching a surface, not by the victim's physical characteristics.

allQuestions.text: A 65-year-old found dead in seawater shows goose skin appearance, easily removable hair, and the right hand forcefully grasping grass weeds. This is most consistent with:
allQuestions.explanation: Forceful grasping of an object (weeds) at the instant of death represents cadaveric spasm — instantaneous muscle locking that proves the person was alive and gripping at the moment they entered the water, distinct from the gradual onset of ordinary rigor mortis.

allQuestions.text: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) causes death via what type of anoxia?
options: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
originalOptions: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
allQuestions.explanation: GBS causes ascending paralysis leading to respiratory muscle failure, preventing adequate ventilation so oxygen cannot enter the lungs — anoxic anoxia, despite normal oxygen availability in the environment.

allQuestions.text: What type of anoxia is caused by cyanide (HCN) poisoning?
allQuestions.explanation: HCN inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), blocking cellular oxygen utilization despite normal oxygen delivery — defining histotoxic (cellular) anoxia.

allQuestions.text: The vagus nerve shares the same anatomical root and exit point with which cranial nerve?
allQuestions.explanation: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and CN X (vagus) both arise from the medulla oblongata and exit the skull together through the jugular foramen, making their close anatomical relationship medicolegally relevant to vagal reflex death in asphyxia

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism of carbon monoxide toxicity?
options: Decreases oxygen delivery to the tissues
Binds reversibly to haemoglobin with an affinity 200–230 times that of oxygen
Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
Shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left
Binds to cytochrome oxidase and impairs oxidative metabolism
originalOptions: Decreases oxygen delivery to the tissues
Binds reversibly to haemoglobin with an affinity 200–230 times that of oxygen
Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
Shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left
Binds to cytochrome oxidase and impairs oxidative metabolism
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Increases oxygen transport to the tissues
allQuestions.explanation: CO forms carboxyhaemoglobin, which lowers oxygen-carrying capacity and left-shifts the curve, so oxygen transport and release both fall. It never increases them.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are NOT true regarding CO poisoning in pregnancy EXCEPT, which statement is true? Which statement is NOT true regarding CO poisoning in pregnancy?
options: Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
Fetal haemoglobin binds CO with a higher affinity than adult haemoglobin
The fetus is more susceptible to CO than the mother
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but eventually reaches a higher level than the mother's
originalOptions: Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
Fetal haemoglobin binds CO with a higher affinity than adult haemoglobin
The fetus is more susceptible to CO than the mother
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but eventually reaches a higher level than the mother's
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Elimination of CO from the fetus is faster than from the mother
allQuestions.explanation: CO is eliminated from the fetus much more slowly than from the mother, which is why the fetus ends up with higher COHb and is more susceptible to hypoxia even when the mother survives.

allQuestions.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning affects the fetus in all of the following ways EXCEPT:
options: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide is eliminated slowly from the fetal circulation
Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but ends higher than the maternal level
originalOptions: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide is eliminated slowly from the fetal circulation
Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
Fetal COHb rises more slowly but ends higher than the maternal level
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Carbon monoxide is rapidly eliminated from the fetus
allQuestions.explanation: Elimination from the fetus is slow, not rapid. Combined with the higher affinity of fetal Hb for CO, this prolongs fetal hypoxia.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the WRONG mechanism regarding carbon monoxide poisoning?
options: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with high affinity
It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
It left-shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
It decreases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
originalOptions: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with high affinity
It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
It left-shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
It decreases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It increases oxygen release from haemoglobin to the tissues
allQuestions.explanation: CO increases the affinity of the remaining haem sites for oxygen (left shift), so oxygen release to the tissues decreases, not increases.

allQuestions.text: What is the mechanism of action of carbon monoxide?
options: Oxidation of ferrous iron in haemoglobin to form methaemoglobin
Right shift of the dissociation curve with increased oxygen release
Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
originalOptions: Oxidation of ferrous iron in haemoglobin to form methaemoglobin
Right shift of the dissociation curve with increased oxygen release
Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Binding to haemoglobin with 200–230 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
allQuestions.explanation: CO competes with O₂ at the haem site and forms COHb, which lowers carrying capacity and left-shifts the curve, causing tissue hypoxia. AChE inhibition is the organophosphate mechanism, and methaemoglobin is formed by oxidation, not by CO.

allQuestions.text: All of the following can cause CO poisoning EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: CO comes only from incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels. An electrical heater involves no combustion and produces no CO.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a source of carbon monoxide?
allQuestions.explanation: An electrical heater has no combustion, so it produces no CO. Firearm discharge gases contain CO, and methylene chloride is metabolised by the liver to CO.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for CO poisoning?
allQuestions.explanation: Increased ambient temperature, not decreased, raises the rate of CO uptake. Cold is not a risk factor.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are features of carbon monoxide gas and its poisoning EXCEPT:
options: The most common type of fatal poisoning in many countries
Produced by incomplete combustion of fuels
originalOptions: The most common type of fatal poisoning in many countries
Produced by incomplete combustion of fuels
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Causes irritative symptoms on inhalation
allQuestions.explanation: CO is non-irritant, so there are no warning symptoms, which is why it is called the "silent killer".

allQuestions.text: CO poisoning is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Sinus tachycardia and ST-segment changes on ECG
originalOptions: Sinus tachycardia and ST-segment changes on ECG
allQuestions.explanation: Despite asphyxiation, cyanosis does not occur in CO poisoning because COHb is bright red; the skin is pink or pale and the lips are bright red.

allQuestions.text: Cherry-red discoloration after CO poisoning is located in:
options: Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
originalOptions: Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Skin, mucous membranes, muscles, and internal organs
allQuestions.explanation: Carboxyhaemoglobin and carboxymyoglobin colour the blood, skin, lividity, mucous membranes, muscles and internal organs, so no single site is the answer.

allQuestions.text: What is the normal COHb level in the blood of a resting healthy non-smoker?
allQuestions.explanation: Background COHb from endogenous haem catabolism is the lowest option, about 1–3% (0.4–0.7% in the lecture). Smokers reach about 5–10%, and symptoms usually begin around 10–20%.

allQuestions.text: In a death from CO poisoning, the cherry-pink colour is absent. This implies that:
options: The cause of death was not CO poisoning
The death was caused by hanging
The patient died too quickly for any COHb to form
originalOptions: The cause of death was not CO poisoning
The death was caused by hanging
The patient died too quickly for any COHb to form
allQuestions.explanation: Resuscitation and oxygen administration lower the COHb level, so the cherry-pink colour fades. Its absence does not exclude CO, and a blood COHb level confirms the diagnosis.

allQuestions.text: What is the mainstay of management of CO poisoning?
allQuestions.explanation: High-flow 100% O₂ shortens the half-life of CO from 3–4 hours on room air to 30–90 minutes, and hyperbaric O₂ shortens it further. Pralidoxime and atropine are for organophosphate poisoning, and naloxone is for opioids.

allQuestions.text: All of the following cause a LEFT shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Acidosis and increased CO₂ cause a RIGHT shift (Bohr effect), which lowers Hb affinity and increases O₂ release. The other four increase affinity and shift the curve to the left.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are risk factors for a LEFT shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Respiratory acidosis (high CO₂, low pH) right-shifts the curve through the Bohr effect, which favours O₂ release. All the other options left-shift it.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause or indicator of child abuse?
allQuestions.explanation: MS is a neurological autoimmune disease unrelated to abuse; multiple bruises, shaken baby syndrome, and Munchausen by proxy are classic abuse indicators.

allQuestions.text: Bruising in which of the following areas is NOT considered a suspicious sign of child abuse?
allQuestions.explanation: Knee bruising is a common, normal childhood injury from falls and play; abuse-related bruising is characteristically found on protected areas such as the torso, back, abdomen, and chest.

allQuestions.text: Regarding Munchausen syndrome by proxy, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
Parents readily admit to causing the illness
originalOptions: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
Parents readily admit to causing the illness
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Parents readily admit to causing the illness
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Parents readily admit to causing the illness
allQuestions.explanation: Munchausen by proxy is characterized by unexplained illness that improves when the child is separated from the caregiver, a lack of clear diagnosis, and negative workup; perpetrators rarely confess to causing the illness.

allQuestions.text: A 31-year-old woman claims sexual assault 4 days ago. Examination shows a recent hymenal tear at the 5 o'clock position. Which statement is TRUE?
options: No informed consent is required before examination
Delay in reporting confirms a fabricated story
Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
Rupture of the hymen is an absolute sign confirming rape
The findings determine the exact time of the assault
originalOptions: No informed consent is required before examination
Delay in reporting confirms a fabricated story
Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
Rupture of the hymen is an absolute sign confirming rape
The findings determine the exact time of the assault
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
allQuestions.explanation: A recent hymenal tear is corroborative evidence supporting the allegation, but it alone cannot confirm rape; consent is required before examination, and delayed reporting is common even in genuine cases.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT true concerning sexual assault victims?
options: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
Post-assault forensic sampling is vital for evaluation
Victims should be assessed for genitourinary health, contraception needs, and counseling
Emergency contraception may include oral contraceptives
originalOptions: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
Post-assault forensic sampling is vital for evaluation
Victims should be assessed for genitourinary health, contraception needs, and counseling
Emergency contraception may include oral contraceptives
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
allQuestions.explanation: This statistic is false — paedophilia and bestiality are not common practices in any population; the other statements reflect appropriate sexual assault management.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognized type of hymen?
allQuestions.explanation: Cribriform hymen (with multiple small openings) is a recognized anatomical variant; notches at 3 or 9 o'clock are considered normal artefacts rather than named types, and "elastic" is not a recognized hymen type.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common cause of erectile dysfunction (impotence) in young men?
allQuestions.explanation: In young men, erectile dysfunction is most commonly psychogenic in origin, whereas vascular causes become more predominant with advancing age.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following cases is considered a medico-legal case?
options: Death at home from a known chronic natural disease
Death in hospital from a known disease under medical care
Death of a person in prison
Expected death of a terminally ill patient under palliative care
Death of an elderly patient from known heart failure attended by his physician
originalOptions: Death at home from a known chronic natural disease
Death in hospital from a known disease under medical care
Death of a person in prison
Expected death of a terminally ill patient under palliative care
Death of an elderly patient from known heart failure attended by his physician
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Death of a person in prison
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Death of a person in prison
allQuestions.explanation: Any death in custody (prison, police, juvenile home) is a medico-legal case regardless of its apparent cause, to exclude foul play and establish accountability. The other options are expected natural deaths under medical care.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a cause of myocardial infarction without atheroma?
allQuestions.explanation: Intense emotional stress causes coronary spasm through a catecholamine surge and can produce infarction in the absence of atheroma. Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and diabetes act through atheroma formation.

allQuestions.text: A prisoner dies from bronchospasm. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A standard death certificate is sufficient
An autopsy is not required because the cause of death is natural
Family consent is required before an autopsy can be performed
The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
The prison physician may release the body for burial without notification
originalOptions: A standard death certificate is sufficient
An autopsy is not required because the cause of death is natural
Family consent is required before an autopsy can be performed
The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
The prison physician may release the body for burial without notification
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The death must be reported by law to the public prosecutor
allQuestions.explanation: A death in custody is a mandatory medico-legal case, so it must be reported to the public prosecutor and followed by a medico-legal autopsy. Neither a death certificate alone nor family consent is applicable, even if the apparent cause is natural.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following causes of death is NOT considered medico-legal?
options: Pulmonary embolism following a hip fracture in a hospitalized patient
Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
Pneumonia in a 16-year-old male in a juvenile home
A 30-year-old brought in dead following a head injury
A 60-year-old man who died suddenly while waiting for an X-ray
originalOptions: Pulmonary embolism following a hip fracture in a hospitalized patient
Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
Pneumonia in a 16-year-old male in a juvenile home
A 30-year-old brought in dead following a head injury
A 60-year-old man who died suddenly while waiting for an X-ray
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Tuberculosis in a 30-year-old refugee under medical care
allQuestions.explanation: Death from a diagnosed disease under active medical care is an expected natural death. The other options involve trauma or its complications, custody, a "brought in dead" case, or sudden unexpected death.

allQuestions.text: When a forensic physician is called to the scene by the public prosecutor, the primary purposes are:
options: Only to confirm that death has occurred
To clean and document the scene
To perform a complete autopsy at the scene
To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
originalOptions: Only to confirm that death has occurred
To clean and document the scene
To perform a complete autopsy at the scene
To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: To identify the deceased and investigate the circumstances of death
allQuestions.explanation: The forensic physician identifies the deceased, determines the time, cause and manner of death, and helps reconstruct the events for the prosecutor. Confirming death or collecting samples are only parts of this role.

allQuestions.text: Which stage of lobar pneumonia is most likely to cause death in children?
allQuestions.explanation: Children most often die in the first stage, from overwhelming toxaemia, before consolidation develops. Red and grey hepatization are later stages, and resolution is the recovery stage.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common cause of sudden unexpected death?
allQuestions.explanation: Coronary artery disease with myocardial infarction, together with hypertensive heart disease, accounts for most sudden unexpected deaths in adults. Respiratory, CNS, metabolic and gastrointestinal causes are far less frequent.

allQuestions.text: Molecular (cellular) death occurs in relation to somatic death:
options: Only after rigor mortis is fully established
Only after the onset of putrefaction
originalOptions: Only after rigor mortis is fully established
Only after the onset of putrefaction
allQuestions.explanation: Molecular death follows somatic death (about 1–2 hours after vital functions stop) and occurs piecemeal, cell by cell. This lag is the basis of the organ-donation window.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about second-degree burns is NOT correct?
options: It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
It is less severe than a full-thickness burn
originalOptions: It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
It is less severe than a full-thickness burn
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)
allQuestions.explanation: A second-degree burn does not suppress the vital signs, so it cannot simulate death. Its features are dermal involvement, blisters and marked pain, because the nerve endings are intact, unlike third-degree burns.

allQuestions.text: A dead body is found in a flat. Rectal temperature is 26.4°C, ambient temperature 18°C, and body weight 90 kg. The approximate time since death is:
allQuestions.explanation: (37.2 − 26.4) = 10.8°C ÷ 1–1.5°C/hour gives about 7–11 hours. A heavy 90 kg body cools more slowly, so the interval is, if anything, longer (Henssge nomogram corrects for weight and ambient temperature).

allQuestions.text: A body is found in an apartment with a rectal temperature of 32°C and rigor mortis not yet complete. The most likely time since death is:
allQuestions.explanation: (37.2 − 32) = 5.2°C ÷ 1–1.5°C/hour gives about 3.5–5 hours. Incomplete rigor, which begins at 2–3 hours and is established by 9–12 hours, fits a recent death.

allQuestions.text: The estimated time since death of a body found cold AND stiff is:
allQuestions.explanation: Cold with rigor present means 8–36 hours. Warm and flaccid is under 3 hours, warm and stiff is 3–8 hours, and cold and flaccid (secondary flaccidity) is over 36 hours.

allQuestions.text: A full stomach with undigested meal at autopsy indicates that the last meal was taken:
options: More than four hours before death
More than six hours before death
Less than two hours before death
More than twelve hours before death
originalOptions: More than four hours before death
More than six hours before death
Less than two hours before death
More than twelve hours before death
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Less than two hours before death
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Less than two hours before death
allQuestions.explanation: A full stomach with undigested food suggests death within about 2 hours of the meal, whereas an empty stomach suggests at least 4–6 hours. It is only a rough guide, since fear, injury and coma delay gastric emptying.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following post-mortem changes begins immediately after death?
allQuestions.explanation: Livor starts as soon as circulation stops and blood is governed by gravity (apparent at about 2 hours, fixed at about 6–8 hours). Rigor appears at 2–3 hours and putrefaction becomes visible at 48–72 hours. Cooling (algor) is a gradual process.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following appears immediately after death in a person who died under intense emotion?
allQuestions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm is instantaneous rigidity at the moment of death, linked to violent death with intense emotion. Ordinary rigor mortis is delayed by 2–3 hours.

allQuestions.text: Rigor mortis is first evident in:
allQuestions.explanation: Rigor is first detected in the small muscles of the eyelids, then face and jaw, neck, upper limbs, trunk and lower limbs (head to foot). The myocardium stiffens early but this is not evident on examination.

allQuestions.text: The fundamental cause of rigor mortis is:
options: Active contraction triggered by calcium channel activation
Breakdown of the muscle cell wall by autolytic enzymes
Coagulation of muscle proteins by heat
Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
originalOptions: Active contraction triggered by calcium channel activation
Breakdown of the muscle cell wall by autolytic enzymes
Coagulation of muscle proteins by heat
Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Depletion of ATP, so actin–myosin cross-bridges cannot release
allQuestions.explanation: Rigor is a passive stiffening, not an active contraction: with low ATP and rising acidity the actin–myosin bonds cannot dissociate. Heat coagulation causes heat stiffness, and muscle turns alkaline again only in secondary flaccidity.

allQuestions.text: The best site for recording body temperature to estimate the time of death is:
allQuestions.explanation: The rectum (8–10 cm above the anus) gives the true core temperature and is the standard site for the cooling formula. The external ear is a recognised site but is not the ideal one.

allQuestions.text: In practice, the most accurate way of estimating the time of death is:
options: Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
originalOptions: Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Scene markers (last seen alive, uncollected mail, dated receipts)
allQuestions.explanation: All biological methods are imprecise, and scene markers are often more accurate. Core temperature is the best scientific method, but it does not outperform circumstantial evidence.

allQuestions.text: "Livor" in livor mortis (hypostasis) means:
allQuestions.explanation: Livor means livid (purple), reflecting blood pooling in dependent parts. Blue is the colour of cyanosis, not of livor.

allQuestions.text: The normal colour of post-mortem lividity is:
allQuestions.explanation: Normal hypostasis is bluish or purplish-red. Cherry pink indicates CO, cyanide or cold, brown indicates methaemoglobinaemia, pale indicates anaemia or haemorrhage, and greenish-black is a putrefactive change.

allQuestions.text: What is the colour of livor mortis in methaemoglobinaemia?
allQuestions.explanation: Methaemoglobin gives brown lividity. Deep bluish violet is seen in asphyxia, and cherry pink in CO poisoning, cold and cyanide.

allQuestions.text: The colour of hypostasis in mummified bodies is:
allQuestions.explanation: In mummified bodies, lividity appears brown to black due to desiccation. Deep bluish violet is characteristic of asphyxia.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT related to colour?
allQuestions.explanation: Congestion means excess blood in the vessels and is not defined by a colour. Cyanosis denotes blueness, vibices are streaks of hypostasis, and livor means livid (purple).

allQuestions.text: Hypostasis in the lower limbs is a sign of:
allQuestions.explanation: In complete hanging the body is vertical and fully suspended, so lividity collects distally in the legs, feet and hands. In incomplete hanging it follows the part touching the ground.

allQuestions.text: Hypostasis in drowning is most commonly seen on:
options: A site that depends on the water current and body posture
Always the front of the body
originalOptions: A site that depends on the water current and body posture
Always the front of the body
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) A site that depends on the water current and body posture
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A site that depends on the water current and body posture
allQuestions.explanation: Moving water keeps turning the body, so hypostasis is often faint and its site is variable. A floating body usually lies face-down, giving lividity of the face, upper chest and upper limbs, but this is not constant.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following produces MARKED hypostasis after death?
allQuestions.explanation: Congestive heart failure (like asphyxia and polycythaemia) leaves more blood available to pool, so hypostasis is marked. Anaemia and haemorrhage reduce circulating blood and give faint or absent lividity.

allQuestions.text: All of the following cause faint, late or absent hypostasis EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Polycythaemia increases the red-cell mass and gives marked lividity. Anaemia, haemorrhage, cholera and the extremes of age tend to produce pale, late or absent lividity.

allQuestions.text: Absence of hypostasis after death is most likely in:
options: Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
originalOptions: Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Anaemia or death from severe external haemorrhage
allQuestions.explanation: Lividity needs enough blood to pool in dependent vessels, and anaemia or massive blood loss leaves too little. Polycythaemia, CHF and asphyxia give marked lividity.

allQuestions.text: Which post-mortem change is related to the red blood cell count?
allQuestions.explanation: The intensity of livor depends on red-cell mass and blood fluidity: marked in polycythaemia and faint in anaemia. The other changes are muscular, thermal or bacterial.

allQuestions.text: Extensive muscular exercise immediately before death:
options: Delays the onset of rigor mortis
Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
Has no effect on rigor mortis
Prolongs the duration of rigor mortis
originalOptions: Delays the onset of rigor mortis
Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
Has no effect on rigor mortis
Prolongs the duration of rigor mortis
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Accelerates the onset of rigor mortis
allQuestions.explanation: Fatigued or exhausted muscles, and increased activity just before death, give rapid onset and short duration of rigor because of rapid ATP depletion. Rested, healthy muscles develop rigor slowly and keep it longer.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are early signs of death EXCEPT:
options: Skin loses its elasticity with facial pallor
Muscles rapidly become flaccid (primary flaccidity) with loss of tone
The eyes lose their intraocular tension
The retinal vessels show fragmentation ("trucking") of the blood columns
The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
originalOptions: Skin loses its elasticity with facial pallor
Muscles rapidly become flaccid (primary flaccidity) with loss of tone
The eyes lose their intraocular tension
The retinal vessels show fragmentation ("trucking") of the blood columns
The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The muscles immediately stop all twitching and never respond to any stimulation
allQuestions.explanation: After death muscles may still twitch focally and respond to touch or stimulation for some hours, because cellular death is progressive. Options A–D are recognised early changes.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are early signs of death EXCEPT:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Rigor mortis (2–3 hours after death)
allQuestions.explanation: Rigor needs 2–3 hours to appear, so it is the odd one out among the immediate changes. Primary flaccidity, loss of corneal reflex and the start of cooling occur at once.

allQuestions.text: A 55-year-old man, apparently dead, is brought to the casualty department. The earliest post-mortem change to appear is:
options: Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
originalOptions: Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Loss of skin elasticity with pallor
allQuestions.explanation: Pallor and loss of skin elasticity appear within minutes of circulatory arrest. Lividity, corneal clouding, cooling and rigor take hours.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are post-mortem changes in the eyes EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: After death the cornea becomes opaque (earlier if the lids are open, within about 10–12 hours if closed), so a persistently clear cornea is not a post-mortem change. The other findings are all described after death.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a post-mortem change in the eyes?
allQuestions.explanation: A clear cornea is a feature of life or of very early death. Corneal opacity, tache noire, anisocoria and falling intraocular tension all develop after death.

allQuestions.text: After death, body temperature may be higher than expected in all of the following EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Rectal temperature is lower than expected after haemorrhage, cholera, CHF and hypothermia. It is higher after infections, asphyxia, pontine haemorrhage, coronary thrombosis, struggle and heat stroke.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a POSITIVE sign of death?
allQuestions.explanation: Putrefaction, adipocere, mummification, rigor and fixed hypostasis are certain signs of death. Flat EEG and absent heart or breath sounds also occur in suspended animation, and corneal reflex loss is unreliable.

allQuestions.text: The diagnosis of brainstem death depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Apnoea after disconnection from the ventilator
originalOptions: Apnoea after disconnection from the ventilator
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Presence of the gag reflex
allQuestions.explanation: Brainstem death requires coma, absence of ALL brainstem reflexes (including gag and cough) and apnoea. A present gag reflex means brainstem function persists.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following organs is MOST resistant to putrefaction?
allQuestions.explanation: The prostate (and non-gravid uterus) are among the last organs to putrefy. The brain, stomach, spleen and liver putrefy early.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the last organ to putrefy?
allQuestions.explanation: The non-gravid uterus and prostate are late-putrefying organs, whereas the stomach and intestines are early. The gravid uterus is also an early-putrefying organ.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following pairs are signs of putrefaction?
options: Waxy, soap-like fat and brittle bones
Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
originalOptions: Waxy, soap-like fat and brittle bones
Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Green discoloration of the right iliac fossa and bloating with foul-smelling gas
allQuestions.explanation: The first visible sign of putrefaction is greenish discoloration over the right iliac fossa (near the bacteria-rich caecum), followed by gas formation and bloating. The other pairs describe rigor, adipocere, lividity and eye changes.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following are two other types of decomposition besides putrefaction?
allQuestions.explanation: Mummification (desiccation in dry, warm conditions) and adipocere (fat saponification in moist conditions) are the special routes of decomposition. The other options are early post-mortem changes or part of putrefaction itself.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following sets contains only signs of LATE putrefaction?
options: Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, rigor mortis
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, tache noire
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, early lividity
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, cadaveric spasm
originalOptions: Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, rigor mortis
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, tache noire
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, early lividity
Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, cadaveric spasm
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Liquefaction of soft tissues, skin slippage, bloating, greenish-black discoloration, exposure of the skeleton
allQuestions.explanation: Late putrefaction progresses through bloating and blistering with skin slippage to liquefaction and eventually skeleton exposure. Rigor, tache noire, early lividity and cadaveric spasm are early or non-putrefactive changes.

allQuestions.text: Adipocere is chiefly composed of which acid?
allQuestions.explanation: Adipocere is mainly saturated fatty acids, chiefly palmitic acid, formed by hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fat. Stearic and hydroxy-stearic acids are minor components and little oleic acid remains.

allQuestions.text: Adipocere formation is associated with which organism?
allQuestions.explanation: Bacterial enzymes of Clostridium perfringens hydrolyse and hydrogenate body fat in warm, moist conditions. Moisture is essential.

allQuestions.text: Adipocere occurs first in:
allQuestions.explanation: Adipocere forms first in subcutaneous fat (cheeks, breasts, buttocks). Internal organs such as the liver, kidney and heart may be affected later.

allQuestions.text: Mummification involves:
allQuestions.explanation: Mummification needs dry, warm conditions that dry out the tissues, preventing bacterial growth. Humidity and bacterial action favour putrefaction or adipocere.

allQuestions.text: Mummification is:
allQuestions.explanation: Mummification is drying and shrivelling of tissues with no microbial growth. Saponification is adipocere, and liquefaction occurs in putrefaction.

allQuestions.text: The most common source of putrefactive organisms is the:
allQuestions.explanation: Most putrefactive bacteria come from the bowel, with Clostridium predominating. This is why discoloration starts in the right iliac fossa over the caecum.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following does NOT significantly affect putrefaction?
allQuestions.explanation: Sex is not a major factor (only slightly faster in females, who have more fat). Temperature, moisture, clothing, age and cause of death clearly alter the rate.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following does NOT retard putrefaction?
options: Poisoning with strychnine or heavy metals
originalOptions: Poisoning with strychnine or heavy metals
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Burial in a shallow grave
allQuestions.explanation: Surface burial decomposes the body more because surface soil has more bacteria and access. Water immersion, coffins, dry sandy soil and metal poisons all delay putrefaction.

allQuestions.text: Cadaveric spasm occurs in:
allQuestions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm affects voluntary (skeletal) muscles only, usually the hands and forearms, particularly those contracted at the moment of death.

allQuestions.text: Suspended animation is:
options: Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
Apparent death in which the patient cannot be aroused
A state that lasts for days or weeks
A state that can never be induced voluntarily
Irreversible loss of brainstem function with preserved circulation
originalOptions: Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
Apparent death in which the patient cannot be aroused
A state that lasts for days or weeks
A state that can never be induced voluntarily
Irreversible loss of brainstem function with preserved circulation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Apparent death in which the patient can be revived
allQuestions.explanation: In suspended animation vital signs are not detectable by routine methods, but the person can be resuscitated. It can even be voluntary, as in yoga practitioners.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)?
allQuestions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism causes true, rapid death. Hypothermia, hypnotic or opiate overdose, electrocution and drowning can suppress vital signs reversibly.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of apparent death (suspended animation)?
allQuestions.explanation: A second-degree burn does not suppress the vital signs. Newborns, heat stroke, hypothermia and cholera are recognised causes of apparent death.

allQuestions.text: All of the following may simulate death EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Cyanide causes rapid true death rather than a reversible suppression of vital signs. Drowning, hypnotic or opiate overdose and electrocution can all produce apparent death.

allQuestions.text: Maggots of a cadaver help in determining the:
allQuestions.explanation: Forensic entomology uses the stage of maggot development (larva, pupa, adult), corrected for temperature, to give a minimum post-mortem interval.

allQuestions.text: Maggots are most useful in forensic practice for:
options: Estimating the time of death in late stages
Estimating the time of death in early stages
originalOptions: Estimating the time of death in late stages
Estimating the time of death in early stages
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Estimating the time of death in late stages
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Estimating the time of death in late stages
allQuestions.explanation: Entomology is most valuable in late decomposition, when temperature, rigor and lividity no longer help. In the early hours those methods are better.

allQuestions.text: When a tattoo has been destroyed, its former presence can be inferred from pigment in the:
allQuestions.explanation: Macrophages carry tattoo pigment to the draining lymph nodes, so it persists there even if the skin is burnt or decomposed.

allQuestions.text: In suspected air embolism, the body cavity to be opened first is the:
allQuestions.explanation: The thorax is opened first so air is not introduced artefactually. The pericardial sac is filled with water and the right ventricle incised under water, where escaping bubbles confirm venous air embolism.

allQuestions.text: "Nutmeg liver" refers to:
