allQuestions.explanation: Nutmeg liver results from chronic venous congestion, usually right-sided heart failure. It shows dark congested centrilobular zones alternating with pale periportal zones.

allQuestions.text: Fatty change of the liver is usually and more commonly seen in:
allQuestions.explanation: Steatosis is commonest in metabolic disorders (obesity, diabetes) and alcohol. Heart failure produces nutmeg liver (chronic venous congestion) rather than fatty change.

allQuestions.text: Fatty change of the liver is seen in:
options: Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
originalOptions: Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Metabolic disease and poisoning by phosphorus or arsenic
allQuestions.explanation: Fatty change occurs with metabolic disorders, alcohol, and poisoning by phosphorus and arsenic. Heart failure causes congestion (nutmeg liver) instead.

allQuestions.text: A black triangular patch appears on the exposed sclera at each side of the iris in a body whose eyelids were left open for several hours. This finding is:
allQuestions.explanation: When the lids stay open for 3–4 hours, drying of the exposed sclera forms yellow triangles that turn brown and then black. This is tache noire, not a haemorrhage or lividity.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the main ethical priority of the physician when dealing with vulnerable children who are victims of violence?
options: Respect for the autonomy of the parents
originalOptions: Respect for the autonomy of the parents
allQuestions.explanation: In suspected child abuse, the physician's primary ethical duty is early detection and protection of the child. This outranks confidentiality and parental autonomy.

allQuestions.text: In which of the following situations is breach of confidentiality permissible?
options: Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
Request by the patient's husband or wife
Request by an insurance company representative
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
originalOptions: Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
Request by the patient's husband or wife
Request by an insurance company representative
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Reporting a notifiable infectious disease (e.g., cholera) to the health authorities
allQuestions.explanation: Notifiable diseases must be reported to the Ministry of Health by law. Requests from a spouse, insurer, employer, or relative do not justify a breach without the patient's consent.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are principles of bioethics EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: The four principles of bioethics are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. "Reluctance" is not a bioethical principle.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT correct concerning valid consent prior to medical treatment?
options: It must be voluntary and freely given
Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
The patient must be informed of what the treatment involves
The patient must be informed of the benefits and risks
The capacity of the patient must be assessed
originalOptions: It must be voluntary and freely given
Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
The patient must be informed of what the treatment involves
The patient must be informed of the benefits and risks
The capacity of the patient must be assessed
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Consent of the husband or wife is always mandatory
allQuestions.explanation: Valid consent requires voluntariness, adequate information, and capacity. A competent adult consents for himself or herself, and requiring spousal consent would violate patient autonomy.

allQuestions.text: A 23-year-old single adult female presents with vaginal bleeding. Which of the following statements regarding consent is correct?
options: Consent must be obtained from her father or husband
Consent of her partner is always mandatory
A court order is required before treatment
She can give her own medical consent independently
originalOptions: Consent must be obtained from her father or husband
Consent of her partner is always mandatory
A court order is required before treatment
She can give her own medical consent independently
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) She can give her own medical consent independently
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: She can give her own medical consent independently
allQuestions.explanation: Any competent adult (18 years or older) has full capacity to consent to treatment without parental, spousal, or guardian authorization.

allQuestions.text: What is the most important rule when performing a physical examination of the intimate parts of the body?
options: The examination must be performed only after police notification
The examination must be performed by a physician of the same gender only
The examination must be photographed before it begins
The examination must be performed in the presence of a guardian
originalOptions: The examination must be performed only after police notification
The examination must be performed by a physician of the same gender only
The examination must be photographed before it begins
The examination must be performed in the presence of a guardian
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) A chaperone must be present
allQuestions.explanation: A chaperone protects the dignity of the patient and the professional integrity of the physician during examination of intimate parts.

allQuestions.text: "Respect for persons" in the ethical approach includes all of the following EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Respect for persons comprises autonomy, integrity, equity, and equality. Following the doctor's orders contradicts patient-centred ethics.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT true concerning the duties of doctors to patients?
options: Respect the patient's right to confidentiality
Always bear in mind the obligation to respect human life
Refer the patient to another physician whenever the examination is beyond the physician's capacity
Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
Act in the patient's best interest when providing medical care
originalOptions: Respect the patient's right to confidentiality
Always bear in mind the obligation to respect human life
Refer the patient to another physician whenever the examination is beyond the physician's capacity
Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
Act in the patient's best interest when providing medical care
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
allQuestions.explanation: Informed consent is required for victims of violence as for any other patient. Only a true emergency in which delay would cause harm waives it.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT appropriate considering ethical standards?
options: Maintain professional competence throughout one's career
originalOptions: Maintain professional competence throughout one's career
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Enhance intimate relationships with patients
allQuestions.explanation: An intimate relationship between a physician and a patient is unethical because it violates professional boundaries.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a declaration of the World Medical Association related to the humanization of medical practice?
allQuestions.explanation: The WMA declarations include Geneva, Helsinki, Oslo, Tokyo, and Sydney. There is no "Declaration of London" in medical ethics.

allQuestions.text: The humanization of medical practice was the main theme of which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: The Declaration of Geneva (1948) is the physician's oath and defines the physician's duties. The Nuremberg Code (1947) concerns consent in research, Oslo concerns therapeutic abortion, and Tokyo concerns torture.

allQuestions.text: The Declaration of Helsinki is related to:
allQuestions.explanation: The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) sets the ethical standards for medical research on human subjects. Torture is addressed by Tokyo and therapeutic abortion by Oslo.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are types of consent EXCEPT:
options: Informed consent for accepting medical treatment
Written consent by a rape victim
Request for euthanasia by the patient
Participation in a research trial authorized by an Institutional Review Board
originalOptions: Informed consent for accepting medical treatment
Written consent by a rape victim
Request for euthanasia by the patient
Participation in a research trial authorized by an Institutional Review Board
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Request for euthanasia by the patient
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Request for euthanasia by the patient
allQuestions.explanation: Euthanasia is illegal in Jordan and is not a type of consent. The other options are recognized forms: implied, informed, written (expressed), and research consent approved by an IRB.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT related to the World Medical Association declarations concerning the humanization of health services?
options: United Nations Development Fund for Women
originalOptions: United Nations Development Fund for Women
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) United Nations Development Fund for Women
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: United Nations Development Fund for Women
allQuestions.explanation: Helsinki, Geneva, Tokyo, and Oslo are all World Medical Association declarations. The United Nations Development Fund for Women is a United Nations agency and not a medical declaration.

allQuestions.text: Breach of patient confidentiality is permissible in which of the following cases?
options: Request by the patient's husband or wife
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
Upon the request or consent of the patient
originalOptions: Request by the patient's husband or wife
Reporting rheumatoid arthritis to the patient's employer
Request by a relative of the patient
Upon the request or consent of the patient
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Upon the request or consent of the patient
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Upon the request or consent of the patient
allQuestions.explanation: Confidentiality may be breached with the patient's own consent, for notifiable diseases, by court order, for child protection, or when there is a serious risk to others. Requests from a spouse, insurer, employer, or relative do not justify a breach.

allQuestions.text: What type of toxicology concerns itself with medical and legal aspects, focused on detecting poisons in medicolegal investigations?
allQuestions.explanation: Forensic toxicology represents the intersection of toxicology with the law, applying poison detection specifically to medicolegal investigations, distinguishing it from clinical (patient management), environmental, and purely analytical toxicology.

allQuestions.text: What color is associated with methemoglobin?
allQuestions.explanation: Methemoglobin (Fe³⁺ state) produces a characteristic chocolate-brown discoloration of blood and livor, and causes cyanosis that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen — distinguishing it from cherry-red (carbon monoxide) or cyanotic bluish-purple (hypoxia) presentations.

allQuestions.text: Activated charcoal is useless in all of the following EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Activated charcoal effectively adsorbs salicylates (along with paracetamol and tricyclics), but it is ineffective for iron, lithium, cyanide, corrosives, alcohols, and heavy metals.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following substances is best absorbed (adsorbed) by activated charcoal?
allQuestions.explanation: Salicylate is well adsorbed by activated charcoal, whereas iron, lithium, and cyanide are not effectively bound by it.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about activated charcoal is TRUE?
options: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
It works by absorption into the toxin
It is contraindicated in all cases of poisoning
originalOptions: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
It works by absorption into the toxin
It is contraindicated in all cases of poisoning
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
allQuestions.explanation: Activated charcoal works via adsorption — binding the toxin to its surface in the gut — thereby preventing systemic absorption, rather than being absorbed itself or inducing emesis.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about activated charcoal is FALSE?
options: It should be given as soon as possible after ingestion
It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
It works by adsorbing toxins in the gut
It is ineffective for metals and alcohols
originalOptions: It should be given as soon as possible after ingestion
It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
It works by adsorbing toxins in the gut
It is ineffective for metals and alcohols
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
allQuestions.explanation: Activated charcoal and syrup of ipecac should never be combined, since ipecac-induced vomiting would expel the charcoal from the stomach before it can adsorb the toxin.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are true about activated charcoal EXCEPT:
options: Give with a sufficient amount of water
It is a finely arranged black powder
Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
originalOptions: Give with a sufficient amount of water
It is a finely arranged black powder
Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
allQuestions.explanation: Ipecac is not routinely recommended and should never be combined with activated charcoal, as it would counteract the charcoal's effect by inducing vomiting rather than improving efficacy.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives at the ER 2 hours after an overdose. What is the correct management?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Activated charcoal if no contraindications
allQuestions.explanation: Within 2 hours of ingestion, activated charcoal is first-line if the airway is intact and there are no contraindications; syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended, and gastric lavage is rarely used (limited to within about 1 hour with a protected airway).

allQuestions.text: Why are alkaline (base) burns generally MORE dangerous than acidic burns?
options: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
They cause coagulative necrosis, which limits penetration
Acids are neutralized immediately upon contact
Bases do not penetrate mucous membranes
originalOptions: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
They cause coagulative necrosis, which limits penetration
Acids are neutralized immediately upon contact
Bases do not penetrate mucous membranes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
allQuestions.explanation: Alkalis dissolve proteins and saponify fat, producing liquefactive necrosis without a limiting eschar, allowing progressively deeper tissue injury; acids instead cause coagulative necrosis, which forms a protective eschar that limits further penetration.

allQuestions.text: Which specific enzyme is reactivated after organophosphate poisoning (before aging)?
allQuestions.explanation: OP poisons phosphorylate AChE; before "aging" occurs (~48h), pralidoxime can remove the phosphoryl group and restore enzyme activity.

allQuestions.text: The drug that reactivates phosphorylated AChE in organophosphate poisoning (before aging):
allQuestions.explanation: Pralidoxime is an oxime AChE reactivator effective only before aging; atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does not reactivate the enzyme.

allQuestions.text: Enzyme reactivated by pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning:
allQuestions.explanation: Pralidoxime specifically reactivates AChE (not pseudocholinesterase/BuChE), and only before the phosphorylated enzyme ages.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about carbamate and organophosphate poisoning is FALSE?
options: Both cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms
Atropine is used for symptomatic treatment
Both can lead to respiratory failure
originalOptions: Both cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms
Atropine is used for symptomatic treatment
Both can lead to respiratory failure
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Both are treated with pralidoxime
allQuestions.explanation: Pralidoxime is not indicated for carbamate poisoning because carbamate-enzyme inhibition does not undergo aging (it's spontaneously reversible), unlike OP poisoning.

allQuestions.text: Management of carbamate toxicity – all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
originalOptions: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
allQuestions.explanation: Treatment (ABC + atropine) must never be delayed for lab confirmation in cholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning, as this is a time-critical emergency.

allQuestions.text: Not a muscarinic sign of organophosphate poisoning:
allQuestions.explanation: Muscarinic (SLUDGE) effects cause urinary incontinence/frequency; urinary retention instead reflects a nicotinic/sympathetic effect.

allQuestions.text: What is the role of atropine in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning?
allQuestions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist that dries secretions and reverses muscarinic toxicity; it has no effect on nicotinic weakness, which requires pralidoxime.

allQuestions.text: Management and treatment of organophosphate poisoning – which is TRUE:
options: Atropine is antidote for nicotinic receptor
originalOptions: Atropine is antidote for nicotinic receptor
allQuestions.explanation: Initial priority is airway management including suctioning of bronchial secretions, followed by atropine for muscarinic symptoms and then pralidoxime.

allQuestions.text: Low dose of organophosphates is NOT associated with:
allQuestions.explanation: Low-dose OP exposure produces muscarinic effects (bronchorrhea, miosis, salivation); paralysis is a nicotinic effect seen at high dose.

allQuestions.text: Organophosphate-induced neuropsychiatric disorder (OPIDP) happens:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) After 1-5 weeks of OP poisoning
allQuestions.explanation: OPIDP is a delayed peripheral polyneuropathy appearing 1–5 weeks post-exposure, distinct from the immediate cholinergic crisis and the 24–96h intermediate syndrome.

allQuestions.text: Antidote of organophosphate poisoning:
allQuestions.explanation: Dual therapy is required — atropine blocks muscarinic toxicity while pralidoxime reactivates AChE, addressing nicotinic and central effects.

allQuestions.text: What is the best blood sample site for forensic toxicology analysis?
allQuestions.explanation: Femoral vein blood is preferred postmortem because it is peripheral and less affected by postmortem redistribution (PMR), unlike central sites (subclavian, jugular) that are subject to drug diffusion from nearby organs.

allQuestions.text: Which sample site is best for QUANTITATIVE toxicology analysis?
allQuestions.explanation: Femoral blood undergoes minimal postmortem redistribution, making it the preferred site for accurate quantitative drug measurement, whereas central blood (heart, subclavian) is prone to redistribution artifact.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of vitreous humor as a toxicology sample?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) More susceptible to postmortem change
allQuestions.explanation: Vitreous humor is actually resistant to postmortem change because it is isolated behind the blood-ocular barrier, protecting it from putrefaction and postmortem redistribution — making the "more susceptible" statement false.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding vitreous humor in forensic toxicology?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Done as a routine procedure
allQuestions.explanation: Vitreous humor is collected only in specific circumstances (decomposed bodies, suspected drug/alcohol use, or when other samples are unavailable), not as a routine procedure.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following CANNOT be determined by analyzing vitreous fluid?
allQuestions.explanation: Vitreous fluid can detect alcohol, glucose, electrolytes, potassium (useful for postmortem interval), and urea/creatinine (renal function), but heavy metals preferentially accumulate in hair, nails, and bone rather than vitreous humor.

allQuestions.text: Which sample is most resistant to postmortem putrefaction, making it valuable in decomposed bodies?
allQuestions.explanation: Vitreous humor's anatomical isolation behind the blood-ocular barrier makes it the most resistant forensic sample to putrefactive change among the options listed.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about vitreous fluid is WRONG?
allQuestions.explanation: Vitreous humor is resistant to (not affected by) putrefaction due to its isolated anatomical location, making this statement false while the others are accurate.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding liver samples in forensic toxicology?
allQuestions.explanation: The liver actually putrefies relatively quickly and is not protected from decomposition, though it remains valuable for assessing lipophilic drug concentrations and tissue distribution.

allQuestions.text: For qualitative assessment (screening) of forensic samples, which is the preferred sample?
allQuestions.explanation: Urine is preferred for qualitative drug screening via immunoassay, while femoral blood is used for quantitation, vitreous humor for decomposed cases, and hair for chronic exposure history.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about urine samples in forensic toxicology is NOT correct?
options: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
Urine can detect drugs and metabolites
Urine is used for qualitative drug screening
Urine is useful for detecting drug exposure
originalOptions: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
Urine can detect drugs and metabolites
Urine is used for qualitative drug screening
Urine is useful for detecting drug exposure
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
allQuestions.explanation: Urine is mainly used for qualitative detection of drug exposure, not quantitative measurement, which requires blood analysis.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT TRUE concerning sodium fluoride as a preservative in forensic blood samples?
options: Inhibits glycolysis, preventing postmortem glucose changes
Used as a preservative in blood samples for alcohol analysis
Prevents postmortem production of alcohol by microorganisms
originalOptions: Inhibits glycolysis, preventing postmortem glucose changes
Used as a preservative in blood samples for alcohol analysis
Prevents postmortem production of alcohol by microorganisms
allQuestions.explanation: Sodium fluoride inhibits bacterial growth and glycolysis, thereby preventing fermentation (and postmortem alcohol production by microorganisms) rather than enhancing it, which is why it is used to preserve blood samples for alcohol analysis.

allQuestions.text: Reporting and documentation of injuries include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Injury location (anatomical measurement from a fixed landmark)
Type of injury (e.g., bruise, laceration, abrasion)
Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
originalOptions: Injury location (anatomical measurement from a fixed landmark)
Type of injury (e.g., bruise, laceration, abrasion)
Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Description of the assailant (left- or right-handed)
allQuestions.explanation: The medico-legal report documents the victim's injuries objectively (site, type, size, age, tenderness). Assailant handedness is an investigative inference, not a clinical finding.

allQuestions.text: According to Jordanian law, a physician is obliged to report which of the following to the Ministry of Health?
allQuestions.explanation: The Public Health Law obliges the physician to notify the Ministry of Health of notifiable infectious diseases (e.g., cholera). It does not extend to all trauma cases or all deaths, nor is it limited to sexually transmitted diseases.

allQuestions.text: Who is responsible for issuing the primary medico-legal report?
options: The senior physician or head of department
The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
originalOptions: The senior physician or head of department
The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The first physician who examines or manages the patient, regardless of specialty
allQuestions.explanation: The primary report is written by the first doctor who sees the patient, usually in the emergency department, whatever his specialty. The forensic physician completes the final report later.

allQuestions.text: The components of a medico-legal report are:
options: Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
originalOptions: Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Heading (preamble), body (history and findings), and conclusion (opinion)
allQuestions.explanation: A complete report has three parts: the heading identifying the case and the requesting authority, the body containing the history and examination findings, and the conclusion giving the medical opinion.

allQuestions.text: A surgeon operated while under the influence of alcohol, and the patient died. The surgeon is guilty of:
allQuestions.explanation: Gross negligence or recklessness (operating while intoxicated) that causes death constitutes criminal negligence. Civil negligence results in compensation only, and therapeutic misadventure is an accident despite proper care.

allQuestions.text: In Jordan, a physician is legally governed by:
options: The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
originalOptions: The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Jordanian Penal Code
allQuestions.explanation: The physician's practice is regulated by all three Jordanian laws together; international codes are not by themselves legally binding.

allQuestions.text: A 60-year-old man underwent arthroscopy with meniscectomy and died of pulmonary embolism. Which aspect of his post-operative care was negligent?
options: He was not informed how serious a headache would be
He was not informed which analgesics to use
He was not told to stay within 2 miles of the hospital
He was not informed of the duration of work disablement
He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
originalOptions: He was not informed how serious a headache would be
He was not informed which analgesics to use
He was not told to stay within 2 miles of the hospital
He was not informed of the duration of work disablement
He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: He was not informed how serious shortness of breath would be
allQuestions.explanation: After lower-limb surgery, shortness of breath is the warning sign of pulmonary embolism, and the patient must be told it requires urgent medical attention. The other omissions are not related to the cause of death.

allQuestions.text: In a suicidal attempt, which finding is most characteristic?
options: Multiple deep wounds scattered over the body
Chop wounds from a heavy weapon
originalOptions: Multiple deep wounds scattered over the body
Chop wounds from a heavy weapon
allQuestions.explanation: Hesitation marks are multiple superficial, parallel, non-lethal cuts made before the fatal cut. Defence wounds, by contrast, are found on the victim of an attack, on the dorsum of the hand and the forearm.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is characteristic of a suicidal cut throat in a right-handed person?
options: Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
Multiple deep, scattered wounds with defence injuries on the hands
A deep horizontal wound with no hesitation cuts
Incised wounds on the back of the neck
A wound starting on the right side of the neck and deepest at its end
originalOptions: Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
Multiple deep, scattered wounds with defence injuries on the hands
A deep horizontal wound with no hesitation cuts
Incised wounds on the back of the neck
A wound starting on the right side of the neck and deepest at its end
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hesitation cuts, with the wound starting high on the left side and running obliquely downward, deepest at its start
allQuestions.explanation: A suicidal cut throat is accessible, is grouped on the side opposite the dominant hand, and is accompanied by hesitation cuts. A homicidal cut is deep, often horizontal, without hesitation cuts, and may show defence wounds.

allQuestions.text: The green colour of a bruise is due to:
allQuestions.explanation: Green appears at about 3–5 days and is due to biliverdin. Brown (1–3 days) is haemosiderin, and yellow (5–7 days) is bilirubin.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about abrasions is FALSE?
options: They are superficial wounds involving the epidermis
Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
They may indicate the direction of the applied force
They may reproduce the pattern of the causative object
originalOptions: They are superficial wounds involving the epidermis
Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
They may indicate the direction of the applied force
They may reproduce the pattern of the causative object
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Their healing is characterized by granulation tissue formation rather than re-epithelialisation
allQuestions.explanation: Abrasions involve the epidermis only, so they heal by re-epithelialisation from the edges and hair follicles under a scab, leaving no scar.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about abrasions?
options: They always heal with a scar
They are produced only by sharp instruments
They involve the full thickness of the skin
Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
originalOptions: They always heal with a scar
They are produced only by sharp instruments
They involve the full thickness of the skin
Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Even if they bleed slightly, they heal without scarring
allQuestions.explanation: Abrasions are epidermal injuries, and even when they bleed a little from the papillary dermis they re-epithelialise without a scar. They are caused by blunt force, not sharp instruments.

allQuestions.text: Which type of injury gives the best indication of the object or weapon used?
allQuestions.explanation: A patterned abrasion reproduces the surface texture of the causative object (tyre tread, grille, buckle, teeth). A brush abrasion shows only the direction of sliding, and a laceration does not reflect the weapon's dimensions.

allQuestions.text: What is the importance of Langer's lines (skin cleavage lines) in wound assessment?
options: Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
Determining the age of the wound
originalOptions: Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
Determining the age of the wound
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Determining the degree of gaping of the wound
allQuestions.explanation: Langer's lines follow the direction of dermal collagen and elastic fibres. A wound across the lines gapes widely, whereas a wound parallel to them gapes little and heals with a finer scar.

allQuestions.text: Crescent-shaped (semilunar) abrasions are caused by:
options: A fall on a rough surface
originalOptions: A fall on a rough surface
allQuestions.explanation: A fingernail pressed into the skin leaves a small crescentic abrasion, or a linear scratch if dragged. Teeth leave two opposing curved arcs (a bite mark).

allQuestions.text: The abrasion produced by a tangential force that scrapes off the superficial layer of the skin is called:
allQuestions.explanation: A graze is produced by tangential sliding force (e.g. road rash). Pressure and impact abrasions result from force perpendicular to the skin.

allQuestions.text: A graze abrasion is the same as:
allQuestions.explanation: "Graze" and "brush" are synonyms for a sliding, scraping abrasion. Crush, pressure and impact abrasions are caused by perpendicular force.

allQuestions.text: A patterned (prominence) abrasion is seen most clearly when it occurs over the:
allQuestions.explanation: The pattern prints best where skin lies tight over bone, as on the scalp. Padded areas such as the abdomen and buttock cushion the blow and blur the pattern.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT necessary for the formation of a patterned abrasion?
options: An object with a textured surface
originalOptions: An object with a textured surface
allQuestions.explanation: Skin over a hard bony base is needed to reproduce the pattern. Subcutaneous fat absorbs the blow and blurs the pattern.

allQuestions.text: Incised-like (split) lacerations can be seen in all of the following sites EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Split lacerations occur where the skin lies directly on bone and is crushed against it. They do not occur over padded areas such as the chest wall.

allQuestions.text: Blunt trauma can simulate an incised wound most characteristically over which part of the body?
allQuestions.explanation: The thin scalp skin is tightly stretched over the skull, so a blunt blow splits it in a clean line that looks incised. Marginal bruising, tissue bridging or crushed hair bulbs still indicate a laceration.

allQuestions.text: One of the following statements concerning bruises is NOT true:
options: The source of bleeding is usually small-calibre vessels such as veins, venules and arterioles
Bruises are caused by leakage of blood from damaged vessels into the surrounding tissues
The size and appearance of a bruise are related to the site of the injured part
Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
originalOptions: The source of bleeding is usually small-calibre vessels such as veins, venules and arterioles
Bruises are caused by leakage of blood from damaged vessels into the surrounding tissues
The size and appearance of a bruise are related to the site of the injured part
Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Bruises occur only in the skin and never in deeper tissues such as muscle and internal organs
allQuestions.explanation: A contusion can occur anywhere in the body, for example in muscle, spleen or liver. "Bruise" usually implies a lesion visible through the skin.

allQuestions.text: Intradermal bruising is characterized by:
options: Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
Gravitational pooling of blood in dependent areas
Migration of the blood away from the site of impact
originalOptions: Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
Gravitational pooling of blood in dependent areas
Migration of the blood away from the site of impact
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Reproduction of the pattern of the causative object, e.g. a shoe sole
allQuestions.explanation: Blood confined to the dermis cannot spread, so it keeps the pattern of the object. Hypostasis is a post-mortem phenomenon, and a deep bruise may migrate along tissue planes.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is TRUE concerning lacerations?
options: They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
They are always the result of intentional violence
They result from a sharp object applied to the skin
The more resilient tissues are always divided together with the weaker tissues
originalOptions: They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
They are always the result of intentional violence
They result from a sharp object applied to the skin
The more resilient tissues are always divided together with the weaker tissues
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
allQuestions.explanation: Lacerations are caused by blunt force, are not always intentional (e.g. falls), and scalp lacerations can bleed profusely. Tougher tissues such as nerves and vessels survive as bridges.

allQuestions.text: One of the following statements regarding a lacerated wound is NOT true:
options: It is caused by blunt force
The margins show abrasion or contusion
Tissue bridging may be seen in the depth
It commonly occurs over bony prominences
originalOptions: It is caused by blunt force
The margins show abrasion or contusion
Tissue bridging may be seen in the depth
It commonly occurs over bony prominences
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Its edges are always irregular
allQuestions.explanation: Over a bony prominence (scalp, brow, shin) a laceration may have a deceptively regular, incised-looking edge. It is identified as a laceration by marginal bruising or abrasion and by tissue bridging.

allQuestions.text: Blunt weapons can usually cause all of the following EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Clean-cut edges are the hallmark of a sharp instrument. Blunt force produces abrasions, contusions, lacerations with ragged edges, erythema and oedema.

allQuestions.text: One of the following is NOT a characteristic of self-inflicted injuries:
options: Grouping on the side opposite the dominant hand
Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
originalOptions: Grouping on the side opposite the dominant hand
Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Usually multiple, deep and scattered wounds
allQuestions.explanation: Self-inflicted wounds are typically superficial, tentative, grouped and within reach of the person. Multiple deep, scattered wounds point away from self-infliction.

allQuestions.text: Fabricated wounds are mostly:
allQuestions.explanation: Self-made wounds produced for secondary gain are usually shallow cuts made with a sharp object on visible, reachable areas, sparing sensitive parts such as the eyes and lips.

allQuestions.text: What is the most frequent type of wound among defence wounds in a knife attack?
allQuestions.explanation: A victim who grasps at or deflects a blade sustains defence incisions, classically on the palm, dorsum of the hand and ulnar aspect of the forearm.

allQuestions.text: Defence wounds are most likely to be found on the:
options: Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
originalOptions: Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Dorsum of the hands and ulnar aspect of the forearms
allQuestions.explanation: These are the sites exposed when the victim raises the arms to ward off a blade. The palm is also involved when the blade is grasped. Defence wounds are a homicide indicator.

allQuestions.text: Regarding hesitation wounds, which of the following is NOT correct?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) They are surrounded by bruises
allQuestions.explanation: Hesitation wounds are superficial, parallel, regular-edged incisions. Surrounding bruising implies blunt force, not a sharp-edge cut.

allQuestions.text: Yellow discoloration of a bruise is expected at approximately:
allQuestions.explanation: Yellow is due to bilirubin at about 5–7 days. Green (biliverdin) precedes it at 3–5 days, and the bruise then fades through straw to normal colour.

allQuestions.text: What is the usual cause of death in extradural haemorrhage?
allQuestions.explanation: The expanding arterial clot raises intracranial pressure, causing tentorial herniation and brainstem (medullary) compression, which ends in respiratory failure. The haemorrhage is usually from the middle meningeal artery after a temporal bone fracture.

allQuestions.text: What is the main characteristic of the wound shown in the image? [img: forensic1stabwound.jpg ]
options: Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
originalOptions: Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Clean, sharp, regular edges without surrounding bruising
allQuestions.explanation: A typical stab wound has clean-cut regular edges with no marginal bruising or abrasion, and its depth exceeds its length. Irregular edges, tissue bridging and marginal bruising indicate a laceration, and a wound longer than it is deep is characteristic of an incised wound.

allQuestions.text: Concerning stab wounds, one of the following statements is NOT correct:
options: A slit-like wound usually distorts after removal of the weapon
An irregularly shaped skin wound may result if the knife is twisted
Movement of the knife may enlarge the wound
The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
One end of the wound is sharp if the weapon is single-edged
originalOptions: A slit-like wound usually distorts after removal of the weapon
An irregularly shaped skin wound may result if the knife is twisted
Movement of the knife may enlarge the wound
The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
One end of the wound is sharp if the weapon is single-edged
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The resulting skin defect is usually exactly the size of the knife
allQuestions.explanation: Skin elasticity, Langer's lines, and rocking or twisting of the blade alter the wound, so it is rarely the exact size of the blade.

allQuestions.text: A fully conscious man sustained a head injury during a fight. Examination shows a boggy swelling of 6 × 4 cm over the right parietal area, and an X-ray shows a fracture of the parietal bone without displacement. The nature of the injury is:
allQuestions.explanation: A linear crack without displacement is a fissure (linear) fracture, the commonest type. A depressed fracture has the fragment driven inward, a comminuted fracture has several fragments, and a complicated fracture involves injury to the underlying dura, brain or vessels.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are types of skull fracture EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Skull fractures are classified as linear, depressed, comminuted, compound and complicated. A spiral pattern is a long-bone fracture.

allQuestions.text: A burn that destroys the full thickness of the skin, appears white or charred and leathery, and is painless because of destruction of the nerve endings is classified as:
allQuestions.explanation: A third-degree burn is full-thickness skin destruction and is painless. A first-degree burn involves only the epidermis, a second-degree burn extends into the dermis with blisters and severe pain, and a fourth-degree burn extends beyond the skin into fat, muscle or bone.

allQuestions.text: During surgery on a patient with a gunshot wound, what is the correct approach regarding the bullet?
options: Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
Remove it and discard it immediately to prevent further injury
Regard it as the property of the surgeon
Hand it to the patient's family
Keep it in the hospital pathology archive without notifying the police
originalOptions: Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
Remove it and discard it immediately to prevent further injury
Regard it as the property of the surgeon
Hand it to the patient's family
Keep it in the hospital pathology archive without notifying the police
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Treat the patient first, preserve or handle the bullet carefully, document its position, never discard it, and hand it to the police under a signed chain of custody
allQuestions.explanation: The bullet is forensic evidence belonging to the police investigation. Handle it with gloved fingers or rubber-shod forceps, because metal instruments scratch the rifling marks, and place it in a labelled, sealed container.
